ALL ARE INVITED TO WALK THROUGH. RESULT OF UNHAPPY MARRIAGE, DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS, Jtc.. perhaps the most favourable opportunity ever offered to those about furnishing In good style is the present. The furnishing in question has been removed from a very large house in the vicinity of Ply- mouth Grove, and everything was made to order only 14 months ago by one of the best houses in the city. The prices quoted are exactly one-half the cost. Nothing like a full des- cription can be given. Inspection is invited. Firstly. the hall is furnished with a grand dark mahogary Louis Stand and pair chairs to match; price 9 guineas. The dining-room is in solid black walnut of magnificent and uncommon design. To attempt anything like a description would be a waste of time • to say the least, it is the most charming and unique, the diningaabie extending with extra leaves, sup- ported by square legs which are beautifully carved; the over- mantel is such that, can only be made by workmen of the highest standard ;itis a work of art. Next comes the truly magnificent Suite, which, of course, are also in solid black walnut, and consists of 12 standard Chairs (the price quoted Is for six chairs, more can be had if required). with double- padded tacks, two extra large lounge chairs, and a grand couch, of large size, sideboard alone is worth £5O Os 9d, the whol forming a noble lot for high-class dining-room. Price 68 guineas- -1 have also the carpets, paintings, and engravings from the same room. The drawing room is furnished in the latest style. and surpasses everything for elegance I hare ever seen. Firstly, the Curio display cabinet at once strikes you as being a marvel of beauty and werkmanshlp It possesses all the requirements o• such an artistic article Next comes the handsome music cabinet with face fron and various divisions, lined with plush ; two curious shape tables, with fancy cut and carved legs ; the overmanted with diamond-shaped glasses, and recesses for the display ornick-nacks ; lastly, but by no means the least, the truly magnificent suite of double gondola settee, for any part of the room; two charming easy chairs, four occasional chairs, and two gossipy chairs. All are upholster ,d in a rich silk tapestry, with raised flowers and sprays. and finished with silk cord and gimp. It may ba remarked that these fittings are suitable for only a high-class drawing-room. There are in all nine bedrooms, space prevents all being described. The best room ot all, I may here state, is suitable for a lady of title or a lord. it cost £l2, and is offered for 60gs. The suite is simply magnificent, the wood is perfeztty solid bright- polished walnut of the choicest quality, the wardrobe is 'lft wide, fitted at either end with hanging compartments which are enclosed with brilliant bevellad Vaxhan plate glass of shield shape, between the doors are drawers, and above are bay-shaped cupboards, with massive carved panel which at once isplays great dexterity with the chisel the whole is crowned with a corn,ce of tower like shape,the dressing table is 4ft 61n. wide. pedestal design, and t.ay-shaped between , the pedestals, which are fitted with drawers, the glass, which supported by carved brackets, is shield shape and extra large. Next comes the 41t 6ln bay-shaped washstand, wit!: marble slab, tile, and glsss back, about 4ft high, the pede,tal towel rail and upholstered chairs forms one of the finest suites money can buy. There are eight other bedrooms Which contain suites at all prices, some as low as 4 guineas and some at 14, 18, and 25 guineas. The suite from the breakfast room is in saddle begs, price 8 guineas ; dining table, 355; sideboard, £7 15a; two recesses bookcases. 75s each. Another carved oak bookcase and a host of other a•ticles are on view. Carpets, rugs, fenders. orna ments. paintings, china, stet glass, all removed to 44, Old- ham-street, Manchester. DON'T FORGET.

AN ATTEMPT.—Mrs. Brown: "How would you define ' tact '?" Mrs. Jones: "1 should say tact is the ability to make your husband believe that he is having his own way." A CLEAR CASE. —Buzzfuzz : "That saying, Marry in haste, repent at leisure,' is all wrong." Sizzletop : "Think so?" Buzzfiizz : "Certainly. After a man marries he has no leisure."

They belong to me son-in-laws." KNOWlNG.—Alberta: "He must be in earnest, and those places where his letter sticks together must be tears." Alethea ? "They're not tears, but they prove positively that he loves me—they are where he dipped his pen in the mucilage." "MR. BILLISS is such a nice young man," said the elderly aunt. "That's all you know about it, said the young niece; he is nothing of the sort. He is just the jolliest company imagin- able."

THE EFFECT OF A SCATHING DENUNCIATION.—Jen- kins: "Didn't that lawyer on the other side, give you.a terrible overhauling?" Thompson: " Didn't he, though? You can bet if I have any more law business I'm going to have him !" VARIETY IS CHARMlNG.—Doilleigh : "I tell you, old man, it is pretty hard work to lay up any money in these times. I have all I want to do to make both ends meet." Bodleigh "In view of the present price of beef, 1 should think you might find it easier to make one end vegetable." A BETTER ARRANGEMENT. —Huggins : " Bissam, had your hair cut?' Kissam : "Yes, dear boy. I found a place where they cut your hair while you wait." Huggins: "That's good, A barber's shop is usually a place where they cut some other man's hair while you wait." VALUABLE WORK.—" Dou you know," she said, "that your volume of poems has become quite indispensable in our house ? " " Indeed ? " he responded with a pleased look. "Yes. Mamma says she wouldn't be without them. She threatens to read them whenever the children are naughty." CHAPPIE : "I know how you must feel, for I've felt the sa me way myself." She (who has lost her mother) : "Have you lost your mother, too ?" Chappie : " No-o ; b.. the doctors made me give up cigarettes ! " HE OBJECTED.—" Mr. Gilley, I'm very sorry, but I can't marry you," replied the maiden sorrow- fully; "but I'll be a sister to you." "No, you won't !" replied Mr. Gilley. "I've got more sisters now than I need. Between the four of them I can't find a necktie when I happen to want one."

A TERRIBLE DISAPPOINTMENT.—Mother: "Why, my dear, what's the matter ? .Something has hap- pened at Mrs. de Music's party, I know. Tell me all about it, my child." Daughter: " 800-hoo ! Mrs. de Music asked me to play, and—and when I told her I was out of practice, she said she was so sorry,' and didn't ask me again, boo-hoo-hoo ABOUT MULES. —lf you're in the right and a man says you're as stubborn as a mule, you may safely take it he merely means to imply that your determination is equal to his own. If you're in the wrong and a man says you're as stubborn as a mule—well, in that case, perhaps the best thing you can do is to think as highly as possible of mules.

As ADVERTISED.—CUStOrner : "What did you mean by selling me that stuff you called hair. restorer, and telling me it would restore my head to its original condition ?" Druggist: "Didn't you like it?" Customer: "No, I didn't. If I had kept on much longer, I would have been entirely bald. Original condition, indeed." Druggist: "Most people are born bald, sir. That is the original condition." "DEAR one," he whispered, "do you think if I married you your father would ever forgive us?" "I am sure he would dear," she asserted softly. "And would he give us a house of our own?" "I know he would, dearest." "And would he give us enough to live beautifully on?" "I am positive of it, Harry." "And would he take me into the firm?" "Certainly he would." "And let me run the business to suit myself ? " "Of course he would, darling." "I cannot marry you," he said hoarsely. "Your father is too willing to get you off his hands." Too MECH.—His Honour Judge is a man of grim humour. One tune while he was holding the assizes at a West of England town, a member of the bar in the luncheon hour was seeking to convey the impression to a group, of whom Judge was the centre, that his income from his profession was very large. "I have to earn a good deal," the lawyer said; "it seems a large story to,itell, but my personal expenses are over a thousand a year. It costs me that to live." "That is too much, Brother S—," said the j udge ; "I wouldn't pay it—it isn't worth it !" No MISTAKES.—When Dr. T. De Witt Talmage was in Atlanta recently he told the following anecdote of Henry W. Gra ly, the famous Atlanta editor :—" Grady said to me one day, while speak- ing of journalism, that he made it a rule never to correct mistakes, and to run the Comtitution on the policy that no mistakes were made. At least, he would never acknoNc leit,e one. One day Grady said an obituary appeared i,l his columns of a man tolerably well knowh. The dead man appeared the next day and demanded a correction, saying he was not dead, and that the obituary was all a mistake. Grady sail he never made mistakes and never corrected errors. The dead man that was insisted in saying he was alive and wanted it understood. Grady then told him that the only thing he could possibly do would be to place him in the birth column as a new arrival."

AN ACCOMPLISHED YoUTIL—A good story is told of a young man who besides being of the spendthrift order, is a splendid mimic, and can imitate his father's voice to a nicety. Not long ago the young man wanted, without delay, some money to pay a bill, au; !ie knew his father would treat a request for the ~,arne with cold contempt. Wating till he knew that his father would he away, he went to a telephone call-room and rang up the office, calling for the cashier. The cashier was forthcoming, and when he was at the other end the young man imitated his sire's voice. "I say, Blank, if that scapegrace of a son of mine comes round arid asks for fifty pounds, don't give it to him. Ohly give him ten." The cashier promised that he would fulfil the commands. Not long after, the son called at the office and demanded fifty pound. He was refused by the conscientious Cas'iier, and., apparently in anger, the young Man contented himself with the termer. When the old man reached the office there was a scene.

div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

In the great cemetery at Woking some of the proprietors of plots have a mania for burying dead dogs, cats, birds,and other pets there,and the atten- dants have to keep a very sharp look out to baffle these manifestations of over-fondness. Perhaps it was knowledge of such facts that led to the open- ing of the dogs' cemetery in Kensington Gardens. Few Londoners know anything ab ,ut it,although it may be seen from the top of the Bayswater omni- bus. It is attached to the lodge of one of the keepers, and contains a considerable number of stones in memory of the dear departed beneath. All were the pets of rich or titled people,and some have had rich and costly funerals. Not long ago, for ex- ample,a lady of high position paid £l7 tor the coffin in which her Fido was to rest in peace.

Gigantic wheels and Eiffel Towers suggest the idea of a big globe depicting the earth, and Mr. Riddiman Johnston has just prepared six specimen sections of a gigantic model for London. A month or two ago Professor Wallace, Darwin's rival in the discovery of the law of natural selection, criticised with great minuteness the monstre project which M. lieclus has projected for the Paris Exhibition, and he detailed a scheme of construction which overcame certain objections to which M. Reclus's scheme is open. Mr. Johnston has the advantage of Professor Wallace's ideas. The model he has in hand is double, the size of the French globe of 1889, but it is smaller than the model M. Reclus has in band. It would measure 84 feet in diameter, and would thus be on a scale of about eight miles to an inch. Thus London would occupy on the model a space equal to half a crown. A spiral gallery would run from pole to pole, and machinery would be em- ployed to cause the globe to revolve on its axis, so that the adventurous and inquisitive who ascended the spiral staircase would be able to examine it at any point of its latitude or longitude.

London is rapidly reaching white heat on the Eastern question, and so the "Times departs from its attitude of reserve to pour cold water on the protest movement. It will be all in vain. Its peculiar logic only serves, as far as I can perceive, to irritate and inflame the public mind. Even its broad hints of a possible war are derided. In some of the chapels on Sunday night there were extra- ordinary outbursts of emotion, notably at the City Temple, where Silas Hocking, the novelist, was preaching.

It is perhaps fortunate that a change is about to be made in the command of the Fleet in the Medi- terranean. Not that any word of reproach can be hurled against Admiral Sir M. Culme-Seymour, whose term of service is expiring. He has done his work well in every way. But the sending out of another admiral—Sir John Ommaney Hopkins— will enable the Admiralty to give him special instructions as to the duties that may he thrust upon him arising out of the Turkish situation. An understanding and even a new code can be arranged that will be very advantageous in the event of prompt and delicate operations being necessary against Constantinople.

The heir to "the assassin who sits on the throne of Constantinople " is not Abdul Hamid's eldest son, but his" Majesty's" brother Mehemmed Res- had who was born in 1844,and is therefore two years younger than the present Sovereign of Turkey. The " Imperial Prince " succeeds his ftether only when there are no older male descendants of Othman, or Ottoman, founder of the Turkish empire. Besides, the mentally afflicted and dethroned Murad Abdul has three brothers in the line of succession—Res- had, mentioned above, Wahid Effendi, born in 1860, and Suleiman Effendi, born in 1861 According to the writer of an article that appeared some months ago in a leading review, Reshad is a State prisoner in the Palace of the Cheragan,his companions being the members of his harem and some Court 3fficers. " He is not," we are told, "allowed to receive s single letter, book, or newspaper, not to mention a visitor from the outer world." To expect a man living year after year in such circumstances to be- come an enlightened ruler would be unreasonable.

The Czar is, in many things, disposed to look up to the Prince of Wales. He aElmires him, he be- lieves that be possesses the magic talisman of popularity, and he recognises in him the past mas- ter of tact and courtesy in public affairs. It seems not improbable that when the Czar reaches Bal- mcral, the Prince of Wales will take an early opportunity of saying a few words to him on tbe desirability ot a talk with the Marquis of Salisbury on Eastern affairs. Great caution will be required to bring about such an informal interview, but I have confidence in the success of the Prince of Wales.. The point of an interview is one oa which attention will be fixed for some time.

Earlier in the year Sir John Gorst was very em- phatic about the misdeeds of rural school boards. We should like to ask him what he thinks of the doings at a rural Voluntary school at Scottew (Nor- folk) during the past month or two. This unhappy village has no school board. Just before the sum- mer holidays the teacher who had been in charge of the school for many years left, having had a serious difference with the inhabitants of the vicarage. Since then the parson has been endeavouring to get another teacher. Teacher after teacher came down,but all refused to take the place. Beside her teaching work she was to be sure and "dress neatly," and to make herself useful at church. At the end of the holidays there was no teacher, and the vicar had to turn into the school himself and conduct the work with the assistance of two moni- tors, chosen frem amongst the village children. Eventually a young teacher, who takes the school as her first place,has been found, apparently ready to submit to the conditions imposed. But what has the Education Department to say about school work proceeding under such conditions, with the parson as a stopgap?

Mr. Toole has innocently amused more people in his life than any other living comedian, and there- for 3 he will be shocked to hear that his theatre in King William-street had to be demolished because the patients in Charing Cross Hospital, hard Iry, were disturbed by stage noises at night, and could not sleep. But his reply will be anticipated. He will say that his tun never irritat,A a living soul, sick or well, injured or sound. It was the men in the flies, the scene shifters, the carpenters, who did the business. However,the demolition of the abode of jollity has begun, and the Charing Cross Hospital manager will lose £l,OOO a year, and Mr. Toole a home. One is sorry for them both.

The Augustus Harris Memorial Fund is being col- lected with great difficulty. After all the talking and writing to which it has given rise, it does not exceed £l3OO, and is not likely to go very much higher. When one contrasts the meagreness of this posthumous honour with the fulsomeness and gush with which the energetic entrepreneur was written about during his life-time, one is compelled to be- lieve that a good deal of the popularity has been somewhat peculiar. And yet it is impossible to forget that the originators of the proposal were the most misled of all, for they even asked Her Majesty to become the patron of their movement.

During the lat five years the ratable value of the metropolis has increased by nearly three millions, and now reaches a SUM of 36 millions. The increase at the pre-ent rate of taxation represents an addi- tion of £lOO,OOO to the County Council annually, of £BO,OOO to the School Board, of £60,000 to the police, and of £65,000 to the water companies. It is not entirely represented by the growth and out- spreading of the metropolis, because the enhanced value of existing buildings largely contributes to tte gain. In the first three ca9es,there is no objec- tion called for, but that the water companies should charge more for their water because the rent al ora house has been raised, say, from £lOO to £l2O a year, is a grievance which is acutely felt by the London public, and yet they have sat under it meekly for generations, and have even now sent a majority of representatives to Parliament who are upholders of the system.

• Sunday next being the .anniversary of the Battle of c Alma, the royal dinner party at Balmoral will be in- vested with rather more ceremcny than usual, for the Queen on this occasion always drinks the toast "To the glorious immortal memory of the blessed dead, who fell fighting for me, and my country, on the heights of the Alma on the 20th of September 1854." It would be in- teresting to know what would have happened if the Russian visit had included Septembtr 20th! A paragriph has lately appeared in many ef the Lon- don papers, wherein the widow of Sir John Millais is described as Effie, Lady Millais. This is erroneous. The new baronet is her own son, and is married, therefore she is the Dowager Lady Millais. It is a well known fact that widows with married sons have of late years tried to avoid assuming the style of dowager, but they are always styled so at Court, and in all official docu- ments. The only instance in which the hated " Dowa- ger " can be dispened with is, when the reigning man is a stepson or only a connection by marriage. The correct thing now-a-days is to spend one's honey- moon on a farm 1 When Miss Consuelo Vanderbilt married the Duke of Marlborough, they spent their h.,neymoon on a farm in Long Island, and iu order to be fashianable Mr. and Alm Moses Taylor, and Mr. and Mrs. Harry Payne Whitney (Miss Gertrude Vanderbilt that was) are now in the solitude of big farms also. Apropos el weddings, the example of the Rev. Sir John Leigh Hoskyns, in celebrating his golden wedding,when he and Lady Hoskyns renewed their vows before the al- tar and were blessed by their son, seems likely to find imitators, for during the past week I have heard of ancther couple who did likewise. The church was beau- tifully decorated, and after the celebration of the Holy Communion the Wedding March was played. At a sub- sequent reception there was a wedding cake, and an ex- hibition of the beautiful "golden "gifts. Quite recently a woman was charged on remand, at one of our London Police Courts, with" talking,reutter- ing and making unseemly comments on the prayers" during Divine Service, in one of our London churches, but the c Ise was adjourned sine die on her brother be- coming security for her, and the defendant expressing her regret for such conduct. Talking and making com- ments during Divine Service is "disorderly behaviour in the eyes of the law but a case is recorded where this inconvenient practice was simply " eccentricity." One of our Royal Dukes of a past generation was in the hab- it of ejaculating remarks aloud all through the service. When the clergyman said " Let us pray," he would re- mark so that everyone round hi ni could hear " Pray Yes, certainly by all means 1" It was fortunate for the Duke that he was not of the lower ten thousand, other- wise a different view, in all probability, would have been taken of these particular preceedings.

Those of my readers who-remember the eccentric Quaker Fox, who insisted upon wearing his bat in St. Paul's Cathedral two or three years ago, may be inter- ested to hear that the first volume of a book, describing his life work, is now to be had. The title is, "The Hat Crusade," and a portrait of Friend Fox is given, by way of frontispiece, hat and all. Speaking of the Quaker and his hit, domestic manners would appear to have dis- tinctly improved since the 17th century, for no gentle- man would now think of sitting down to dinner without removing his headgear. In Pepy's Diary, and the little Samuel certainly ranked as a gentleman, we read,undar the date of September 22nd,1644. "Home to bed,having got a strange cold in my head by flinging off my bat at dinner, anti sitting with the wind in my neck.' Lord Clarendon twig who died in 1674,says in his essay on the "Decay of Respect paid to Age,"—"ln my younger days I never kept my hat on before those older than myself 'except at dinner.'" Why it was necessary for a man to wear ah. t during dinner it is difficult to imagine. It is however, an item to be grateful for that the fashion is not in vogue nowadays. Those of us who possess damaged collars and muffs of fur will welcome that narrow finger depths will be much used for trimming late autumn and winter gowns.l have noticed several up-to-date tweed skirts boasting a nar- row band on the hem, but I would strongly urge my readers to beware of this mode. It is an effective one, of ceurse,but it must be remembered that fur clogs with notorious ease, and declines to be restored to freshness after contact with mud.

The correct walking skirt of the moment is just a little shorter at the back than in the front, and will clear the ground. The comfort of this particular mode we cannot fail to appreciate. The dust and mud no longer has a chance to cling by the dustpan-full to the hem. and we have not nearly so often to " re-bind" our skirts, an odious task which every woman dislikes intensely. We have scarcely been able to get veiling,' wide enough during the past few months, but it seems that a change is about to take place, and the short veil just covering well the nose, is to be in high favour, during the coining winter. A rumour too, concerning the revival of mittens has reached one, from Paris, but in all probability they will be reserved as the complement of toilettes affecting styles peculiarly suited to them,and including Marie Antoinett," fichus, or th. 3 round bertha of 1830.

It is no longer correct, when greeting a friend, to raise one's hand to the level of one's shoulders before attempting a languid handshake, the more graceful and hearty handshake we were wont to indulge in some two or three years back is now in vogue. Apropos of our method of greeting one another, the Australian natives practise the singular custom, when meeting, of sticking out their tongue at each other, while the South Sea Islanders fling a jar of water over the bead of a friend. The Japenese removes his sandals, crosses himself, and cries out "spare me" and the Hindu falls in the dust before his superior. A Chinaman dismounts when a greater man goes by. Arabs hug and kiss each other making simultaneously a host of enquiries about each others health and prospect., while the Turk crosses his hands upon his breait and makes a profound obeisance thus manifesting his regard without coming into persona contact with its object. A friend in Paris sends me the news that the gay capital is just now in the clutches of the "prophets," who moreover have an organ, " The End of the World " which is vended in the streets by a dejected looking gentteman dressed entirely in black. This caper state that our planet wil be "consumed by fire in November." At present it looks much more probable that it will be washed away with rain, and at a much earlier date too!

I am frequently asked by correspondents for a good recipe for furniture polish. The old rule we " plenty of elbow-grease," and I think this was really the best of polishes. Next to that, vinegar and oil, mixed in equal nr.pGrtions is a good polisher and cleanser. Then comes beeswax and turpentine,which more especially for oak is excellent. In reality, the simpler the polish th 9 better. and the less the amount used. Servants hive, all of them,a strong tendency to putting on large amounts of everything in the way of polish, and to rubbing very little of it off.

ITALIAN SPONON.—Dissolve one ounce of gelatine in one pint of milk,put it in a saucepan on the fire till it nearly boils,beat the yolks of two eges,with four ounces of white sugar and stir into the saucepan with the milk until it thickens. Put it aside to cool and when it be- gins to set add the whites of the eggs, beaten to a stiff froth, and a little flavouring. Beat for a few minutes and pour into a wetted mould.
" MADGE."
OR, A WAR OF THE HOUSEHOLD.
By the Author of "The Double Life," "Th. Bailiff's Scheme," &c., &c.

div.head: MY DEAR Nmun,
div.p: MY DEAR Nmun,

It would seem that the day of the cape has well- nigh departed, and that now the autumn has come round and outer garments become once more a necessity they take, for the most part, the farm of neat, smart little jackets. Fulness in the basque is gradually getting less, and the little coats, which are worn quite short, look exceedingly smart and pretty. They are much more becoming to the figure than capes, and the absence of the abnormal development of sleeves renders them really feasible garments now.

A very stylish and handsome driving coat is of fawn box-cloth, double-breasted, and fastening with big buttons of smoked-pearl, and with huge revers of sable or mink. Another coat may be made close fitting of Royal blue cloth, beautifully cut, and kaving vest, a high collar and cuffs of Persion lamb.

The close-fitting, tailor-built jacket bodices are quite the smartest of the smart this autumu. A delightful costume, combining one of these bodices with a becoming cape, which is detachable, and can therefore be put on or off at pleasure.
The dress is of fine fawn beaver cloth, the bodice having large revers of brown velvet, edged with a band of the cloth. The shoulder-cape is attached under these revers.

Millinery is still in a transition state; and the milliners, like " Brer Fox" of immortal memory, " lie low" at present, so it is difficult to prophecy with accuracy concerning hats and bonnets. How- ever, we shall not wear erections resembling hay- stacks ; while velvet and felt will, as usual in the cold months, be in the ascendant. Plaited chenille will also be used for shapes much more than it was last year.
A very suitable hat for cycling, travelling, or i wearing at the seagide s made of Panama straw, and trimmed with black satin bow and two smart wings.

There are some remarkably and quite attractive looking hats for early autumn. One has a toque of black velvet, with high, narrow crown, spreading out at the summit, and sown closely with glitter- ing green beads, with here and there a beetles'-wing jewel ; the brim was entirely composed of curled ostrich tips, and at the front was a large butterfly bow of brilliant green velvet, clasped with an antique paste ornament. Another charming hat has a full Tudor crown of black velvet, and a straight brim of plaited chenille, rather wide in front, and shaped off to nothing at the back, where arose a panache of seven black plumes secured with a rather large clasp of antique paste, and two small tips curled downwards on to the hair. A smaller hat, also of black velvet, may turn right up at the left side, and the inevitable plume of black feathers adjusted there with a coquettish bow of poppy - red velvet underneath.
Your loving JENNIE.
"WOMEN'S CHAT."

Considering the fa.ci.tliTt.t-Fie'Cia-riPa was never per- 'pitted to have a veritable evening gown until she was sixteen, and then only of the plainest possible descrip- tion, the toilettes she is now in a position to indulge in, must appear all the more magnificent by comparison. The young Empress, who is winning all hearts during her tour of visits, has a most graceful presence, and her beautiful face, tinged with melancholy, recalls some- what the serious sweetness of her mother, the Princess Alice, one of the most loved, and most htlpful of Her majesty's daughters.

div.head: CHAPTER Ix.
div.p: CHAPTER Ix.
ALONE.

The funeral at Chessom Grange was over. The body of the good old squire had been taken to its rest in the country churchyard. His generous heart, with its quick sympathies, its pulsations stilled forever, was hidden away under the damp sods. The bluff and jovial face, the kindly eyes, the smiling mouth, were all hidden from the long- ing eyes of those who had loved him. He was gone; and the girl he had loved and cherished as his own, whom he had sheltered from every childish grief, and whose path had lain among the sun- shiny places, by reason of his tenderness and love, was left alone. How utterly alone she was soon to know.

It was the day after the funeral. In the pleasant sitting-room, the windows of which were open to admit the warm sunshine and fresh summer breezes, doubly grateful after the late funereal gloom, the new proprietor of the Grange was striding slowly to and fro. As the reader knows, he was Edmund Ches. som, the squire's only son, yet no greater contrast than he presented to his late father can readily be imagined. . . . . . . . .

Ice was not tall, but slender, with an angular figure, and slow and cautious movements. Not more than five-and-twenty, he yet looked ten years older, possessing a thin face, sharp features, and shrewd, unsmiling eyes. His thin lips were com- pressed closely, and as if hl ually. He was not a man to feel, much less to give way to, generous impulses, but he prided himself on being scrupulously just. Hard-headed, cold-hearted, cautious, more thoughtful of himself than others— such was he upon whom the mantle of the im- pulsive, generous and noble old squire had so un- expectedly fallen. There was a complacent expression on his face, as he halted by the window and looked out upon the smooth green lawn and the cool grove beyond. "Not a bad inheritance to come into at my age," he mused. "It's a pity poor father had to leave it so suddenly. In the right hands, it can be made twice as productive as it now is. lam a fortunate man."
He contemplated his possessions a little time in thoughtful silence, and then roused himself ab- ruptly, as he heard a light step in the hall. The next instant Dora entered the room.

She was dressed in the deepest mourning. Her face was very pale, and her eyes were red and swollen with weeping. She had a stunned and be- wildered look, as if she could not even yet realise the blow that had fallen upon her. "Good morning, brother," she said, with a faint and woful little smile, and with a strong effort at self-command. "Jane told me you wished to see me."

Mr. Chessom took her hand, giving it a faint pressure, and led her to a chair near the window. "Yes, I sent for you, Dora," he exclaimed, resuming his slow walk. "I want to have a con- versation with you concerning your -cuture—yours and mine. Of course, my father's death necessitates many changes. Have you bestowed any thought upon the matter ?" "No, Edmund. I have not thought of my- self at all—only of papa. Poor, poor papa ! ' and the sweet young voice broke into quivering sobs. _ _

Edmund Chessom frowned involuntarily. Dora's anguished cry irritated rather than touched him. "Then you have not thought of your future ?" he asked. "You have formed no plans ?" "None, Edmund," and Dora's voice had in it an accent of surprise. Mr. Chessom quickened his steps a little. "Humph 1" he said. "How old are you, Dora?" "Seventeen."

"Ah —yes. Nowlet us understand each other, Dora. I want to have a frank talk with you. I don't doubt the sincerity of your grief, my dear girl. It's all very natural for you to feel badly, under the circumstances; but if you could control your emotion, I should be able to speak more freely." His formal tone and unsympathetic rhlnner affeQted Dora much as an unexpected showerbath might have done. She gave a quick, faint gasp, choked back the sobs she had been unable to control, and bee me strangely quiet. "There, that will do," said Mr. Chessom, approvingly. "You will find self-control a most necessary virtue, Dora; and the sooner you learn it the better. But to proceed with what I had to say: I have a revelation to make to you—a revela- tion which will utterly astound, and perhaps' over- whelm you. Can you bear to hear it? Shall I go on ?"

"Yes," said the girl, in a whisper. "Can it be possible that you know what I mean ?" asked Mr. Chessom, regarding her fixedly. "Are you aware, Dora, that you are not—not my sister? That you are not the daughter of my parents ?" Dora nodded dumbly. She could not trust her voice to speak. " Ah, my father told you, then ?' Again Dora nodded. Mr. Chessom drew a sigh of relief, and resumed his walk, which had been momentarily inter- rupted. lam glad to hear it," he said. "I was afraid the discovery that you were but an adopted child of my parents might overcome you. The way is now clear to complete understanding between as. First, let me tell you of my plans. I shall settle down at the Grange, in my father's place. The life of a country gentleman will suit me exactly. lam engaged to be married to a lady who lives in London, but our union will be deferred a year on account of my father's death. It will not look well to have bridal gaieties at the Grange within a year of my father's funeral. And so you have thought of nothing as yet for your- self ? " " Nothing." Mr. Chessom took another turn or two, and then exclaimed :

_ "Of course you know enough of the world to know that it will be impracticable for you to remain at the Grange? yor the next year this will be but a bachelor establishment—not at all the home suit- able for a young girl of no kin to the proprietor. The lady I expect to marry would righly object to your stay. People would talk—" "But no one knows that I am not your sister, Edmund." "You know it. I know it. The lady lam to marry knows it. The secret can remain a secret no longer, nor is it desirable that it should. So long as my parents lived they had a right to do as they chose in the matter, and of course I have a similar right to do as I think best. lam your friend, Dora, but I am not your brother, and I do not see that there is any use in keeping up the false pretence of being so." A sobbing sigh burst from Dora 'a lips. With a piteous look, she turned her face to the window. "Don't mistake me, Dora," said Mr. Chessom, with a vague uneasiness, touched by her look. "I think as much of you as ever. You are a dear little girl, and I want to do right by you. I hear from the servants, of whom I have made some in- quiries, that the young squire comes here very often. Arc you engaged to be married to bun? Dora shook her head. "Do you love him ? " Dora answered by a gesture. "I am sorry. Squire Weir would have made you a good husband. Who is this Warner who has been here so much? Not the Warner who is con- nected with the noble family of Champney ?" "Yes. He is the cousin and secretary of Lord Champney," said Dora, in a low, quivering voice. " Indeed ! He hasn't been here since my father died. He is not a very devoted lover. Where is he?"

"He does not know of—of papa— He went to London last week. I had a note from him the morning after papa—" The tremulous voice broke down in a gust of passionate sobs. Mr. Chessom walked the floor, frowning im- patiently, until the sobs had died away, and the slight figure grown still and the pale face calm again. "Then he is in London now?" Dora bowed her head. "You haven't written to him the sad news?" "No—oh, now 1"

" Perhaps it's as well. Mr. Warner might be pleased to marry into the Chessom family—as no doubt he would. More than one Chessom has married a noble. But it would be quite another thing to marry the penniless daughter of a pair of vagrants—a child picked up by chance on the road, and adopted out of pity for its helplessness and beauty,, Ur. Warner is a man of the world, not a
Quixac, not a knight of chivalry, and he will act as men of the world act. You have seen the last of your fine lover, Dora."

Mr. Chessom did not mean to be cruel. He believed that he was setting the facts before Dora in a sensible nnwner. He lacked the delicate tact ard the fine symplthies which belong to the finest type of men, and did not dream that his every word cut into Dora't3 sensicive soul with the keen- ness of a knife.
As the girl did rot answer, Mr. Chessom soon resumed :

"You have, therefore, no lover, and no pros- pects. Is not this so ?" "You have not judged Mr. Warner rightly," cried Dora, in her impetuous way. "You wrong him. He will come to use. He loves me—not my birth, not my supposed wealth—but just me!" Mr. Chessom smiled with conscious superiority. "I judge of a man of the world as a man of the world," he said, quietly. " Don't deceive yourself with false hopes, Dora. Mr. Warner's family would prevent his misalliance, even if he were giddy and thoughtless enough to insist upon marry- ing you. Would you go into the Champuey family to be looked down upon? Would you he the cause of your husband's disgrace with his relatives? You have no idea of the haughty pride of these titled people. They do not care so much for fortune, I have heard, as for good blood—"
Dora shivered. "Don't," she said, putting up her band plead- ingly. "You may be right, Edmund. I will never consent to bring disgrace or trouble upon Mr. Warner !"
"Then, what remains? My father made no pro- vision for you. He left you totally dependent upon me—"

"He meant to provide for me!" interposed Dora, rousing herself. "That last day he went to see his lawyer, who was out of town. He made an appointment to meet him the next day. Papa told me himself that he meant to leave me a fortune—the same as if I had been his very own daughter." "Then why didn't he?"
"You kno;v why, Edmund!" cried the girl, in an anguished voice. "The end came that very night. Oh, papa! papa!"
"Dora, it will injure you to give way like this to a useless grief. Tears won't bring my father back ! "

Dora calmed herself by a desperate effort. "As to my father's intentions," continued Mr. Chessom, calmly, "I can't help but think that if he meant to provide for you, he would have done so 1 He had many years in which to do it, if he had so desired. You must have mistaken his meaning, Dora." "Oh, no, I did not, Edmund. "But the facts bear me out in persisting to think so. You could not have understood him rightly. If he had meant to leave you something, he could easily have made a will at any time during the past seventeen years. Doubtless he thought, as most men would have thought, that he had done his part by you. He took you out of the highway, adopted you as his own, provided you with governesses and teachers, dressed you like an heiress, and gave you every advantage that money could purchase. And to-day, Dora, you are competent, or ought to be, to earn your own living by teaching. How would you like to be a governess ? " " I—l don't know." "You certainly cannot want to retnain at the Grange after what I have said ?" "Oh—no, no 1"
, "Then you'll have to become a governess. There is no other resource for you that I can see. You have no taste for painting, I suppose—no fancy to become an artist ?'
Dora replied in the negative. "There is nothing you would prefer to teach- ing ?" " I can't think, Edmund. My brain is in a whirl. You must decide for me."

"Then you will be a governess. I have already bestowed considerable thought on the matter. You had better proceed to London. I know of lodgings there that will just suit your purse and condition. I'll give you a line to the landlady, and she'll make you comfortable. I will also give you a letter to Miss Coningsby, my promised wife. She has younger sisters' and will use her influence to procure you pupils. You will soon fall naturally into the position of a daily governess, and will enjoy eating the bread of independence." "And you will enjoy being rid of me 1" cried Dora, with a passionate bitterness. "I have nothing to say, Edmund. But papa loved me so 1 It would have grieved him to the soul could he have foreseen this hour for me. Until this moment I have not felt how terribly friendless and alone I am. Alone—alone t" She dwelt on the word with a teh-ible despair. Mr. Chessom was not unmoved by her emotion, but he hastened to say: "You will not be alone, Dora. I would not permit one so young and beautiful as you to go out into the world alone. Listen to me. There is a woman over at the Hare and Hounds—a patient, sorrowful woman, whose husband and children—all but one child—lie buried in a foreign land. This woman is poor and destitute, and turns to her only surviving child for help and support. This woman is your mother, Dora!" "I have seen her."

_ "She did not say so. I went to see her last evening, having received a message from her. Of course, Dora, a mother's claims are paramount. Even if it were best for you to remain here I could not keep her. Neither would I bribe her to go away, as she wished me to do. I never approved my father's course in adopting a poor child out of the streets as one may say. You see I speak frankly, Dora. But he had a right to do as he pleased, and I have no wish to reflect upon his memory. But with my father's life the whole pretence must end. You will go away with your mother, Dora, and be a support to her declining years." "But I don't like her," cried Dora. "I don't feel as if she were my mother. I can't have her cold eyes for ever upon me—l can't! I can't! I will go away, Edmund. I will work hard. I'll give half my wages to—to that woman, but I can't have her near me."
"Dora 1" ejaculated Mr. Cheasom, in a cold re. buke.

"All I ask is to go away by myself," said Dora, impetuously. What you want is an impossibility," said Mr. Chessom, coldly. "I am surprised at you, Dora. If you pay no heed to duty, let me tell you that you are under age, and that your mother is your rightful guardian. You must yield to her au- thority." The heat, the rebelliousness, the quick, impetu- osity, all died out of Dora's manner. She became quite calm and still; but it was the calmness and stillness of a profound despair. "There, that is better," said Mr. Chessom. "You had best resign yourself to the inevitable. I have had a talk with your mother on the subject, and I shall resign you into her care to-morrow morning. It is, I hope, unnecessary for me to re- mind you that you should adopt a filial attitude toward this poor woman." - - -
" It is unnecessary," exclaimed Dora, bitterly. "If Mrs. Narr is my mother, the law is on her side and I must go with her. But the law can't make me like her." . .
"Dora !" again ejaculated Mr. Chessom, rebuk- ingly. "I am shocked at your rebellious spirit." He sighed, and walked back and forth in a per- turbed manner. -

"I must leave you to yourself," he said, finally, his face clearing. "You must work out your own. destiny, Dora. I have but one thing more to say. You will need some funds until you get stazted, and it will be prudent to keep a small sum by you in case of sickness. You can take with you all your personal effects, clothing, jewellery, books and music. Here is the address of the lodging- house keeper, also the address of Miss Coningsby, upon whom you will call without delay. She will expect you. Here also is the sum of one hundred and fifty pounds, all that I shall probably ever give you." He handed her the addresses, and the banknotes representing the sum he had mentioned. Dora hesitated about accepting them, but finally drew out her already well-filled purse, and stuffed in the additional notes, saying proudly: "I take the money, Edmund, but not as from you. Papa intended to provide for me, and I take this as my right. It is only a small part of what he intended to give me." Mr. Chessom's face flushed, but he made no response. "I can pack up my things in a couple of hours," continued Dora. "and I shall then be ready to go, if you will kindly send me to the station. Mrs. Narr can meet me there. I don't want to see her this side the station.

" You had better wait till to•morrow, Dora l" No. I cannot stdy. I thank you for your civility, Mr. Chessom, but I shall feel better to go." ," Perhaps it would be as well, then, that you should go. Still, you are quite welcome to stay till to-mm.ow! The carriage will be at the door in

two hours from now. i will send word to Mrs. Narr immediatel , so that she may be waiting for you at Horsham. After all, lam not sure that you are doing well in going off so abruptly. There will be many of the neighbours in to call to-day, and explanations would be very disagreeable for you. We part friends do we not, Dora ?" "I suppose so," said Dora, drearily. "I have forgotten what friendship means." "I will not see you again. Partings are always disagreeable. I hope you will prosper in your nevi vocation, Good-bye, Dora." He touched her cold hand lightly as the girl arose and paused a moment on her way to the door.

"Good-bye I" echoed Dora, faintly. She tottered on to the door, and halted on the threshold for a last look at the pleasant room, endeared to her by so many pleasant scenes, hal- lowed to her by the squire's sudden death within its walls. A last, long look—and then Dora went up to her room. When the carriage came to the door, two hours later, Dora, deeply veiled and clad in mourning garb, descended the stairs ready for departure. The old fatoily servants, who had been informed by Mr. Chessoin that Dora had been only an adopted child of the Chessoms, and was now going away with her on mother, crowded around her with tears and sobs.

There was a brief scene, and then Dora got into the carriage, the trunks were strapped into place, and the next umment the young girl was leaving behind her the dear old Grange, with all its tender memories and pleasant associations. She sank back in the corner of the carriage, pulling her veil over her face and weeping silently. Only once on the way to Horsham did she arouse herself, and that was when they drove pat Weir Hall, the home of young Squire Weir. Then she started up, and looked eagerly at the stately mansion and pleasant grounds' but the, young squire was not visible and she sank back, with a half-uttered moan on her lips. The journey to Horsham was in due time accomplished. Dora was driven directly to the station—a train being on the point of de- parture. Mrs. Narr was waiting on the platform, and came forward to greet the young girl, but Dora quietly repelled her embrace and greeted her with cold politeness. For her life, she could not have welcomed her warmly. Mrs. Narr's face clouded, and she was about to rebuke Dora, or to reproach her, when the train glided into the station. Then came the bustle of departure, and soon after Dora was speeding on her way to London, in company with the woman whose maternal claims upon her her heart rejected, yet alone—terribly alone I The battle of life was before her. Would she perish in it, or come off conqueror? What would be her fate?
(To be continued).

div.head: PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION.
div.p: THE PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION.
BY MR. H. WHITHA.M.

A few of my Warrington friends ask me for my opinion as to who is likely to be the next Presi- dent. lam no prophet and therefore cannot say. Yet I meet with lots of prophets, but the trouble is, they all differ about the matter. With American politics I have no sympathy. It is a something, I am bound to say after ten year's looking on, that I have no de•ire to meddle with. I am a little in- clined to think that the Democratic party are, in this campaign, and against the wishes ot some of its leading men, trying to ring out the old an ring in the new with the introduction of the silver question as a leading plank in the Democratic plat- form, hut of that even I cannot be sure. There is no doubt of one thing—the political situ- ation is as nice a tangle as anyone could &sire to unravel. On the one hand we shall have to vote for protection and a gold standard as represented by McKinley. On the other for a moderate free traie and the double standard, or free silver, as the party headed by Mr. Bryan puts it. It is acknow- ledged all round that the coming election is the most important one that America will have seen since the Civil War. Mr. Bryan, a comparatively unknown man, by a single speech, alm mt by a single phrase, leaped at a bound to the front and has made it possible, nay, exceedingly likely, that the Democratic party will tak- a new lease of life and for another four years reign at the White _ .

The Democratic party has little to say, and little to print on the tariff question, but on the silver question it is immense. Speaking for the people, it says in the words of its silver-tongued orator, "they shall no longer be crucified on a cross of gol J." The Republican's deal as gently as possible with the silver question preferring rather to stake their all on the tariff question. They insist upon point- ing the attention of the people to the tires of the mills and factery's which they say are out, while your own mills and factories in Birmingham, Brad- ford, Sheffield and Leeds are running full time, and filling the States with cheap goods" Made in Kng- latid," and all in consequence of Cleveland's unpa- triotic tariff measures. _ _

The position of the Bepublican party is anything but satisfactory to its members. To begin with,the siloer question as a political " cry " should be as much at home on their platform as on that of the Democrats. All its leaders are in favour of free sil- ver,from McKinley down. There is scarcely a lead- ing Republican paper in the country but is pledged to bimetalism, but they all excuse them- selves out of the question by saying that it is no use meddling with the money standards until Eng- land signifies her willingness to co-operate along with other European nations in the adoption of a universal money standard. In McKinley they have a leader who is certainly an incapable man, and not at all able to cope with Bryan. lie has proved that it is protection, and that only, that he can talk about, and quite a number of republicans are begin- ning to think that protection as a panacea for all their ills has proved a rotten reed to lean upon, and it is from these disgruntled ones that the Populist party has swollen its ranks. A complete fusion is likely to come about between the Populists and Democrats, and as a consequence McKinley may see all the race. But what is making more against the Republican party than almost anything else is the unfortunate selection of Mr. Mark Hanna as the chief boss of their show. This man has a record second to none in its vile attitude towards labour. As a large employer he has neglected no opportunity to tread out trade uniouistn. As a syndicate, trust and com- bination " boss" he shoulders through the crowd arm in arm with R Thefeller, Armour, Sage, and other notable millionaires. This man's love for his country is unbounded, but its population is all under his own hat. Be makes the" call "on Wall- street, and millions pour forth, and, would anyone believe it, all to protect the poor workingman trom being paid a fifty cent. dollar. Yes, Wall-street is pouring out its millions. A campaign fund is spoken of reaching to as much as five million pounds. This has its significance to workingmen, and they chuckle, and in whispers speak of the ballot box. Hanna recommends employers to adopt the English methods, stop the engines, and call the men together for a talk. Let the consequences be puinted out to the men, should Bryan be elected. This is not intimidation. Oh, no. Simply a`friendly talk. It was also fsiendly advice when the insurance agents sent notices round to the farmers that should Bryan win they would have to foreclose and make what they could out of the farms. Same when bankers stop the flow of gold and government scrip. Let me say as a matter of 'fact from what I have beard and seen, that not one of the political moves that dis- graced England previous to the reform era will be wanting in this campaign by the unscrupulous gold bugs of the Republican party. Throughout the country there is great distress. farmers are at their wits end, not knowing which party to trust, or where to seek for relief. Their farms are gradually slipping out of their hands, mortgage is eating all up. Their produce brings nothing. Hundreds, nay thousands, of cases are named where,when all charges are paid,a season of toil leaves nothing for the toiler —all is eaten up by the money changers. In the cities it is the same, no work and men walking the streets, or compelled to work for wages that bring no livelihood. I know of one large concern here where the men have two aid three months wages owing; they cannot get a cent. and scarcely dare ask for what is their due. Men seem determined to vote silver even if it brings all the disasters that the Republicans say it will. For myself I don't think I shall vote at all. I cannot unravel the tangle, and I shall not cast a vote for mere desperation's sake. But I think Bryan will run McKinley very 'close, and he may very likely be the next President. A mere looker on at this great political fight will be struck with one peculiar and significant feature. The division between the two camps is sharp and acute. The rich and the poor are facing each other in battle array. It almost. seems as if we were en- tering upon the great struggle so long foreseen by the social student. This massing of wealth for a political fight is looked upon with dismay, and it is feared that the old land marks that have been used to shelter the covetous and the grasping are being assailed. In the Republican camp are to be found the bankers, financiers and promoters of trusts, owners of monopolies, big manufacturers, and officers of all the great corporations. Where twenty years ago the number of rich millionaires could be counted easily, they abound in numbers now in every city and State,and their influence and money is on the Republican side. It used not to be so. A man's social position was no. guide to his political proclivities. The Democratic camp is a very cave of Adullam. All who are dissatisfied with things as they are, are to be found shoulder to shoulder with the rank and file of the workingmen, farmers, and farm labourers. This division seems to be drawing the line sharply between capital and labour. Labour has proved by experience that capital is unfit to govern. To it oast wars and present rumours of wars can easily be traced. The poor see plainly that the building up of rich corporations is the building up of soulless and merciless machines, under which their lives are ground out of them. Such is my answer to those who wish for my opinion,and this is how it all appears to me. If Bryan wins then a peaceful revolution, If Mc Kinley a French revolution may not be far off.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC.

The traffic o-t-1 the canal last week was unusually heavy, 185 ships, with an aggregate net registeied ton- nage of 53,770 tons, navigating the waterway inwards and outwards, as compand with 138 ships of 44,837 tons in the preceding week. The foreign traffic in par- ticular was considerably above the avnage.

It is officially announced by the \Var Office that the five officers of the army who were convicted of taking part in the raid into the Transvaal " have beeo pn- mitted to retire from Her Majesty's service." Eight officers who were discharged at Bow-street Police Court have been severely censured by the Adjutant General and ordered to return to duty.

div.head: ALLEGED MURDER AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE ALLEGED MURDER AT WARRINGTON.
PRISONER AGAIN BEFORE THE
MAGISTRAT ;.
CONIIIIML TO THE ASSILES FOR TRIAL.

An evidence of the great amount of interest taken in the proceedings against the prisoner James Bate—who has now been committed to take his trial on a charge of wilful murder—was given on Monday morning, when he appeared before the local bench of magistrates consisting of the Mayor (Councillor James Fairclough), Alderman Fran- comb, Councillor William Pierpoint, Dr. Gornall, Messrrs Thomas Birchall, J. W. Hayward, and S. Wright. For some considerable time before the Court opened large crowds congregated in the vicinity of the Court-house, and a body of police had to be put on duty in order to keep the thoroughfare clear. It was net until the fingers of the p )fice court clock pointed to 10.30 that the case was proceeded with, the time since ten o'clock having been occupied by a number of other police cases. The prisoner was accommodated with a chair in the dock, and was then charged with the murder of his wife. Mr. W. H. J.Jenkins,solicitor, appeared on his behalf, and the prosecution was conducted by the Town Clerk (Mr. J.Lyon Whittle). There was a perceptible change in the appearance of the prisoner since he was in Court on the Wednesday previ- ous. His eyes had lost all their brilliancy and he looked careworn and pale. He followed the evidence atten- tively, aril did not speak until the close of the hearing of the case when hie solicitor asked him to repeat after hint the words " I reserve my defence." The hearing of the case lasted until four o'clock when the magistrates committed him to take his trial on the capital charge at the Liverpool Assizes. The number of magistrates had dwindled from seven to three by the time the hearing concluded, and the decision was given by Councillor William P.erpoint, There was a large attendance of the general public in the well of the Giurt during the pro- ceedings. A large crowd outside—chiefly composed of women—was kept from entering the Court by a num- ber of police officers. The lamentable event was the topic of conversation amongst them, and when anyone emerged from tho Court he was freely questioned. On learning the result the crowd dispersed and there was no demonstration of any kind. The prisoner before being taken to the cells shook hands with the solicitor and his clerk. Early on Tuesday morning he was removed to Walton Gaol where he will remain until the trial, which will not take place until November. FURTHER POLICE PROCEEDINGS. '

The Town Clerk, in opening the case on Monday, said he appeared on behalf of the Crown to prosecute the prisoner on a charge of wilful murder. The prisoner was not upon his trial that day. The duty of the Bench was to ascertain from the evidence whether in their judgment it was sufficient to justify them in com- mitting prisoner to take his trial en the capital chargeat the Aisiv‘s. _ _ _ _

Mr. Jenkins : I should like,before the case is opened,to thank the Chief Constable for the great kindness he has shown to me in this matter, in giving me every possible assistance in conducting the defence. It is with very great pleasure I have to say so. The Chief Constable: lam very glad to have been of assistance to you. Mr. Jenkins said there was another matter to which he wished to refer—a matter in which he could assist Mr. Whittle. He suggested that the medical evidence he taken at time to be defined. The cross-examina- tion of the medical then was a very important element in the prisoner's defence, and it would necessarily take up a considerable time. It was bound to be done slowly and patiently. The Town Clerk expressed his willingness to such a course heing taken. It was then decided to adjourn for luncheon at one o'clock, and to call the medical evidence at two o'eleck. The Town Clerk continuing, pointed out what the duty of the magistrates was,and said it might be possible that there were circumstances of extenuation which might be found in reducing the charge to manslaugh- ter. Having read the law regarding murder, the Town Clerk said they had to assume in the first place that the prisoner was guilty of wilful murder. He need net trouble the magistrates with the details as they had already been disclosed, and appeared in the public Press. The prisoner was a chemical labourer, and lived at 11, Oliver-st. He (the Town Clerk) bad had plans pr-pared of the house which Mr. Jenkins was willing to accept as correct. The prisoner kad four ehildren, and he was informed that the prisoner and his wife had lived unhappily together. On Monday, the 7th inst.,the pri- soner got home, and there was no tea provided for hie. His wife was drunk,and the prisoner went off in a tem- per and visited several public-houses during the even- ing. The prisoner's wife went home at ten o'clock. She was drunk, an she was seen to fall outside her house. He would leave the attack on the woman to the wit- nesses. He (the Town Clerk) did not wish to shield the woman -,ho was the prisoner's wife. She seemed to have been a drunken, careless woman, neglectful of her duty as a wife and mother. He would now call the evidence. ' John Sutcliffe, civil engineer and surveyor, said he was an associate member of the Civil Engineers and ' Assistant Borough Surveyor of Warrington. He went to the house, 11, Oliver-street, at ten o'clock in the morning of the 10th, and made a detailed exansination of the house at four o'clock. life had prepared the plans produced. The building were very old, more particu- larly Nes. 9 and 11. All the property was in a dilapi- dated condition, and the walls of Nos. 9 and 11 were settled and bulged outwardly, leaving a cavity of one inch at the front and an inch and a half at the back. Standing in either house-9 and 11—it was possible to see into the other house through the cavity. The inner wall was plastered on both sides and was a 44 inch wall. The witness proceeded to give various details in connec- tion with the construction of both houses. In the front bedroom of No. 9 there was a hole in the lathe and plas- ter of the ceiling about ten inches in diameter which was clege to the pantry wall. The floors of the bedrooms of No. 11, were in a rotten condition and the back bed- room floor was composed of boards and joists only. The beards were very old and rotten. Inspector Spinks and Sergeant Cheney had gone to the house with him and they made exper;ments with regard te the transmission of sound from one house to the other. Witness stood in the bedroom of No. 9 and distinctly heard the voice of Sergeant Cheney in No. 11 in an ordinary tone of voice. He put certain questions and received correct answers. This was about five o'clock in the evening, and traffic in the streets was going on and there was a considerable crowd outside. Similar experiments were made in No. 13, and he could hear them in the next house but not so distinctly. Cross-examined by Mr. Jenkins: The bloodstains were at the far end of the room, in the back bedroom. He called it a bloodstain for convenien:e. He had had considerable ~.xperience in empty buildings. By the Town Clerk : The bedroom was 9ft. 4in. by Bft. 11 in.

Margaret Bate, 10 years of age, said her father was named James Bate and lived at 11, Olivet-st. She then proceeded to repeat the evidence given at the inquest. In answer to the Town Clerk she said her mother told her that she had fallen down outside. Eler mother never said she was hurt. She did not notice any marks of blood on her mother's face when she came in. Her mother used to get drunk nearly every Saturday and Monday night. Her father was as bad.

div.head: CARD

fßs Mr. Jenkins: Did you tell Mrs. Stewart that " mamma " fell downstairs when going to the outhouse? —I don't remetnber.—She did tell neighbours that her mother fell down. Her mother was often drunk, and her father had often to work without food. She did not know that her father went to work without breakfast on Monday morning. Her mother was drunk on Saturday night, and she had beer on Sunday. She didn't get up on Monday morning. After her father bad left the house on Tuesday morning Uncle John Kelly took her to grandma Kelly's. Her grandma was very angry with her father and she said to him "you have killed her" and he replied "you are a liar." She stayed a day or two there, and her grandma asked hcr "how her father did it." She told her that he kicked her in the mo• th, stomach, and back. On Tuesday morning after she told her father that "mammy was white "he said "Oh Maggie your mammy is dead. It is only what I thought this drinking and falling would bring her to." She did tell her father that he had not killed mother. Her .mother had a severe cut on the head a few weeks ago. It was on her head now. She remembered her mother saving that a man had kicked her. It was about a fort- night ago. When her father asked her to get the rag he said "It would be bad to look at if anyone came in." There was a lot of blood in the corner. The bloA on the face was on the mouth, and her father wiped it off with a. wet rag._ . _. .. . . ...

By the Town Clerk: She was there when her father called her grandma a liar. Her grandma then said " Long threatenings have come at last, you often threatened to do it, and you have done it." She re- membered her mother having her head cut and going to the Infirmary. It was a long while ago and she did Pet complain of her head. The Town Clerk: It was in April. Mary Jane Fearnley, 15 Oliver-street, gave evidence corroborating what she said at the Coroner's inquiry. The prisoner was at her door on Monday night, in a drunken condition and she took him home. He used threatening language towards his wife and said what he would do for her. She ran out of his house. ‘Vhen the Prisoner's wife came home she fell. on her knees and rolled over.
By Mr. Jen)iins : The deceased woman might have hurt her head and witness not have seen it.

Victoria Whelan, 13, Oliver-street (next door to prisoner) said she saw deceased on Monday night. She had seen her worse drunk on other occasions. She re- peated her evidence as to what she heard from 11.30 p.m. to nearly midnight on Monday. The row continued for about twenty minutes alter witness had been awakened. She heard deceased say" Oh Jim you have murdered me," or" Oh Jim you are murdering MO." She did not know which. The prisoner replied " You want mur- dering, you'll have no more of my money you—lrish pig." She heard no more of the deceased's voice. The prisoner continued talking and cursing. She hcard a noise of something bumping on the floor and she could hear the vibration in her room. The prisoner afterwards took the children to the next room. He said " Maggie haven't I been a good daddy to you," and the girl re- plied " Yes daddy you have." She heard a gurgling noise. Her (witness's) daughter was in bed with her. She had been disturbed by rows in the prisoner's house before.

Fly Mr. Jenkins ; if the prisoner was stamping about the bedroom with his heavy boots on it would shake her room. Deceased was a strong woman. By the Town Clerk: She could distinguish the foot- steps from the bumps on the floor. By Mr. Jenkins : Might it not have been possible that she was bumping her husband ?—lt might have been possible but she thought there would have been more noise than there was. Elizabeth Shaw, widow, said she slept in the same bedroom as her mother (the last witness) on Monday night. She saw the prisoner returning home. He was singing and staggering. She saw him speak to Mrs. Fearnley who run away. She heard a " thunging " noise on the floor several times like " bumps" on the floor after the prisoner .entered the back bedroom.

By Mr. Jenkins : _ When you heard the bumping noise didn't you hear prisoner say "It is every Monday alike. I'll work no more for you ?"—Yes he did say that. By the Town Clerk : The " thunging "noise did not see-n to be like footsteps. Henry Gibbons, general labourer, 9 Oliver-street, said he was in the front bedroom on the night of the 7th, when he was awakened by the pesoner saying " Where is my b— supper." Be appeared to be calling from the foot of the stairs of prisoner's house. Shortly 'afterwards he heard him go upstairs. He had boots on. He could tell by the noise he heard. Prisoner used bad language and witness heard some bumping going on. He heard a woman's voice say " Oh !" By the Town Clerk: He could distinguish between the stamping of the prisoner's boots and the bumping on the floor. _
____ _...... At this point of the proceedings the Court adjourned for luncheon. On resuming, the first witness called was

.• _ Ellen Brown, Oliver-street, who stated that on Tues- day morning at 9 15, prisoner sent for her and she went across to his house. He was standing near the middle door, and she asked prisoner where Kate was, to which he replied " Oh, I am in a bit of trouble, Kate is dead." prisoner was then crying. He asked her to assist to remove the body from the back room to the front. The deceased was lying on the edge of the bed en her back, and was then dead. She assisted to remove the body and then went home.

Margaret Kelly, mother of the deceased,residing at 30, Foundry-street, said the deceased was 33 years of age. She had never seen the couple living happily together. She heard of her (laughter's death on Tuesday morning at ten o'clock. She saw the prisoner and said " Jim what in the world is amiss with Kate." he said " I don't know, she fell downstairs drunk." She then said " Jive, you have killed her," and he said " No, it is a lie." She said "Long threatenings have come at last; you said you'd swing for her." She saw blood had been wiped off the floor near the head of the bed in the back bedroom. _

By Mr. Jenkins : She had often seen bleod-shed in consequence of quarrels. Sergeant Cheney gave evidence as to arresting the prisoner and charging him with causing the death of his wife. He repeated the reply of the prisoner given in our last issue. He was in company with witness, John Sutcliffe and Inspector Spinks at Oliver-street, to test the transmission of sound from one house te another. lie spoke in an ordinary tone of voice from the middle of the back bedroom at No. II to Inspector Spinks and Mr. Suteliffe. He could hear what was said te hint. By Mr. Jenkins The crevices in the party wall only apply to that between 9 and U. au had known the woman for a great many years. She was a drueken woman, but kind withal. He had known her to fight. The police record produced was that of the deceased woman. She had been up in that court tor drunkenness, breach of the peace, and assaults. He never had occas- ion to speak to her.—You have heard the evidence of the doctors, I suppose, that she died from contused wounds? —Yes, I have but the terms used were of such a profes- sional character that I could hardly grasp them. (Laughter.) Dc.T.Starkev Smith gave the result of his post-mortem examination Of the deceased related at the inquest. The cause of death was an effusien of blood on the brain, caused by direct violence. The bruises on the body were sufficient to cause death. He thought the injury to the forehead was them et likely one to bathe cause of death. He did not think it would be long betweon the infliction of the injut v and death. A suggestion that the dneased fell downstairs was not consistent in his opinion with the injuries he found. After the blow to the forehead unconsciousness would follow, and death would ensue from the clot of blood on the brain. He had examined the boots produced, and the injuries he found upon the deceased might have been caused by them. Ple went into the back bedroom and near the head of the bed there was a patch 13in. by llin. where blood had evidently been wiped up from the floor. Above the patch of blood and inclining on the right hand,there were several spots of blood on the wall. He thought there were eight or ten. He had examined the handkerchief and piece of bed tick produced and found,micrescopically and chemi- cally,blood stains. He could not say vi hether they were recent. _ _ _

By Mr. Jenkins: The medulla oblongata was at the back of the bead, and the brain had direct communica- tion with it. Tiee congestion was on the anterior por- tion of the brain, and its course followed more to the base of the brain. che formation of the clot of blood in the substance of the medulla oblongata would Cause death more quickly than if it were on the outside. He did not think a fall on the setts would have produced injury to cause death. It was extremely improbable, but it might be just possible for her to get to her bed- room after receiving the injury.—Tbere is just that chance P—Witness : She could hardly have done so. It is just possible. Continuing, the doctor said that the only evidence of deceased taking drink was the enlarged liver and dilated stomach. Her kidneys were healthy. She appeared chiefly to have drunk beer. He did not think that the injuriee he bad mentioned were caused by a fall. The injury to the deceased's nose must have been caused by a terrible blow, and could not have been caused by falling. Ile thought that the blood spots on the wall had spurted from the nose. By the Tewn Clerk : The injuries were consistent with the idea that the woman was undressed at the time. lithe injuries to the forehead had been caused by a fall on the setts he did not think she would have been able to get home. speak rationally to her children, and undressed herself.

He-examined by Mr. Jenkins: He did not think the injuries had been caused by the tips of the boots except perhaps that on the right side of the chin and the left ear. Dr. 13.)wden said that in company with Dr. Starkey Smith he made a post-mortem examination on the body. He corroborated his statement. Cross-examined by Mr. Jenkins : Supposing the woman had fallen on the setts shortly before getting in- t) bed, possibly that i'night have been the cause of death. She might possibly have been able to reach 'a er bed- room.
