The Town Clerk: Da you think she could have gone home, had some supper and undressed hcrself after- wards ?—lt is very unlikely, but I cannot say it is im- possible. In,pector Spinks said he went to the house of the de- ceased and made an examination of the whole of the premises and found no ,do d except in the back room. He received the handkerchief produced and cut out a pieee of the bed tick. He handed a portion of the bed tick to Dr. Smith. He corroborated the evidence of Sergeant Cheney regarding the arrest and transmission of sound from cne house to the other.

Cross-examined by Mr. Jenkins : He had known the deceased since 1880, and she had been convicted several times. She had come up about once each year. She was violent when drunk but ha,mless when sober.
The prisoner was then charged in the usual manner and speaking after Mr. Jenkins, lie said " I reserve my defence."
The Chairman (Coun. Pierpoint) then said : You are committed to the Liverpool Assizes to take your trial on a charze of wilful murder. The prisoner was then moved from the dock.

div.head: REMOVAL OF THE PRISONER.
div.p: THE REMOVAL OF THE PRISONER.

After the committal of the prisoner, many people were anxious to know when he would be removed to Walton Gaol,in order that they might be able to see him. The police, however, in order to prevent any demonstration, very wisely refrained from divulging the time of his de- parture. Sergeant Cheney on Monday evening went round to the prisoner's friends and relatives to inform them that they could see the prisoner for the last time, prior to his removal to Liverpool. This opportunity was taken advantage of and the meeting between the pri- soner and his friends was of a heartrending character. The departure ut the prisoner was at 530 on Tuesday morning. Detective-Sergeant Monaghan and Detective Roper accompanied him in a cab to the Central Station, and thence to Walton Gaol. The officers met with little or no observation by the few persons who were in the neighbourhood of the station at this early time of the morning. A cab was in waiting at Liverpool and the prisoner arrived at Walton a little after 7 o'clock.

div.head: NUGGET OF GoLD ORE.
div.p: THE NUGGET OF GoLD ORE.
" That," said my friend, in reply to a question of mine, 'is a very large and very rich nugget of gold ore. It was taken many years ago from a mine in Australia."
" How much is it worth ?" I asked. He looked at me with a shrewd smile and replied : "It is worth just nothing at all." I thought that a queer thing for him to say, but asked no more q.iestions.

Two years later I again visited his house in London, and this time I missed Vile big nugget from the shelf where I had first seen it. But I asked no questions. Perhaps, recalling thi incident of two years before, my friend said :" I have something to shciw you," and, opening a closet, he produced a magnificent gold vases remarking : " That nugget of gold ore has taken this form. Exclusive of the labour involved in the trans- formation, the .old alone is now worth £100." What curious similit des there are between things essentially unlike ! Here is one which it may be in- structive to follow up. It is suggested by the following sentence from a woman's letter :—" In spite of all the nourishing food I took, nothing seemed to give me strength." New,why was that P Perhaps the history of the pre- vious three years of her life may help to account for it. In January,lB9o,she had an attack of influenza which, she says, left her low, weak,and languid. So far as we are able to ascertain, influenza is caused by a certain p ison of the blood developed during peculiar conditions of the atmosphere. Its early symptoms are these of fever ; they are always sudden and often alarming. Yet,as in nearly all causes it ends in recovery in a week or two, it does not explain the mystery of Mrs.Westall's centinued weakness and prostration. She tells us that her appetite was poor, and that eat- ing was immediately followed by great pain in the chest, back, and sides. Hoping to overcome this state of things she took much nourishing food. That an in- crease of strength should result from the eating of plenty good food would seen% reasonable. How else can one ever gain strength ? Yet, strange to say, no such result followed. On the cont rary, the pain became worse, so that— to use her own words—she was "completely racked with pain " all over her, and so weak she could scarcely put one foot before the other. Besides this, the condition of the stomach was far from encouraging. That organ is the source of all power in the human body, and should feel warm, comfortable and quiet. In this lady's case it was full of uneasiness and vain. She speaks of a craving, gnawing, sinking sensation in it, which was not relieved either by food or by any medical treatment. Certainly, something quite different from a f-irmer attack of influenza went to the making of that ; we must look deeper to find the real trouble.

Chemists often determine the character of a poison by observing the colour it creates when applied to litmus paper ; and—in addition to the general symptoms—it is sometimes possible to tell the nature of a disease by tak- ing notice of what cures it. N3w there is sue univers- ally known remedy which never fails to cure one subtle, comprehensive, and yet deceptive disease. Happily it was finally employed in Mrs. Westall's case. In c3ncluding her letter, dat.,d December Ist, 12, Rucklidge Avenue, Willesden, London, NW., 1892—she says "At the time when my condition was very critical and ray family very anxious, my son-in-law Mr. Deacon, of Shepherd's Bush-road ,told me how in an illness of his own he had been cured by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup ate advised me tio begin using it at once. I did s 3, and soon my appetite returned and my food digested : and by the time I had consumed two bottles I was strong as ever, and have kept in the best of health ever since.—(Signed) Yours traly, Mary West all

This remedy, as the public is well aware, is adver- tised to cure indigestion and dyspepsia and its consequ- ences—and nothing else. Yet these consequences in- clude nearly every ailment with which we are familiar. Even influenza seldom attacks any save those whose blood is first poisoned by indigestion and dyspepsia. And as to that nugget of gold ore ? Ah, pos.—Gold is worthless until it is manufactured. Food is useless unless it is digested. Betwszo the ore and the vase is workman. Between food and strengtk also a workman —the stomach.

div.p: NORTHERN UNION.
LANCASHIRE SECTION.

At a meeting of the Lancashire section in Manchester on Thursday night, J. Acton, of Widnes, for striking a player in the Salford match last Saturday was suspended up to and including October let. The following import- ant recommendations were drawn up for submission to the General Northern Union Committee :—SVhen a player wishes to serve a new club he may do so provided be obtains a letter from his old club stating that they hay, newer to give or withhold the transfer at their ab- solute discretion. If from any cause an inquiry be held. this union shall have power to order the payment of the costs of such inquiry and of the clubs and witnesses as it may think fit, if the transfer is between clubs in the same county to which the club belongs shall deal with the matter, but if the transfer be from a club in one county to a club in another county the matter shall be dealt with by the North Union Committees. This union may grant power to recognised governing bodies to increase the stringency of this rule, provided such alterations be submitted to and approved by it. The game of the Lancashire and Yorkshire match on ' November 21 was fixed on the Oldham ground,the same as last season. The date unfortunately is the same as that for the match between the two counties under Rueter 'anion laws. DEATH OF AN OLD RESIDENT AT THELWALL.

Many will regret to hear of the death of Mr. William Wright, landlord of the Pickering Arms, Thelwall. Mr. Wright, who was in his 62nd year, died on Monday night, after an illness of only two or three days' duration. He had lived in Thelwall for about 20 years during which time he had formed an extensive circle of friends both in Thel- wall and the district. POLICE COURT MISSION WORK.

Mr. C. W. Harris, of Lichfield, has been selected out of 61 applicants by the Diocesan Executive of the C.E.T.S. for the post of Police Court Missionary at the Wigan County Petty Sessions, Newton Petty Sessions, &c., and he will commence work at once. He will thus relieve Mr. Henry Taylor,the Warring- ton missionary, from attending the Newton Court, which he has done for four years.

div.head: MUSIC IN THE PARK.
div.p: MUSIC IN THE PARK.

The bandstand at the Park was occupied on Sun- day by the St. Paul's Church brass band, under the conductorship of Mr, R. Smith. There was a large attendance. The programme was as follows : Hymn, " Dresden " (J. Frost); quick march, " Bruns- wick " (J. Jubb) ; selection, " Maritana " (W. V. Wallace); overture, " Symphonia " (Victor Buot) ; " Kyrie " and "Gloria," from the "12th Mass" (Mozart) ; anthem, " To Thee, 0 Lord " (Metcalfe) ; "God Save the Queen." THE RECENT ACCIDENT AT MESSRS. CROSFIELDS' WORKS.

We understand that the employas of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited, have raised amongst themselves a handsome sum towards assisting the widow and children of their fellow workman, Henry Bristol Jackson, who met with a fatal accident in attempting to enter a hoist whilst in motion at the works on the Ist instant. Mr. Thomas Rigby acted as secretary to the fund, and the appeal met with a ready response from the men, and a sum of £l2 17s. 6d. was raised, which has been forwarded to the widow, together with a vote of condolence in her sad and sudden bereave- ment. This sum is in addition to and apart from what the firm had previously done for the widow. The secretary wishes to tender his sincere thanks to the subscribers.

GOOD TRAIPLARY AT LATCHFORD.

The Bonehill Branch Lodge of the 1.0.G.T. held their weekly .meeting in the Temperance Hall on Monday evening. Bro Councillor Ellison presided. There was an excellent attendance of members and visitors. Communications having been read and other business transacted? the programme was pro- ceeded with, which consisted of a paper, entitled "happiness," by Bro. F. A. Jenkins, which was lim- tened to with great interest. Bro. A. Ford, in open- ing the discussion, moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Jenkins, and in a lengthy speech Bro. J. J. Corbett seconded it, and it was well supported by Bros. H. Fletcher, H. Blease, B. Few, A. Hampton and the Chairman. The essayist suitably responded, and the meeting terminated. QUOITS.-A WARRINGTON PLAYER AT WINSFORD. A large number assembled at Winsford Railway Hotel enclosure on ?Saturday to witness a quoiting match between T. Hatton, Winsford, and J. Bryce, of Warrington. The conditions were to play a game of 101 points up. Bryce to stand 19 yards and Hatton 18 yards, any weight of quoits, for a stake of £5O. Both are well known players, and a fort- night ago Hatton defeated Woodward, of Radcliffe, by a single point, for £5O at the same place. Tbe betting closed at 5 to 4 on Hatton, but after Bryce had got one in at the first end the betting changed to evens. The came was even until the scores were called Hatton 20, Bryce 15. From this point the local pitcher began to forge ahead, and reached 30 to 18, 41-22, 50-24, 61-25, 71-32, 90-43, and 91-41, and eveutually scored a ready victory by 54 points,the full scores being—Hatton,lol ; Bryce, 47.
TILE APPOACHING MARRIAGE OF MAJOR W.ll. WALKER.

In connection with the approaching marriage of Major W. H. Walker, of Liverpool, and Miss Sophie Sheridan, of Frampton Court, Dorset, which takes place t the close of this month, Major Walker has made arrangements fot festivities in the park ad- joining his residence, Gateacre Grange, on the Ist of October in celebration of the happy event. In- vitations will be sent to about 2,000 employes of the firm of Peter Walker and Son, Limited, and to the tenants on the estate,and they, with their wives or sweethearts, will be entertained to luncheon in the grounds. In the evening the park will be thrown open to the villagers, who will join the general company in witnessing a grand display of fireworks. Light refreshments will be served dur- ing the day to the guests, and neither pains nor ex- pense will be spared to provide amusements and games in which both young and old can take part.

On Tuesday afternoon, the marriage of Mr. Charle3 Jones, eldest son of Mr. John Jones, of Preston Brook, and Miss Annie Ryder, eldest daughter of the late Mr. Joseph Ryder, of Preston Brook, was celebrated at the Daresbury Parish Churen, a very large congregation being present to witness the interesting ceremony. The Vicar offici- ated. The bridesmaids were Miss Ellen Ryder (sister of the bride), and Misses Ethel and Mary Jones (sisters of the bridekroom). Mr. Fred. Jones acted as best man, and the bride was given away by Mr. Henry Ryder. Copious showers of rice were thrown over the happy pair as they left the church for their residence at Daresbury, where a large com- pany at down to the usual wedding breakfast. Shortly after, the newly-married couple left Dares- bury amidst the hearty congratulations of everyone present for Scarborough, where the honeymoon is to be spent. They were the recipients of many presents.

div.head: SERIES OF SMALL FIRES.
div.p: A SERIES OF SMALL FIRES.

About 9.45 on Sunday night, the fire-bell was rung and two or three minutes later the Fire Brigade turned out under the command of Superin- tendent Turner. It was said at first that the con- fiagation was at the General Post Office, but the rumour was quickly dispelled when information was received at the hre-engine station to the effect that the men were to proceed to Latchford. It was stated that the shop of Mr. T. Green, greengrocer, was on fire, but on the brigade and engine arriving th?.re it was found that owing to an accident the bedroom curtains had become ignited but the flames had soon been extinguished. The services of the brigade were, therefore, not required.—en Monday afternoon, Mr. Thomas Brookes' chipped potatoe shop in liewsey-street was observed to be on fire. Information was at once conveyed to the fire engine station. The firemen were quickly on the scene, and the fire was speedily got under subjection. The damage done was very slight, and does not ?,xceed £3. The cause of the rant break is unknown.—A fire bloke out at the house of Mr. Jackson, baker, Pinner's-brow, at 10.20 the same night. The brigade was sooa at work, and got the flames under at 11 o'clock. The fire was caused by the falling of a lighted lamp on some paper. The damage to the stock and property is estimated at abont £5O.
CUTLBRIC and Bleetro-Plated GOODS.—GARLAND, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. WARRINGTON FORESTERS AT CHESTER.

On Saturday, the officers and some of the mem- bers of the Court Mercy of the Warrington district held their annual picnic, to Chester. Although a severe thunderstorm broke out at the time ap- pointed to start, a goodly number put in an appear- ance at Bank Quay station, and on arrival at Chester the storm had abated but slightly. However as the afternoon progressed a change for the better took place, and the various places of interest in the city were visited with comfort. Many of the party made an inspection of the Cathedral, others en- joyed a sail up the river to Eecleston Ferry, also visiting Eaton Hall—indeed no. place of any impor- tance being neglected. At 5.30 the party sat down to an excellent repast prepared by Bro. L. J. Jones, the host of the Red Lion Hotel, and a prominent member of Chester Forestry. At the social function afterwards Bro. G. May bury apologized for the ab- sence of Bro. B. Hulse, secretary of the Chester district. Bro. G. Smith, hon. treasurer to Court Mercy, spoke of the pleasure these annual outings provided, and remarked that they had a tendency to still further cement the good feeling which al- ready existed between Foresters. Notes of thanks were passed to the host and hostess, after which the party made their way to the station, Warring- ton eventually being reached at 9.15. All expressed themselves highly pleased with the days outing, and a compliment was passed to the managers for their enuarours to make.the picnic a success.

div.head: ARMENIA..
div.p: ARMENIA..

There was an average attendance at the meeting of this society on Sunday afternoon. Mr. J. Haley was chairman and in his address referred to the Armenian atrocities. He said he thought the time had come for the workingmen of this country, irrespective of creeds or political parties, to speak out in condemnation of the cruelties that were being perpetrated by the Turks with Use sanction and connivance of the Sultan. He believed that the present English government only needed the assurance that the people had made up their minds on this question to enaNe them to act with a firm hand and a determination that these horrible massacres should coale to an end. If they as a society believed in the brotherhood of man as implied in their motto it was their duty to take the initiative in this matter in War- rington. He suggested as a step in that direction that the society should send a petition to Lord Salisbury on the matter.—The Rev. John Yonge at the conclusion of the meeritie, in alluding to the Chairman's remarks, said they were timely and well said. He took it that every- one of them who read their newspipers had not been able to do so recently without feelings of indignation at the infamous monarch who was crushing down his Christian subj,cts in the empire of Turkey. He (Mr. .Yonge) felt perfectly sure that at last the temper—or at least the spirit—of this country was rising, and before very long they would see a marked expression of feeling all over the land.He hoped that Warrington would not b• behind in that particular kind of work. (Applause.) He believed it was contemplated by some in the town to have a meeeing for the purpose of the discussion of that great and grave question. He hoped the Mayor would take the lead in tio • matter, and he further hoped that any word of his (Mr. Yonge's) might reach his ears and move his heart. Their human sympathies were above political considerations, and they would be wanting in humanity to say nothing of Christianity if they did not speak out —and speak out promptly—by a movement that would tend to stop the great massacres which were going on in • Turkey. For the present he would suggest that a peti- tion mieht be sent up from that P.S.A. Society.—Mr. Thomas King, of Manchester, delivered the address for the afternoon, in which he urged his hearers to set a good example to their fellows, and not to place tempta- tion in the way of anyone. The service was also taken part in by Mr. C. T. Owen. It was announced that 3S new members had joined that afternoon, bringing the total membership to 1.000.

div.head: WYCLIFFE COCKHEDGE MISSION.
div.p: WYCLIFFE COCKHEDGE MISSION.

The Sunday school anniversary services in connection with this mission were held on Sunday, and were of a most successful cbaracter. The preacher for the occa- sion was Mr Alfred Cornev,of Warrington, and his dis- courses cv(•re much appreciated. The Sunday school children were present at the morning service. Special hymns were sung,and the choir sang "Come unto Me." In addition to the sermon, Mr. Corney delivered a brief, but interesting address to the children. The afternoon service consisted of the performance of a service of song, entitled " Time Reformation, or the life•work of Martin Luther." Mr. Richard Travis conducted, and the chil- dren sang remark ,bly well. The connective read- ings were given by Mr. A. Corney. Solos were sung by Miss Pemberton, Miss Senior, Miss Rushton, Mr. Lightfoot and Mr. Barton. At the evening service, the mission room was crowded. Mr. A. Corney, again preached. The musical portion of the service was improved by the assistance of an orchestral band. A festival anthem entitled" Great is the Lord" was sung in addition to the "Sanctus," "To Deum,"and a chorus, "Round about the starry throne." Collections were tak-n at each service on behalf of the Renovation Fund. The room had been decorated for the occasion with plants and flswers by a nnmber of teachers in the Sunday school.

Two events have almost entirely The Events of the Week. monopolised public attention this week. One of these events is

the agitation en behalf of the afflicted Armea ians Which has within the last few days developed into Vigorous national protest against the infamies of the SULTAN Of TURKEY. The other event is the UR- 'exPected and startling arrest of four American- Irishmen who were, it is alleged, engaged in pro- rnoting a dynamite plot of a sensational character. .With regard to the agitation, it is now clear that the:supposed "apathy" of the people of this coun- try in reference to the Eastern horrors that was lamented by many people during last week, was really in the nature of a calm before a storm. The English people have, it is now evident, bean deeply moved by the tragic story of massacres I 1 the Turkish Empire. The old spirit which has been stirred in times past on behalf of struggling autionalities has been thoroughly roused by the sufferings and helplessness of the Armenians. All over the country meetings are being held and resolutions are passed which certainly lack nothing in the way of vigour or directness of language. In this agitation the national opinion 13 practically unanimous. Everybody agrees in abhorring the atrocities, and in urging upon the ver nm en t to endeavour to find out some I:aethod of putting an end once for all to these too frequent manifestations of Turkish barbarity. In several towns meetings of the inhabitants mai- Vened by the Mayors have already been held, and during the next few days many similar meetings will be held in various parts of the country. Mr. GLADSTONE has given a conditional consent to at- tend a meeting at Liverpool, and it is not at all improbable that the voice of the "Grand Old Man" will again be the most potent instrument in arousing the country as it was in the case of the Bulgarian atrocities. It may, therefore, now be said that so far as the public opinion of this coun- try is concerned Lord SALISBURY is armed with a full mandate to use all the resources at his cora- taand, diplomatic or warlike, in order to protect the Christians of Turkey from the insensate fury Of the Sultan. The position of the Premier is one of extraordinary responsibility, and it will test his statesmanship to the utmost. Is he lowered to act with or without the "Concert 4. Europe" --a "concert" which seems to 11 ekdly out Of tune and badly in need of a leading mind. If we may accept the opinions expressed in Austrian and German newspapers there will be no effective interference on the part of united Europe even if the Sultan openly decreed the extermination of every Armenian Man, Woman and child. Some of the German news- Papers declare with true Bismarkian brutality that the whole Armenian nation is not worth the life Of one Pomeranian grenadier. Language of this sort can,it is evident, have no other result than to alacourage the Sultan in carrying out his nefarious schemes. If the Armenians are to be saved from the bludgeons of their fanatical enemies, it will have to be impressed upon the Sultan that this kuntry is prepared to interfere by force if neces- sary either with or without the assistance of any Other Power. ABDUL HAMID has always hitherto Yielded to the display or the serious threat of force. It is the one argument which he under- stands or cares for and it depends largely upon Lord SALISBURY whether or not it is used on the present occasion. With reference there has, as to the arrest of the dynamiters yet, been very little information given to the public as to the charges that will be brought against them. They may or they may not have harboured designs against the TSAR on his visit to England, but considering the easy manner in Which the police almost simultaneously laid their hands upon the whole group they must be a very triple or a very clumsey kiad of conspirator. It iS said that the detectives of Scotland-yard hold a Poor opinion of dynamiters in general, and if that he so their professional contempt for this criminal fraternity will probably be deeper than ever after their recent experience. The stupidity of the Present " plot" seems to be only equalled by its futility and wickedness.

The extremely heavy rainfall which has continued for the past three wetics is baling no good for local farmers, in most cases second hay and wheat. barley and oats crops are lying in the fields and the weather has been so bad that some cf the corn has not even been set up in sheaves. Much of the Produce is now hardly worth getting in, as it has been lying so long, so that for many, a bad harvest Will have been experienced. In these times of agricultural depression a bad harvest is more felt by the farmer than the clnsunaer whose wants are cehiefiy supplied from abroad.

Dr. Adams has adopted a practical way of providing the Dutton Workhouse boys With muscular exercise by offering to supply R football on condition that the chairman of the Board :of Guardians starts the first game by kicking off. The doctor expresses an opinion that the boys need exercise quite as much as the boys of or fortunate parentage and with his expression Utost people will agree. There are a few people who look upon all outdoor games with a doubtful eye, and these are the only likely objectors to the in- toration at the Workhouse. Anyhow the Board have decided to provides field, and the game will be countenanced by the Chairman who will kick OIL

The action of the Runcorn Guardians in detain- lug tramps two days has called forth the approval of the Local Government Board who 'are endeav- ouring to secure a general uniformity in treatment. filo far we are in a position to say that the new order of things has made a slight reduction in the 4Umber of visitors "put up" at Dutton workhouse.

We understand that a prominent member of the IttincornTistrict Council was defeated in committee trying to establish a project for the provision of electric light for the town. Councillors are prone to be rather backward in dealing with improve- ttents,and the idea was rejected owing to the town tot being in a position to bear the cost of the in- 'atallation ; yet it sometimes happens by virtue of borrowing powers and favoutable circumstances (which are present in this case) tha`:, improvements eq)st the town little or nothing.

div.head: ILLNESS" OF DR. MCDOTIIIILL
div.p: ILLNESS" OF DR. MCDOTIIIILL

We are pleased to be able to state that Dr. McDougall,. who has recently undergone a serious ilium, is now recovering as rapidly as can be expected under the cir- cumstances. PILLIARD HANDICAP AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

The executive of the Runcorn Liberal Club have ar- ranged a billiard handicap and also a tournament for the coming season.As there are good entries for the two events, they are likely to provide amusement for the club frequenters until well up to Christmas.
SEVERE THUNDERSTORM.

On Saturday another very severe thunderstorm passed over Runcorn, Widnes and district. The storm com- menced about one o'clock and for over a hour vivid flashes of lightening were followed by heavy thunder- claps. No damage has been reported in the town, but a cow was killed in a field at Sutton. The rainfall dur- ing the past few weeks has been very heavy.
NAtiliow ESCAPE FROM DROWNING; AT -RUNCORN,

On Tuesday evening a child belonging to Harry Seaalley,a boatman employed by Messrs. Speakman and Co., had a narrow escape from drowning at Runcorn. The boat was moored in the canal at Top Locks, and it is supposed that the child either fell from the toat or the canal side. Anyhow, the first intimation of the danger of the child was in arose from its screams while in the water, and a boy on the boat hearing th2m quickly ran and brought the child out. As it was then insensible. Efforts had to be made to restore it,:and with some diffi• culty the efforts were successful.

div.head: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH HARVRST FFSTIVAL RUNCORN.
div.p: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH HARVRST FFSTIVAL RUNCORN.

The first service in connection with the annual harvest festival took place in the Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, on Thursday night. The church was beautifully and appropriately adorned with the choicest of harvest pro- ducts and reflected great credit on the ladies who attended for the purpose of decorating. Special music was given by the choir. The Rev. Canon Woodrow of Ormskirk preached an effective sermon. The collection taken together with the collections to be taken at the continued services on Sunday go to the augmentation of the Curates fund. DRUNKENNESS AT RUNCORN, A 44TH APPEARANCE._ _ _

On Thursday at the Runcorn Police Court before Messrs. F. J. Norman and S. Taylor C.C. Ellen Gandy was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mersey- street, Runcorn, on September 16th. P.C. Wylie proved the case, and it was stated that prisoner had appeared before the magistrates 44 times. In consideration of this lamentable fact prisoner was sent to gaol for one month.---At the same court, Annie Miry Connolly who is also known under the name of Mercer was fined 20s. and 6s. 4d. costs for disorderly behavioar the previous night in High-street Runcorn. P.C. Gregory proved the case.

div.head: RIINCORN CYCLISTS AT CHESTER PARADE.
div.p: RIINCORN CYCLISTS AT CHESTER PARADE.

A good number of the Runcorn Cycling Club, turned out on Wednesday afternoon. Delamere was the first place visited and after tea, which was served at the Abbey Arms, the cyclists remounted and went on to Chester. Here a number of the party took part in a parade, held under the auspices of the County Club. It may be said that the Chester parade was very success- ful, though the bad condition of the roads somewhat marred their proceedings. After the parade a dance was held in the Market Hall, for cyclists in costumes so that with a so well arranged programme of amusements the Runcornians spent a pleasant afternoon and evening —The Saturday section of the Runcorn Club abandoned. their run, owing to the unfavourable condition of the weather. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITT BE.

This committee met in the Town Hall, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening, present in the chair Mr. W. Handley, together with Messrs. T. Riley,J. Pritchard,and the Rev. Dr. Gaetaldi, and Mr. J. D. Jones (librarian). Arrange- ments were made for the" Library Lectures," the first three lecturers being Dr. Bowman, Mr. W. Handley, and Mr. Argent (Liverpool) who will deal with "Three Famous Books,"" Hock Savage,a study in local history," and" Music,how our fathers played and sang" respec- tively. Accounts amounting to £2B Bs. id. were passed for paynaent.The following gifts were received :—by Mr. W. Handley "Queen of Love" (Baring Gould), Rev. C. Voicey (author) ; "Testimony of the four gospels concerning Christ," Sir J. T. Brunner ; " Parliamentary report of Common and Shlrt Titles Bill," together with library reports from Layton and Northwich. The librarians report showed that the receipts with library rate (£5O) were £5O 18s., and after paying salaries and other expenses there was a balance in hand of £44 15s. During the month 1,890 books were lent being an in- crease of 343 on the corresponding period last year and 31 books were lent for reference. RUNCORN ANGLING SOCIETY.t

This newly formed society is giving evidence of be- coming a thriving institution. With a capital list of officers and a good membership of enthusiastic devotees of the piscatorial art, there is every reason to predict a prosperous future for it. On Wednesday afternoon, under the auspices of the society, the first fishing match was held in the Shropshire Union Canal at Ellesmere Port. About 12 competitors took the bank side and for two hours endeavoured to lure to tempting bait the fishy denizens of the canal. The weather was decidedly unfavourable, as rain fell for the best part of an hour. At weighing in time Mr. E. John- stone was placed first with a handsome roach, weighing 11i ounces while next in order were Mr. George Hayes, Mr. John Bate, Mr. Samuel Bailey and Mr. W. Coventry all of whom qualified for prizes. Despite the unfavourable weuther the outing was thoroughly enjoyed, and all the competitors were satis- fied with the afternoon's sport.—lt may be mentioned that the society have secured fishing rights over the old nasal near Runcorn, and while there is already a fair amount of fish in it they intend to stock it during the next close season.

The services at St. Edward's Catholic Church, Run- corn, on Sunday, were specially devoted to asking for divine assistance on behalf of the persecuted Armenians in Turkey. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi in brief addresses explained that it waa high time some of the European Powers interfered so as to put a stop to the horrible carnage at present going on in Constantinople for the extermination of the Christian Armenians. He showed how England and Italy seemed to have manifested themselves ready for action, and spoke of the pity it was that the Oriental question was not properly settled in 1855, or in 1877, for if so the horrors recently wit- nessed would have been impossible. Mr. Gladstone had called the Sultan an assassin, but that word was too mild an expression. Considering the hellish thirst for blood be had displayed by his deeds, he was an arch- demon. He (Dr. (Jastaldi) prayed, if the carnage con- tinued, that God Almighty might inspire this noble nation, in conjunction wi'la others,to not simply remon- strate in language, but to show proof of their determin- ation that the massacres shall cease by the bombard- ment of Constantinople if necessary. This desire was already beginning to be manifested by the people of England, and they knew the old adage," Vox populi, vox Dei," the voice of the people is the voice of God. Further procrastination on the subject would add to the history of Europe another page of disgrace and shame.
RUNCORN TONIC SOLFL PnizE CHOIR.

On Monday evening last the members of the above choir held a social evening in the Ellesmere-street school room. A good.start was made at 7.30 with an excellent programme consisting of songs, games, &c. The laAies of the committee,under the direction of Mrs. John Stubbs provided ample refr:Aaments, and their efforts were well appreciateu. During the evening songs were sung by Miss R. Edwards and Messrs. S. Harrison and J. Brown, that hy Miss Edwards earning a well-deserved encore. Miss Mabel Pope, who was the accompanist, also gave a pianoforte solo which she executed with such taste and skill as tO, be called on for an encore. A special feature, which added greatly to the evening's pleasure was au address by Mr. F. J. Norman, the presi- dent of the society, Ho was very .grateful to the choir for the honour they had done him in electing him to such a position, and Assured them that his interest in the choir had always been great,and that he would do what- ever he could to encourage them in their new work. He referred to the good work done by the choir in the past and thought that a good future lay before them. He was pleased to note that they had decided to strengthen their ranks by the admission of staff readers, and hoped that their desires would be gratified. In placing two miscellaneous concerts in their programme for the present season Mr. Norman thought the committee had taken a decided step in the right direction. He thought that the public would appreciate the step, as tbay pre- ferred simpler music to high-class works vfhich they could not understand. Mr. Norman's remarks were much appreciated •by the company, and on his bidding them good-night they struck op the old song " He's a jolly good fellow." Altogether a very pleasant evening was spent aid the proceedings closed at eleven,everyoae expressing themselves delighted with the evening's pastime. A good season is being looked forward to and it is hoped that all members will stick to their guns and help to make th;n,gs succeed.

div.head: EXAMINER SAITTIW AY, SEPTEMBER 19 lag.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SAITTIW AY, SEPTEMBER 19 lag.
RUNCORN BOARD OF' GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday at the Dutton Worktouse present—Mr. J. Xnowles (chairman), the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., A. R. Norman, T. Lea, and S. Yar- wood, together with the members of the Rural District Council with Mr. Ashton (clerk), and. Mr. G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: FOOTBALL FOR TEM BOYS
div.p: FOOTBALL FOR TEM BOYS

The Master reported that the Medical Officer of the House had promised to provide a football for the boys to develope their muscular powers on condition that the Chairman kicked off the first game. The House Com- mittee recommended that the offer be accepted and the Guardians ratified that recommendation outside.

div.head: SCHOOLS FOR THE CHILDREN.
div.p: SCHOOLS FOR THE CHILDREN.
The Master reported that during the fortnight 13 in- fants had been sent to Preston-o'th-Hill school.

The Clerk explained that he had seen Mr. Linnaker, clerk of the Dutton School Board, who told him that there had been a meeting of the Board, and the membeTs did not seem inclined to accept the girls. _ _ _ . _

- Mr. Taylor asked if they had power to refuse them. The Chairman, replying, stated that he would not like to put the Board to any expense. The Clerk explained that there were only three chil- dren eligible to go there. If they knew that, perhaps the Board would accept them. Would it not be well to call a meeting of the committee appointed to deal with the subject so that they could see Mr. Linaker and give him that information. _ _ _
Mr. Heywood suggested that they write to Mr. Linaker and ask him to get the Board to accept the children.

Mr. Brandreth felt they were not giving proper atten- tion to the children and if any father or mother outside did not send their chilaren they would be summoned. This had been going on for three months. Mr. Baxter said they could not admit 10 or 12 chil- dren without enlarging Dutton Schools. The building was ouly made to accommodate 0 children and they had experienced hard work in keeping the average at- tendance to that so as to save enlarging school. _ _ .
It was decided that the Clerk should write to Mr. Linaker pointiag out that they had only three children in the hou3e eligible to attend Dutton School and ask for them to be admitted.
ASSISTANT RELIEVING OFFICER.
Mr. Lea proposed that Mr. Allison, the echoolmaster. be appointed assistant relieving officer at a salary of £5 per year.—Mr. Aaron seconded the motion which was carried.

div.head: FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE.

Mr.Reywood moved that the representative to attend the foothcoming conference of the North Western Poor Law be Messrs. Wright, Devonport, Woodward and the Clerk:and that their experses be borne by the Board.

_ . Mr. Aaron seconded the motion. Rev. Dr. Gastaldi moved as an amendment that the members who attended the conference should do so at their own expense. Mr. Yarwood seconded, saying the ratepayers should not be called upon to pay the expenses of the outing. He failed to see what benefits had accrued from the Board being represented. On the vote being taken 4 were in favour of the amendment and 12 supported the original motion which was carried.

div.head: FINANCILL
div.p: FINANCILL
Mr. Heywood submitted the report of the Finance Committee and showed that the amount of outdoor re- lief for Runcorn was £9O, Frodsham £2B and Budworth £2l. The balance in hand was £2,550.

div.head: ESTIMATES
div.p: ESTIMATES

The basis of contributions required from the overseers for the ensuing half-year was submitted, The total capital for the current half-year amounted to £11,411 and the nett probable expenditure estimated at £8,843, which showed a balance at Michaelmas of £2,568. The probable expenditure during the ensuing half-year as set out in the detailed estimates was common charges £2,300, county rate £4,043, balance and contingency £3,500, making a total of £7,843. The total amount required after deducting the probable balance in favour of the townships at Michaelmas 1896, was £7,275. The rateable value of the Union was £242,272, an increase of £1,578, as compared with the corresponding period of laqt year. A rate of lid. in the £ would produce £7,571, and it was recommended that a call for the sum of £27,275 be made upon the overseers being the same as the corresponding period of last year. The foregoing calculations were subject to alterations which might be made in valuation lists, previous to the contribution orders being signed as there were several new and sup- plemental valuation lists to be rec6ived. Mr. Heywood moved the adoption of the estimates, and Mr. Woodward seconded the resolution which was carried.

div.head: TREATMENT OF VAGRANTS.
div.p: TREATMENT OF VAGRANTS.

The Lecal Government Board writing on the 3rd inst. expressed satisfaction that the Guardians had in- structed the Master cf the Workhouss to conform to the regulations with respect to the detention of vagrants contained in the order of the Bth December, 1892.—Mr. Baxter : Has the order been going on long ?—The Chairman: Only a month.—Mr. Baxter : How is it going on P—The Chairman: There is a slight reduction in the number of vagrants.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF A LADY MEMBER.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF A LADY MEMBER.
Mrs. S. Renton,of Frodsham,havinf; removed to Clay- ton-le-Moore,Lancashire,resigned her post on the Ladies' Visiting Committee. The resignation was formally ac- cepted.
RUN CORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of this board was held at Dutton Warkhouse on Tuesday, present Mr. J. Mclntyre J.P., (chairman) Admiral Parry, J.P., Messrs. H. E. Heywood, S. Woodward, J. Brundrett, C. Roylance, T. Baxter, C.C., W. Ellison, Joseph Spencer, J. S. Jones,W. Bradford, J. B. Chadwick. E. Aaron, T. Wright, T. Lewis, J. Weir, J. Knowles. J. Whitlow, J. M. Williams, J. Darbyshire, A. Greenway, J. Ashton (clerk) G. Ashton (deputy clerk) .1. Farrington (nuisance in- spector), Diggle and Swinton surveyors.

div.head: ISOLATION QUESTION.
div.p: THE ISOLATION QUESTION.

The Urban District Council of Datinfield invited the Roncorn Council to be represented at a proposed confer- ence re as to the County Councils action re the County medical officers scheme of isolation hospitals.—A resolu- tion was proposed stating the Council was willing to take action in the matter and the resolution was carried.
THE DARESEURY HIGHWAY BOARD LOANS.

With reference to the question for the re-payment of the loan of £2,700 raised by the late Daresbury Board the Local Government Board stated that the matter was one to be settled by agreement or arbitration under the provisions of section 63 of the Local Government Act. 1894.—The Clerk was instructed to send a copy to the clerk at North w i ch.
ESTIKATES.-THE NEW ELM

The basis of contributions required from the overseers for the ensuing half-year ending Lady Day 1894 was submitted for consideration being calculated on the rate- able value as per valuation lists in force. The total capital for the current half-year ending Michaelmas 1896 amounted to £4,710 and the nett probable expenditure was estimated at £2 649 which showed a balance at Michaelmas of £2,061. The probable expenoiiture dur- ing the ensuing half-pear was—general expenses, public health £746, highway expenses £2,66B,balance and con- tingency fund £2,000, total £5,414. The total amount necessary for the ensuing half-year was £5,214 and after deducting the probable balance in favour of the parishes at Michaelmas 1896 the amount by contribution crders for the overseers was £3,353. The estimate for highway expenses was based upon the surveyors estimates for the year according to which the probable expenditure for highway expenses would be 6d. in the £ on the rateable value of the district. A call of 2-.1-d. in the £ was levied last half-year and it was now proposed to make a call of aid. in the L. It was also 'proposed to make a call of led, in the £ for sanitary purposes making the call for the year equal to those made during last year. The rateable value of the district was £183,818 being an in- crease of £2,776 as compared with toe corresponding period of last year. A rate of 4A,1. in the £ would pro- duce £3,446,and it was recommended that a call for the sum of £3,353 be made upon the overseers.—The esti- mates were adopted.

THE SEWAGE AT WILDERSPOOL. The Clerk presented a lengthy report dealing with arrangements arrived at by himself and the Town Clerk of Warrington, as to the sewage outfall at Wilderspool. Ho pointed out that the agreement was drawn up and signed at the: time of the Local Government Board inquiry for the extension of the borough of Warrington. At the pregent time the Town Clerk of Warrington desired to insert words which gave the agreement wider meaning and were calculated to involve the Runcorn Rural Counoil in mcre expense than was contemplated. —After hearing the Clerk's statement his action was upheld by the Council.—Mr. Heywood, while comment- ing upon the I own Clerk of Warrington's actiom in the raatter, said it would be better when the whole thing was settled in as open a manner as possible.

div.head: REAPPOINTMENT OF NUISANCE INSPECTOR.
div.p: REAPPOINTMENT OF NUISANCE INSPECTOR.

Mr. Heywood moved that Mr. Farrington be reap- pointed inspector of nuisances and inspector under the Dairies, Cowsheds. and Milkshopr Order, 1885, for one year ending the 29th day of September, 1897,at a salary of £l4O per annum, and that he be appointed inspector of canal boats for the same period, at a salary at the rate of £lO per annum.—Mr. Williams seconded this re- solution.

Mr. Aaron mewed as an amendment that the salary be increased to £l6O per year, and pointed out that the duties had been very much increased since the inspec- tor was appointed. He had had to attend a number of parochial committee meetings, and had a very large area to cover with no railway fares allowed. If they wanted a man to do the work well they would have to par him well for his services. Mr. Jones seconded, and stated the duties had in- creased fourfold, and the salary had not increased in proportion. Mr. Heywood and Mr. Williams accepted the amend- ment, which was carried by 9 votes to B.—Afterwards Mr. Brand reth moved that ths salaries of the officials be referred to the Finance Committee for consideration. This amendment was carried by 12 votes to 2.

div.head: CHINESE DISCOVERY OF AMERICA.
div.p: CHINESE DISCOVERY OF AMERICA.
A " PICrURESQUE TRADITION."

The visit of Li Hung Chang to America may be relied upon to revive here and there among geogra phicaf dilletanti the old fantastic theory of a Chinese discovery of America antedating the landing of Columbus by some 0,000 years, says the "New York Daily Tribune." Ac- cording to this picturesque tradition, which has been fostered by some savants and „more amateurs,there was a certain audacious Chinamau who sailed away about 500 years before the Christiart era across the "azure sea "ef the Oriental maps. Twenty thousand "Ii" to the westward he sailed, and at .last moored beside the kingdom of Fousang ; in other words,a land of remark- able vegetahle and still more remarkable peoples, to which some inedern research 'LNas been fain te apply the name of the American continent. Flatterers of Li Hung Chang may well pour into his ears their belief in a notion in which he is himself probably most willing to acquiesce. But it would be interesting to know if this eminent Statesman and personage from a highly " literary" nation knows the true value of such hypotheses. The point in question ia most effectively handled by M. Henri Cornier in the first number of a periodical of ethnographical and geographical research lately founded in Paris. In this " Journal de la Societe des Arn4ricanistes de Paris," there is a paper entitled " Etat Actuel de la Question du ' Feu-sang,' " wherein M. Cordier successfully appeals to eminent European authorities to prove that it is impossible to identify Fou-sang with America. That the Chinese may at some remote time have reached these shores he freely admits, but their Fou-sang is as yet, he protests, a terra incognita for the geographer and scientist. All the documents in the case, such as they are, belong among the most obscure and confusing ef Oriental literature, but in so far as their facts are comprehensible they point unmistakably to the existence of some land other than America in the Fousang of tradition. M.Cordier cites the latest impor- tant contribution on the subject, that of Dr. Gustave Schlegel, of Leyden, and the investigations of the latter mainly confirm his position. The value of this essay of M. Cordier's would be appreciated anywhere, con- tinues the journal, but it is especially gratifying to find it in a journal which has been established with a scholarly enthusiasm for the study of purely American themes. The aim of "La Socie:6 des Americanistes de Paris the scientific and historical study of America, and its inhabitants, from the earliest eras to the present day. The Duc de Loubat has inter- ested himself in the society, which has made him hon- orary president. MM. Ma ,pero and Oppert are honorary, vice-presidents, and many distinguished savants are as- sociated with them. Dr. Hamy, of the Institute, is pre- sident,and the three regular vice-presidents are Prince Roland Bonaparte,General Meredith Read, and the Mar- quis de Peralta. The secretary is M. Henri Cordier, the treasurer is the Marquis de Bassano,and the six members of the council are MM. Gabriel Marcel, Charles Maunoir, the Marquis de Nadaillac, Desire Pector, Felix Regamy, and Count Louis de Turenne d'Aynac.

div.head: MOTIVE POWER OF THE FUTURE.
div.p: THE MOTIVE POWER OF THE FUTURE.
THE APOTHEOSIS OF THE GAS ENGINE.

In" Cassier's Magazine" for August there is a very interesting article on "The Future :of Power Develop- ment," by George S. Strong. According to Mr. Strong no method of generating power can be compared for a moment, for economy and efficiency, with a gas engine. Great as have been the triumphs of gas in the past, it is quito recently that its application for purposes of loco- motien have been commercially profitable. Mr. Strong says :—Taking gas engines, which derive their energy from coal or other carbon gases or from hydro-carbon gas, we open up a comparatively new iield,for while the gas engine has been known and used for many years in a small way, and with remarkably good results as far as economy goes, it is only since a short time that its merits have been fully appreciated. It is now, with the introduction of new methods of gas production, by the use of by-product-saving appliances that go far towards paying the original cost of the fuel, and thus reducing the cost of the fuel gas to a very low figure, doing much to solve the problem of cheap and effective power. As these gases are low in illuminating qualities they are very much better suited to give the highest effi- ciency in the gas engine. Another gas that has recently been discovered has remarkable qualities under compres- sion, and can be reduced in volume 400 times at 800 pounds and when expanded will burn with twenty times its volume of air, requiring only 0•4 of a pound of it when compressed to develop one horse-power per hour Each cubic foot of it at this pressure weighs 30 pounds and,therefere,contains 75 H.-P. hours,being the greatest storage of energy ever known for a given weight. This opens a wonderful field for the development of power for motors for tramcars and other classes of motor vehicles, as well as pleasure boats. Gas eagines, working with this new fuel gas, are likely to have a very large use in all stationary work and for propelling boats, and it may not be beyond the boands of all possibility to drive ocean steamers and locomotives of the future by gas engines. A ton of soft coal will produce 125,000 cubic feet of Eas of 160 heat units, about 45 feet of which will produce a horse-power in a properly designed and well constructed gas engine, or about 2 777 H.-P. hours for each 2,240 pounds of coal. At the same time, about 90 to 100 pounds of sulphate of ammonia are recovered from this coal, which, at present, is worth about 50do1s. (£10) per ton, which, after paying all the cost of operating the producing plant and making the gas, yields about one cent. (id.) per pound. The gas from blast furnaces can also be used and is found to give wonderfully good re- sults, considering its poor quality. Recent discoveries in mechanical power transmission have made it possible to run a gas engine at full speed in one direction and vary the speed of the driven shaft from zero to full speed in either direction without frictional gearing and without appreciable loss of power. This makes the gas engine applicable to any purpose to, which the steam engine is suited, and makes it especially suitable for boats, Street cars, and motor wa.ggens. It is altogether more probable that the gas engine will be used direct as a locomotive, commencing with the smaller motors for tram-cars and motor waggons, and gradually grow in favour as its utility is demonstrated, until the full-fledged railway locomotive is developed, carrying its gas producer on a tender,entirely automatic inits operation. The fireman, as such will be done away with and become the engineer's assistant in oiling and looking after the operation of the machinery. This will bring the, coal consumption per horse-power per hour from about 5 down to about lb of a pound, and it will be done without adding greatly to the present first cost. For street car work, compressed gas with the gas engine makes it possible to run a car 750 miles with one charge and at a cost of less than one-third what it now costs to run the same car by electric motor, or one-third what it is likely to cost for the compressed air motor.

div.head: ODDFELLOWS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: ODDFELLOWS AT WARRINGTON.
ANNIVERSARY CELEBRATION.

_ The 35th anniversary of the Loyal Garibaldi Lodge, Warrington, was celebrated on Saturday. The members went for a drive to High Legl4 and Arley and returned ar little after six o'clock to partake of a knife and fork tea at the Little Horse Shoe Hotel, Horsemarket-street, Warrington. After tea a meeting was held, the Chair- man being the Past Provincial Grand Master P.P.G.M. Smith ; deputy chairman the Grand Master of the dig trict, Mr. 'F. Keight.—The Chairman proposed " The Queen and the rest of the Royal Family," the company rising and singing the National Anthem.—The Chairman then gave "The Army, Navy, and Auxiliary Forces," which was responded to by P.P.G.M. Sergeant Bramall. —A humorous sketch was rendered by Bro. Scarisbrick. --" The Order" was proposed by P.G. Hughes, and was responded to by the Grand Master of the Order (Mr. Jephcott), of Birmingham, who spoke at great length on the question of old age pensions. The Order, he said, numbered about 86 districts and about 556 lodg,es, and contained 57,000 adult members. There were also in connection with the district lodges 8,700 juvenile male and female members, making a total membership of 67,000.—A song was sung by P.O. Richardson.—" The Garibaldi Lodge" was proposed by D.G.M. Atkinson, and responded to by the Secretary (F. Dickinson).— There was a recitation by P.G.M. T. Knight. " Mark the Spot."—" 'The District" was proposed by P.G. Hill, and responded to by D.S. Joseph Crosby. In his remarks he said that up to 1886 the Warrington lodges belonging to the Macchester district in September of the year severed their connection with Manchester and became a district of their own, and with a nucleus of £2O granted by the Manchester district they formed a funeral fund. At the time the district comprised tOlidges, the "Garibaldi ' and the " Garibaldi Sons Lodge."' In the same year the "Garibaldi Sons Lodge "was dissolved, and the" Gari- baldi Lodge " became a district lodge. Up to 1890 the district was worked on the equal levy system, and with interested accumulated and money levied from the equal levy system the capital was raised to £lB9. At that time there was an alteration in the rules, and in six years, up to 1896, the capital had been raised to £32O.—P.G.M. T. Knight proposed the toast of " Kindred Societies," and P.G. Hughes responded to it.—A humorous sketch was rendered by Bro. Scarisbrick.—The meeting concluded about half-past ten. About 56 members joined in the proceedings.

At Liverpool Police Court on Tuesday Thomas Mont- gomery Joy was committed to the sessions for trial en a charge of obtaining stamps by means of false pretenses. Joy, it was shown had advertised that "Messrs. Joy and C 0.," being desirous of advertising the "Overland" ' cycle, would give away one ef their best £2O cycles to each of ten persons sending in the most words composed from the. letters in thi; world " Overland." In answer to the advertisement, which, it was contended, was of a wholly fraudiiir•nt nature, 5,000 letters containing pinny poetage stamps had been sent to the prisoner's effice, and 3,0?,0 mare. which had not been delivered, ROM now it the hands of the postal authorities,

div.head: I INTERESTING LOCAL MARRIAGE.
div.p: I INTERESTING LOCAL MARRIAGE.
DUTTON-GRIME.

The prettily situated village of Helsby was en fete on Thursday, the occasion being the marriage of Miss Edith May Grime, second daughter of Mr. Thomas Grime. of Clifton, Helsby, and carrying on business in Bridge-street, Warrington, and Mr. James Fairclough Dutton,eldest son of the late Mr, William Dutton,and of the firm of Messrs. J.and IV. Dutton,and of Messrs. Hesketh and Dutton,Sankey- street,Warrington. Both parties are well-known in the town and district,and considerable interest was taken in the marriage. A large number of persons —chiefly connected with the business establish- ments of the two parties at Warrington—journeyed to Helsby in order to witness the ceremony. Prior to proceeding to the church, an inspection was made of the future home of the bride and bride- groom, which has been given the name of Gorse Hill. It is delightfully situated a short distance up the hill and commands a fine view of the Welsh hills on the left, and also a panoramic view of a part of Cheshire. The rooms have been richly furnished, and the visitors were greatly pleased with their inspection of the house and the large collection of wedding presents. The number visit- ing the house was so great that they had to be conducted through the building in parties. The wedding ceremony. which was fully choral was timed to commence at 2.l in St. Paul's Church, Helsby, but long before that time the invited guests commenced to arrive, and when the bride entered the church, every seat in the sacred edifice was occupied. At the time appointed, the choristers proceeded to the entrance door of the church, and afterwards, headed by the Vicar (Rev. A. Spafford, M.A.) who conducted the service, they marched up the aisle singing "'1 he voice that breathed o'er Eden,' the congregation also joining in the singing. Shortly afterwards the bride arrived, and walked to the altar rails leaning on the arm of her father.. She looked exceedingly handsome in a dress with train, of white satin brocade, relieved with pearl trimming and lace. She wore a tulle veil and carried a beautiful shower bouquet. Her ornaments included a diamont pendant, the gift of the bride- groom. (She was given away by her father. There were four bridesmaids in attendance, viz. : Miss Amy Grime and Miss Line Dutton, sisters of the bride and bridegroom, and the Misses Elsie and Lucie Greening (nieces of the bride). The two first named wore dresses of yellow silk, trimmed with white chiffon and with chiffon fichus. They also wore large white felt hats with white plumes. Their bouquets were composed of white and yellow roses, and each had a diamond and pearl brooch, presented by the bridegroom. The two young nieces of the bride wore white silk frocks and large white felt hats. They looked very pretty, carrying satin slippers filled with marguerites and other flowers. Both received a present of a gold bangle from the bridegroom. Mr. William Dutton, brother of the bridegroom, fulfilled the duties of best man. During the service the 67th Psalm, "God be merciful to us," and the hymn "Thine for ever God of love," were sung. Mr. Hill presided at the organ and played appropriate music during the assembling of the congregation. As the wedding party left the Church, he played" The Wedding March.'s A reception was afterwards held at Gorse Hill and refreshments were dispensed in a marquee on the lawn. Between two and three hundred guests were present. A small orchestral band under the conductorship of Mr. R. it Pearson, of Warrington, discoursed sweet music. The wedding party and the bride and bridegroom were photographed by Mr. Thomas Birtles, of Sankey-street, Warrington. Later in the afternoon, the newly-married couple proceeded on their honeymoon, and they will visit Switzerland and the Italian Lakes. WILL OF MRS. HELEN M'CORQUODALE,

Probate hag been granted of the will, dated the 31st July, 1893, of Mrs.klelen M'Corquodale, of 11,Montague- terrace, Richmond, who died on the 17th April last,aged ninety-six years, the widow of Mr. Hugh M'Corquodal3, and daughter of Lord Edward Fitzgerald and his 'rife Pamela, who was a daughtee of MAdame de Geniis and Egalite Orleans. Probate of Mrs. M'Corquodale's will has been granted to Sir John Cowan, of Beeslack, Mid- lothian, Bart., surviving executor, the other executor, testatrix's brother-in-law, Mr. George M'Corduodale, of Newten-le-Willows, having died in the lifetime. She be- queathed to Alexandra Lucia Elizabeth and Mary Augusta M'Corquodale each and any two articles from her personal effects excepting the picture of Lady Edward Fitzgerald and her child; £l5O each to her com- panion, Helen Parrot,and her servant, Hannah Howard ; £25 each to two other servants, £lO to another, £5O to her goddaughter Helen Ellis, and £5O to Janet Augustua Mills. It was the intention of the testatrix to dispose of the portrait of Lady Edward Fitzgerald and some other articles by a separate paper, but no such paper had been found, and these will therefore go with her residuary estate to her servant, Hannah Howard. Mm. M'Corquodale's personal estate has been valued at £482 17s. id.
CROFT HORTICULTURAL 60CIETY. TWELFTH ANNUAL EXHIBITION.

The twelfth annual exhibition of the Croft Horticultu- ral Society was held in the Board School,Croft,on Satur- day. The inclemency of the weather prevented the at- tendance of many who had made up their minds to be present at the opening ceremony. Nevertheless the num- ber present testified to the fact that great interest is taken in the welfare of this society locally. The number of exhibits amounted to about 400, and the garden en- tries to 12. The number of members in the society is 23. Prizes were offered in the shape of copper kettles and other articles for the neatest and beat cottage garden. The president of the society is the Rev. H. I. Wadeson, and the committee is composed of the following gentle- men—Messrs. W. Fazakerloy, E. Monks, T. Abbey, 'l'. Bold, H. Jennion, W. Taylor, jun., J. Worthington, J. Green, George Aspinall,W. Birchall,James Shaw (chair- man), J,ihn Sanderson (treasurer), and J. Cawthorn° (secretary).

There were present amongst others—Captain Withing- ton, Mrs. Withingtan, Mr. Owen. Mr. and Mrs. Peter Ingham, Mr. and Mrs. J. Ca wthorne, Miss Smathern,Miss Clare, Mr. and Mrs. Hammond, Mr. E. Staley, and others.

Captain Wallington, in opening the show, said he had always taken an interest in the progress of the society, and had noticed with pleasure the improvement year after year. (Hear, hear.) It was more noticeable in the quality than in the quantity. He remarked on the splendid quality of the carrots which were displayed before them. In conseqnence of the inclemency of the weather the show was not so full as it deserved to be. He moved a vote of thanks to the judges, Messrs. Jack- son, Thomason, Gilbert Marsh and Harrison. _ _

After it had been seconded, Mr. Harrison, in reply, said he was very pleased to see the room so full. For eleven years he had come to judge for the show, and the progress made was something marvellous. He was pleased to see not only the old competitors there but new ones. (Applause.) Mr. J. Cawthorne hon. seeretarv, moved a vote of thanks to Captain Withington and otheis, which was seconded by Mr. Owen and carried. Captain Withington suitably responded, and said they must thank the lady judges of the children's bouquets of wild flowers, Mrs. Withington, of Culcheth Hall, and Miss Comber , of Middleton Hall. (Hear, I•ear.) Ho then announced the successful competitors of the best cultivated cottage gardens and the points gained by each. The names of these are-1, E. Monks, 74 ;2, W. Oakes, 72 ; 3, J Green, 68 ; 4, T Shaw, 65 ; 5, W Fazakc rley, 64 ; 6, William Birchall, 62. The judges of the cottage gardens were Mr H Jackson, bead gardener to the late Alderman Smith, Newton,and Mr R Ilanison. head gardener to Mr T J Gillespie, JP, Newton. The judges of vegetables were Mr Thomason, Croft, and Mr Gr March, Newton. THE PRIZE LIST.

div.head: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.
div.p: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held in this church on Sunday, when sermons were preached ny- the Rev. John Yonge. Witnin the communion rails a choice collection of flowers and plants was displayed, and gene- ally admired. At the morning service the preacher based his remarks on this text " Give unto the Lord, 0 ye kin- dreds of the peonle,give unto the Lordgiory and strength. Give unto the Lord the glory due unto His name;. bring an offering and come unto His courts- " Psalms 36; v. 7 and 8. Tee choir very effectively rendered the anthem " 0 taste and see" (Goss). Tuere was a large congre- gation at the evening service which was commenced by the intoning of the general confession.. Two anthems were exceedingly well sung. In the lira, "Ye shall dwell in the Laud." (Stainer), Mr.W.Hs Wallington was the soloist, and the quartette was taken, by Mrs. R.. H. Pearson, Miss F. Booth, Mr. Griffiths, and,M.r. Walling- ton. " The eyes 01 all wait on Thee" ,:itivey) waa the title of the second anthem. Mrs. Pearson very tastefully sang the soprano solo,, and in company with Miss Booth and Mr. Joseph Knowles she also sang in the trio. The singing throughout was exceptionally good. Mr. George Wallingtcn conducted the choirs, and Mrs. W. H. Payton presided at the organ. The Rev. John Yonge preached from- the words " The eyes of all wait upon Thee. and Thou gi vest them their.meat in due season, Thou openest Thine hand, and satisfieth the desire of every living. th' nia " (Psalm cxiv. 1.546). In the course of the sermon Mr. Yonge observed that he • took it they had all felt the wondrous thrill ct this glow— ing psalm of praise. Especially when life had brought to them some new and powerful consciousness-of divine goodness, they had been able to enter into the,f'salmist's. adoring feeling as be said, " I will extol Thee,. my Gods. 0 King, and I will bless Thy name for ever and • ever. Every day will I bless Thee, and I will praise Thy name for ever and ever." " The eyes of all wait upon Thee." Let that sentence remind them that night of that tunda-• mental fact ot life which they frequently so strangely forgot. They were utterly dependent creatures,' Even the most resourceful, the best provided, the most pros- perous and well-to-do were absolutely dependent.. " Every blessing we enjoy comes to us from God." They might fancy that because somebody left them a competency, or because by shrewdness and carefulness that therefore they became independ- ent, and so they would walk along life's path holding their heads pretty hip possibly giving themselves a good many airs; but ii they depended alone upon hu- man providence, their own or that of anybody else,they might find some day to their chagrin that the best in- vestments might fall in value and the grandest property might fall. If God in His bounty had liberally supplied their wants they should try to understand that Be had been committing the surplus to their care as trustees. Never let anyone forget his entire dependence upon God. Their very breath was in His hands. Health was His gift, every time the meal was before them on the table. be the fare plain and simple bread and butter, or be it dainties fit to put before a king, it was His hand that furnished the bounty, not their providence but His. They were dependent creatures, dependent every mo- ment upon Him, indebted every moment to Him. In conclusion Mr. Youge said there were four things that the good providence of God, as seen in annual hervests, or in personal experience, should produce in anyone of them. Be named them, as follows gratitude, trust, service, generosity. "Freely ye have re- ceived. freely give." Special collections were taken on behalf of the church funds, and an effort was msde to raise £6B in order to meet extraordinary ex- penses of the year and the extra cost incurred in supply- ing the pulpit during the pastor's illness. The collections at both services realised the satisfactory amount of 177 9a. 10d.

div.head: ST. CROSS, APPLETON THORN.
div.p: ST. CROSS, APPLETON THORN.

The eismbined dedication and harvest festival was duly observed in this church on Sunday. The weather was not all that could have been desired, an important item on these occasions, but it did not preveat large con- gregations from attending. The decoration of the church was as earefulty and tastetully undertaken as in times past, the staff of lady workers being as follows— Mrs. Ash, the Misses Ash. Holt, Minards, Barber, Sut- ton, Beswick, Hindley, and Preston. Tne large quanti- ties of flowers and fruits used in the decoration were, with a limited exception, contributed by the parishioners themselves. The music at the choral celebration was Simper in E. lat. The preacher at evensung was the Vicar. The Maguificat and Nunc Dialittis were sung to settings ley Sir John Stainer, and the anthem "The eyes of all wait upon Thee," by Edwin Clare. The anthem was not an easy one, but was carefully sung. The whole of. the services were extremely wel:end devotionally rendered, and the choir deserve gre.b credit for the trouble taken in the difficult task of getting up the music cozrectl7. The congregations, both at the morning and evening ser. vices, were large, at evensong particularly, and a large number of extra benches and chairs were required.

div.head: DARES BURY.
div.p: DARES BURY.

On Sunday, the harvest thanksgiving services were held in the Parish Church, when the sermons at both the morning and evening services were preached by the Rev. Canon Upperton, vicar of Tarvin,• and rural dean of Chester. Despite the inclemency of the weather the congregations were large, especially at the evening ser- vice. Special hymns, psalms, &c., were creditably ren- dered by the choir,and also the anthem "Sing ye merrily unto God our strength," the solo portions in whicn were sung by Messrs. Isaac James, William and John Oulton. As usual on this festival, the sacred edifice was most tastefully decorated with corn, fruit, flowers, &c.,. reflecting credit up-in those who had kindly undertaken the work. The Misses Litton were responsible for the chancel screen ; Mrs. Clark, Mrs. White, Mrs. Wood and Miss Seeker for the chancel and reredos ; Mr. D. Calder for the pulpit ; Mr. Owen, the lectern ; Misses M. E. Darlington, Hatton, Ishckson, and Mr. Hayward for the windows; while the belfry screen, which was much admired, was the work of Messrs. Hamblett, Oulton, DePrez, Clare and Priestly. The offertories at the close of each service were devoted to the support of the Sun- day schools at Daresbury. Moore, Hatton and Preston Brook, and realised about £ll.

div.head: ALLEGED DYNAMITE PLOT.
div.p: ALLEGED DYNAMITE PLOT.
IMPORTANT ARRESTS.

The practically simultaneous arrests of Tynan at Bou- logne, Bell in Glasgow,and Haines and Wallace at Rotter- dam wore due to the fact that the four men were sus- pected of being engaged in a conspiracy to carry out a series of of outrages with dynamite in this country. Tynan is said to have been arrested under a warrant issued against him for complicity in the Phcenix Park murders in 1882, while Belt is charged under a section of the Explosive Substances Act of 1883. Tynan was brought before the Deputy Public Prosecutor at Boulogne on Monday, but the proceedings were limited to the formal taking of evidence of arrest.and the establishment of Tynan's identity, which . he is said to have freely ad- mitted. An application for his extradition will be made in due course. Bell was brought before the magistrates at Glasgow on Tuesday and formerly remanded. The IThe house in which the two men Haines and Wallace , lived has been thoroughly searched,and materials for the manufacture of explosive bombs have been discovered• All four men have been most carefully" shadowed "for past. It is alleged that they had allied them- selves t witeh Russian Nihilists and foreign Anarchists for the purpose of perpetrating crimes of a most terrible nature in Great Britain. It;is even averred that a part lof their plot was an attempt to be made upon the life of the Czar during his coming visit ta the Queen. The police in Glasgow and London are busily engaged in preparing their case against .the men arrested on Saturday and Sunday last. Bell. the man apprehended in Glasgow, is said to have made a statement, in the course of which he.said his father waaa Scotchusan and his mother an Irishwoman. while he himself was born in the States. He describes himself as a stockbroker carry- ing on business in New York,. and declares that he came to Europe for a pleasure trip and,after visiting Antwerp,. Berlin,and London,arrived in Glasgow a week ago. He had intended to leave Liverpool on Viednesday for New York. While admitting that he is a member of a politi- cal societe in New York, he denies that ho is in any way' connectei with dynatnitards or conspirators of any kind. Beater's correspondent at Rotterdam paid a visit to the man Wallace in his cell on Tuesday. The prisoner refused to reply to any questions, and a similar attitude was ;maintained by the other prisoner, Haines. In a letter addressed to Wallace,and now in possession of the police the following passage occurs :—" If you do not care to go to Scotland, come to Boulogne, and we can then talk it over. e tCowardice cannot be tolerated among our brother's."

A SUSPICIOUS CASE.—John Birmingham. 18, Percival's Fold, was charged with being found in possession of a pair of leggings and unable to give a satisfactory account of the same. —Det. Sergeant Monaghan stated that at seven o'c ock the previous night he saw the prisoner in sompanv with several companions and his father and mother in Walker's Vaults, Bridge-street. Witness noticed that the prisoner was trying on a pair of leggings and offering them for sale. Witness questioned him as to how he became in possession of the leggings and he made different statements concerning them. At first he stated that he had had them given him in the breaking up of the Militia. He had served six years in the Militia and he stated that the authorities gave the leggings to him. Alter being further questioned, prisoner stated that a man named Duffey b ion Sing to ;be pottery works,had given them to him, and afterwards stated thae he had been three years in the Militia. The prisoner had been offering the leg- gings for sale in several places but the people knew they were. midtary leggings and would not buy them. He knew that hil had no right to be in possession of them.—P.C. Berry stater' that he was in company with D. ergeant Monaghan and col. roborated his statement.—P.s. Phillips said the prisoner haa no right whatever with the leggings. They were worth about 3s. 6d.—Prisoner was fined 20s. and Costs or one month's imprisonment.

THEFT OF HIS Femmes BIRD CAGE. —Thomas Braney. 18, Percival's Fold, was charged with stealing on Monday evening a bird cage the property of Michael Braney, his father. —Detective Barlow stated that he received a report from Michael Braney that his son had stolen his bird cage. He went to the house and round the prisoner lying drunk on the floor. On making inquiries he found that the bird cage had been sold by the prisoner for ninepence at Clare's shop in Q-olborne-street. property of the London and North•Westem Railway Com- panv.—Mr. Fama prosecuted on behalf of the Railway Com- pany, and said the circumstances of the ease were out of the usual run of larceny cases. On the 29th of July the two defendants were on EarlestJwn Station inteeding to proceed as passeng. ra to Warrington. At that time a goods train was standing in the station from Holyh ,ad bound for Man- chester In one of the trucks there was was a I.rge crate of fowls, and one of the bars becoming loose some of the fowls made their es ape from the crate. The defendants saw them escape and caught two of them, pocketed them, and sold them in Warrington When charged with having stolen the fowls they declared that they had not seen the fowls.— James Charles Ashton. booking clerk at Warrington, residing at Huyton, stated that he WAS a passenger to W.rrington on the date named by the 6-15 a.m. train. He had to change at Earlestown,,nd whilst there he saw the fowls escape from the crate. The two defendants got one each, and lalrhurst put his in Hayes' pocket.—William Hodges deposed that he saw the defendants take a fowl each.—William Holland, ticket collec-or at Warrington. spoke to seeing the defend- ants returning to Earlestown by the 9.15 p.m. train. He stopped them and questioned them about the fowl . They at first denied asty knowledge of them but afterwards admitted that they had sold them. Frank Clarke employed at the Patten Arms Hotel. arrington. spoke to buying the fowls for one shilling each from the defendants.—Detective Parsons also gave evidence for the prosecution. The defendants said they did not take the fowls with the intention of stealing them. Hayes said they thought they had as much right to them as anyone else, and if they had not picked them up they might have got killed. (Laughter.)—Hayes was fined 10s. and costs, and Fairhurst ss. and costs.
