div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
SCENE IN THE BOROUGH COURT.

There was an unusual scene in the Warrington Borough Court on Monday when a young woman named Annie Smith who is an inmate of the Workhouse was brought up on a charge of being c isorderly and using threats to the Workhouse Master (Mr. Ward) on Satur- day afternoon. Further charaes of assaulting P.C. Gibbs whilst in the execution of his duty and also with break- ing b. window in the cells were preferred against her. On being charged with the offence she pleaded guilty and in a loud voice she said "Yes,and I will do it again." —Mr.B. Shearer said he appeared on behalf of the Guar- dians to prosecute. She was quite incorrigible. Sue was either in the gaol or in the workhouse and they could not manage her.—The Prisoner : I don't c ire what you say, and 1 dJn't care how long I get.—Mr. Shearer : We really cannot do any good with her.—The Prisoner : That's" Charley's Aunt."—Mr. Shearer : She was left here by someone when the Ship Canal was being made. —Prisoner : I will go to gaol again and do it like a bird.—Mr. Shearer: When the police came on Saturday she would not leave the Workhouse but threw herself down. She threatened the Master and committed other offences.—Prisoner : " Charley's Aunt" is not dead while you are there.—Mr. Shearer :—When the House Committee are going about she is defying everybody. Be would ask the magistrates to make an example of her.— In answer to the magistrates, Mr. Shear,r s iid the de- fendant was not drunk. She had been in the Work- house for the last five or six weeks and had been kept without any intoxicating drink P.C. Gibbs said he was called into the Warrington Workhouse on Saturday for the purpose of quelling the disturbance. He found prisoner in the wash-house. On seeing witness she threw two tins of water at him and struck him in the face. She made use of very bad lan- guage and threw herself into the water. Since she hid been confined in the cells she had brok,n windows.—The Mayor: Is she all right P—The Chief Constable: When she was up here before I thought it was a case for her condition to be enquired into. This was done but it was thought: her mental condition was all right— The Prisoner: They tried their best to send MA to the asylum, but they could not.—The Chief Constable: She is a perfect dem.,n, there's no mistake.—The Prisoner: I will do it again.—The Chief Constable: This is he twenty-first appearance.—The Prisoner: It is only twenty.—The Chief Constable: She was sentenced to three months imprisonment on the last occasion.—Pri- soner: lam able to do six months.—The Chief Con- stable: She is better in gaol.—The prisoner made use of disgusting language.—The Mayor sentenced her to 21 days for disorderly behaviour, six months for assaulting the poiice, ani two months for the damage done to the cells.—The Prisoner: That is eight months, twenty-one days. I will do that on my head. She then uttered threats against the Chief Constable and Mr. Shearer.— The Chief Constable ordered Sergeant Chantler to re- move her as her language was unbearable. She wrestled with the sergeant, and while doing so got her band free and threw a piece of stone at the workhouse master,Mr. Narcl,which just missed hins.—The Chief Constable : I am glad to say that she is not a native of Warrington.— The prisoner was then removed to the cells below.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY. —Before- -gr. R A-rmitgge (chairman) and Mr. Wm. Houghton. OBSTRUCTINO THE FOOTPATH,—Frank Appleton and Jos Hewitt of Houghton Green, were charged with having on the 30th August at Poulton; obstructed the free passage of the footpath by standing thereon.—P.C. Johnson proved th case and stated that he saw the defendants standing in the foot- path for twenty minutes A. great many people had to leave the footpath in consequence. —Both defendants were fined ss. each. _ _

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES—Ambrose Timmins, 11, Howard-st., Sankey Bridges, was fined 53. including costs for neglelting to cause his child to attend senool regularly. For smiler offences. Joseph Terner, 159, Howard-st., Sankey Bridges; Frederick Hancock, 14, Wright-street, Sankey Bridges ; and Richard Jenkins, Wright-st., Sankey Bridges were also dealt with. Mr. B. Shearer prosecuted. TRESPASSING INT SEARCH or GAME.—Arthur Parker, Wat- kin-street, Warrington was charged with having on the 30th August trespassed on land in the occupation of Mrs. James Warburton at liurtonwood in search of game.—Mr. B. A. White, solicitor, prosecuted, and stated that the defendant was seen by a gamekeeper to be on a field in the occupation of Mrs. James Warburton, and it was a likely Mace for pheasants and partridges. There were six others in company with the defendant and they had two dogs - a fox terrior and a whippet—in addition to two guns. The men were on the hedge side and they commenced to walk slowly %long the field and two shots were fired in the air. The defend- ant was the only one caught. The ease looked like a deliberate case of poaching in a wholesale manner and it was aggravated by the fact that it was on Sun- day, It was not necessary for him to prove any actual poaching. All he was called upon to prove was that the de fendant was on land where he had no right to be and that he was there for the purpose of taking game. Irnmedi itely the gamekeepe r came up the men ran away. The defendant was caught by another gamekeeper who happened to be near at the time. He was found in possession of a double-barrelled gun but no game, the only birds in his possession being two swallows and.two sparrows,— Jonathan Chapley, gamekeeper for Mr. Tobin, stated that on Sunday the 30th August he was on duty on the Canal side at Burtonwood when he saw the defendant and six other men on Mrs. Warburton's farm. they were in a field of clover root off wheat stubble where there were a number of pheasants and partri iges. Hej saw the men spread themselves out and walk along the field. Two shots were fired in the air. He could n,t say what they were firing at.—Defendant admitted being on the land but said he did net know there was game there.—He was fined 10s. and costs.—George Cosgrove, of Regent-street, Hades- town and James Baines, of 57, Houghton-street, Earlestown were also charged with having on the 31th August at Burton- wood committed a trespass in search of game on land in the occupation of William Bend.—Baines was further charged with refusinz to give his name and address when requested to do so by John Thornley, a gamekeeper. Baines did not eppear.—Mr. A. E. White again prosecuted and stated that Mr. Thornley, a gamekeeper in the employ of Mr. Tobin saw the defendants in Alder-lane. Burton-wood accompanied by a lurcher dog. He saw them get over a stile and walk along a footpath running through a wheat stubble field. Cosgrove then took off the dogs collar and Baines went on the field with the dog which commenced lurching. The gamekeeper went up to Cosgrove and he admitted that he was responsible for the dog. He had been previously warned. Baines when asked for his name and address refused to give it. He w+s followed by the gamekeeper to Earlestown and his address afterwards obtained in company with P 0. Burns.—Bvideme in /Hippo -t of Mr. White's statement having been given by the gamekeeper, the magistrates fined Cosgrove 10s. and costs, and Baines. 20s. and costs. The advocate's fee would be al- lowed in the costs.

div.head: NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS. FIRST COURT.
div.p: NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS. FIRST COURT.
SATITRDAY.—Before Mr. T. J. Gillespie (chairman) Captain Withington, and Mr. R. Stone. _ _

A CYCLIST IN TitnUBLE —Deward Cooper, Winwick, was fined Is. and costs for h wing ridden a bicycle at nine p.m. on the 24th August without having a lighted lamp. A BR am oF CANAL BYELAWS —Samuel Darlington. captain of the flat George was summoned for a breach of the Canal Byelaws on June 18th, by neglecting to erect sufficent stageing when discharging a cargo of manure at Winwick lock.—Mr. Penn', soli, itor, prosecuted on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and stated that the proceedings were taken under a special act dated 11th May, 1830 for the reguiatfon of the St. Helens Canal. A section of the act stated that any ins discharging a vessel without planks or stage being laid Sc as to prevent rubbish from falling into t'as canal should pay a sum not exceeding £5. It was the second case th, company had been ()Aged to bring into that Court,but it was net against the same captain, but a captain of the same boat. A great many were engaged in unloading at Winwick Quay and the majority of them very properly obeyed the instructions but some were very obstreperous and the company was ebligtd to take these steps in order to made them comp y with the orders and to keep the canat wholesome and clean. The defendant who had previously ben cautioned, on the date in questien used no planks or stage to prevent the manure wh ch was being un- loaded falling into the canal. It was falling into it in large quantities, and the defendant en being told about it, got a pitchfork and lifted a large piece of manure out of the water. The lapse of time since the offence was in consequence of their being unable to serve the summons on the defendant.— Evidence corroborating Mr. Fenna's statement was given by Joseph Paine, Henry James, Inspector Cookson and Thomas Gool.—lnspector Coookson said manure was floating down the canal for 100 ards from the defendant's boat.—Tbe de- fendant who did not appear was fined 20s. and gusts. A TRUMPEaY C ,SE.—Joseph Marsh was summoned for having on the 26th August assaulted Martha Clarke, and there was also a croas-summons charging Clerke with an assault upon M..irsh. Mr. H. J. Longton represented the female defeatiant. and Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, the male de- fenclant.ln stating his case,Mr.Longton said it arose throngh some extra officiousness on the part of the defendant Marsh. A dispute had aria n between two little boys, one the arm of his (Mr. Longton's) "heat, and the other the brother of Marsh, Marsh urged his brother to strike Mrs. Clarke's son and he did so. Mrs. Mar:h then went to her son's assistance and Marsh then hit her on the mouth —Martha Marsh and Mrs. Elizabeth Derby. Wood-st.. Earlesto an gave evidence in support of Mr. Longton's statement.—Mr. W. H. J. Jen- kins said the case was a very small matter and he was sur- prised that people would waste their money in court fees and bring them there to listen to such trumpery rubbish. The ease was due to two little boys falling out Sides were taken and Mrs. Clarke interfered. His (dr. Jenkin's) client ad- mitted that. ha did accidently touch her in toe face in push- ing her away, but in return Mrs Oa ke hit Marsh with a cloth and threatened him with a poker which he had to take off her for his own safety. He ventured to think that th, Magistrates would be of tae OJinion th a the most serions assault was by Mrs. Clarke. Josenti Marsh and a boy name I Theme' Payne having given evidence, the magistrates dis- missed both cases, stating that they were ot a trumpery des- cription. _ . .

.98‘AULT ON A WIFE.—John K, na•ton was charged with having on the 10th September assaulsa and beaten his wife Sarah Jane Kynaston. --Defendant pleaded guilty. The complAinant stated that the defendant came tor his dinner on the date named and afterwards commenced calling her. div.head: MOND COURT.
div.p: MOND COURT.
Before Colonel Wood (In the chair), Mr. C. B. F. Borron and
Mr. S. S. Brown.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Fines were imposed upon the undermentioned persons for being guilty of drunkenness and disorderly behaviour :—Lawrence Dunn, Michael Mannion. and James Prescott. A similar charge was brought against James Rimmer but was aism,ssed. •

ALLEGED THREATS.—Elizaboth Hughes brouc,ht, a summons against Michael Lawless for using threatening language against her on the 19th August. but not being able to satisfy the Bench as to the guilt of the defendant, the summons was dismis.ed. • Vigil I TRESPASS AT GOLBORNE.—WiIIiam Howard. Th,mas Red- yard, Adam Ince and Elizabeth Latham, were all summoned by Richard Fearns, farmer, of Golbqrne, for trespassing upon and damaging hay grass to the value of 4d.—one penny each. —Complainant asserted that he saw the four defendants walking across his meadow grass at Golborne, on the 3rd bast , which was "a short cut ' from one part of the district to another, The land was properly fenced round, and it was strictly private and no public footpath being across it.—Defendants pleaded gui:ty.—Superinte, dent Brassington remarked that trespassing upon farmers land had become so common that the County Council had issued posters warning offenders that proceedings would be taken against them as soon as their often le was discovered.—Com- plainant stated that the defendants were all neighbours of his,and he did not want to press the case. All th ,t he wanted was to warn other people who might be in lined to offend The Chairman said that as the prosecutor had expressed the wish that defendants should be leniently dealt with, they wou d be fined 6s 6d. including costs. ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD THE LONDON AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.—John Fletcher was charged with hav- ing ridden on the London and North Western Railway with- out a ticket and with intent to defraud the corr pany.—Defendant admitted the offence.—Mr. Fenna, who prosecuted for the Company, stated that defendant was a passenger by a train between Wigan and Golborne on the evening of the 9th instant. He was seen by one of the company's servants to alight from a third class oompartrr ent after which he lingered about the platform for some length of time. When all the other pas- sengers had cleared away from the plittorm he walked in the direction of the barrier, He was met by one of the com- pany's collectors who asked him for his ticket. At first the de- fendant denied having come by the tr in but after interroga- tories he admitted that he had come from Wigan and that he hadn't a ticket. He refused for some time to offer the fare but ultimately handed lid. saying "That is quite enough for you." and at the same time using very obscene language. At last the company's servants were compelled to hand him over to the custody of the police and ha was locked up.—Defend- ant said he was under the influence of drink at the time and he should have gone to Brynn from Wigan instead of to Golborne.—He was fined ss. and costs.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MoNDAY.—Before Messrs. F. J. Norman and Samuel

Taylor. DOG AT LARGF..—Williani Jmneson, of Weston, was sum- moned for allowing his dog to go unmuzzled or without a collar in Church-street, Runcorn, on A.ug tst 13th. —P. C. Kendrick proved the case. Defen !ant said he was away from home at the time and the dog broke loose. Defendant was fined ss. including Costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Murphy was charged with being drunk and die irderly in Mersey-street on Satur- day night at 10 o'clock. P.C. Hughes proved the case and P.C. Gregory statel that defendant was a lodging-house keeper and harbourei sailors and disorderly women. The men went there and got drunk and were turned out into the street to fight It was getting disgraceful.—Superintendent Okell said it was a disgrade to the town.—The Bench fined prisoner 1)s, and costs. DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—SeIina Giblin was sent to gaol for 14 days for disorderly conduct in Mersey-street on the 12th Inst.

KNOWLES said he desired t 3 call the atten- tion of the Council to the fact that someone had put up a new fence near Longford Bridge on the road to Win- wick.—The Surveyor: The Highway Bard have full charge of the roads.—Mr. Knowles said he believed the fence was being put two or three feet nearer the road than the hedge was. He understood that that Council would some time have charge of the reads, and if they ever wanted to put a footpath there they might be called upon to pay through the noses for it.—The Chairman: I think the Highway Board are pretty vigilent in that respect.—The Surveyor said if his assistant went near the spot he would get him to take notice of it.

div.head: TEE DEPIITATI'-'.N TO NEWCASTLE.
div.p: TEE DEPIITATI'-'.N TO NEWCASTLE.

The CLERB said Mr. Halton and himself attended the congress in connection with the Sanitary Institute from September let to sth at Newcastle. Tney were present at the preliminary meetings, reception, opening of the Health Exhibition, and such of the lectures, and papers, and discussions as were likely to be of use to them. Some of them were purely medical. Oe the whole they gained much information,and he thought the experience gained would be of use to the Council.—Mr. then reada report he had prepared. In referring tHhaelyt Halton d to drainage arrangements, he remarked that Northum- berland was better supplied so far as waterways were concerned than Warrington and district,but he ventured to think that they would not be able to make progress without a system of thorough drainoge combined with a tidal way which was necessary to flush that drainage and sweep it away. So far as dealing with excreta in Warrington and district, he thought they ought to use every means in their power tó have water closets in every household where it was possible, and then aeain, all outfalls such as ditches which caused pollution should be piped in order to prevent the nuis- ance that might arise from time to time Referring to a paper on a port sanitary authority by ?dr. A. H. Barber, chairman of the London Sanitary Authority, he ( said the writer mentioned the necessity of employing in- spectors to keep a watchful ye en incoming ships, steamers, and barges importing food stuffs. He (Mr. Halton) agreed that such should be done for scarcely a month passed without some quantity being condemned as unsound food. In conclusion he said he believed sub congresses had a beneficial effect.—Mr. John Houghton: Yes,it is a nice out for you. (Laughter.)—The Chairman remarked that he did not agree with the suggestion of the universal use of water closets. But he thought their thanks were due to the deputation for the report.

HALTON BRIDGE ONCE MORE. Mr. DIGNum wished to know whether anything was being done with regard ts Halton Bridge at Penketh. It would be a great improvement if the work could be carried out. It had been dinussed by the Highway Board on many occasione.—Mr. Warburton said it was a very dangerous place.—The subj,et then dropped. THE SURVETnR'S REP3RT.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. LEIGH.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. LEIGH.

The Warrington first team made their first appearance at home last Saturday, and the occasion was taken to re-open the ground after the alterations te the stand. Unfortunately a severe thunderstorm burst over War- rington about an hour before time for the kick off, and although the weather had cleared before 3.30 p.m. the attendance was very much interfered with, although there would be about 4,000 spectators present. The ground was very heavy going, but the game which ensued was very fast. Barber took his position as cap- tain for the first time this season, and the following was the composition of the two teams :—Warrington : Heesom, full back ; Barber, Isherwood, Cross and Law- less, three-quarter backs ; Bate and Higginbottom, half backs; Taylor, Warburton, Swift, Hill, Higham, Savage, Barrett and Burrows, forwards. Leigh : Coop, full back ; Wallwork, Spillane, Anderton and Jackson,three- quarters ; T. Taylor and Officer, half backs; McMasters, Davies, Fraser, R. Taylor, Blackburn, Edleston, Winstanley and Boardman, forwards. After Hill's kick off, an unaccountable series of mulls gave Warrington a foothold, and Taylor was very conspicuous in working the ball down the field. After a few scrimmages near the visitors' line, the hall was sent over, and Bate had the hardest of luck in not gathering the ball and only a minor resulted. After the kick out, Wallwork was prominent with a fine sprint along the field, and this was supplemented by a grand passing run by Spillane and Anderton. The danger to Warrington was put an end to by Cross. Midfield play followed without much advantage to either side, and rather monotonous play was at length relieved by a free kick to Warrington. Taylor took the kick, and ex- change kicking took place between him, Wallwork, Barber and Coop, the latter of whom by a well judged kick found touch in Warrington quarters. Even play still continned, and though it was fairly interesting, nothing worthy of special comment occurred, until an outburst of passing was witnessed between Higgin- bottom, Bate, Barber, Cross, and Lawless, the latter of whom found Coop in the way, but much ground had been gained by the movement. The Leigh forwards, headed by Davies were now prominent with a fine dribble, and Heesom was applauded for a splendid save near his own goal line. Warring- ton were hard pressed for a few minutes, but they defended manfully, Hee.om, Barber, and Bate being especially prominent. Swift was the means of getting the ball away by a flying kick, and Bennett was only just prevented from following this out with something tangible by being knocked in touch by Wall- work. A lone kick by Anderton, immediately after, al- most caught Heesom napping, for while waiting for it to get over the line in order to touch down, Spillane and Anderton were almost on him, and he only just touched aown in the nick of time. After wonderfully even play, half time arrived with no score. Hill restarted, and some dreadful mulling by the home backs almost re- sulted in Leigh scoring, Barber howeier, proved the saviour of his side. Scrimmages ensued at a very un- desirable place from a Warrington point of view, and a pretty bit of passing between Higginbottom, Bate, Isherwood and Cross, brought no relief, the latter being up-ended by Jackson before he could get free,—and Leigh were again attacking hotly. A score seemed cer- tain, when 'Lawless rushed up and kicked the ball in touch. Hill and Burrows now tried to start a passing movement, but they were promptly pulled up, and for an infringement ot the roles a minute later Warrington were penalised. Coop had the ball placed and kicked a goal from near half way. This caused the play to be faster, and Warrington made desperate efforts to equalise. Taylor took a penalty kick and he could not get the ball over the plste and still Warrington were be- hind. A desperate struggle on the Leigh line followed a dribble, and the ball wee literally forced over, and Bur- rows managed to fall upon it in a favourable position, and thus aroused the drooping spirits of the Warring- tonians. Heescm took the easy place, but failed to land a goal. The ensuing play was very disappointing to the Warringtonians,Leigh evidently holding out the longest, and having muc the better of the play. Still, there did not appear to be much finish in their play, and though the Warringtonian backs failed lamentably to play a combined game, they defended fairly well. Time was almost up, and a draw seemed certain, when Officer got the call from a scrimmage and passed quickly to Spil- lane. The latter parted at the critical moment to Ander- ton, and to the utter astonishment of everyone, he rushed right round the whole of his opponents at light- ning speed, and grounded behind the goal posts. The place kick was taken by Coop and was promptly des- patched over the bar. Immediately after this was done and before anything else could be done,the whistle blew, Warrington being beaten by two goals (eight points) to one try (three points).

div.head: RUNCORN v. SWINTON.
div.p: RUNCORN v. SWINTON.

For the first time in three years Swinton visited Run- corn, and the match in the local arena was followed with keen interest. The violent thunderstorm previous to the match deterred many from attending but there was a fair gate nevertheless. Both towns had the best teams possible the names when the respective teams faced each other being Swinton.—R. B. Makin, back; J. T. Lewis, J. Valen- tine, J. Goodman, and F. Atherton, three-quarters; W. Pearson and W. Hanson, half-backs; F. Ainsworth, P. Greenhalgh, W. Evans, R. Tickle, W. Kilner. J. John- son, S. Hall, and S. Norton, forwards. Runcorn.—Houghton, back; Warder, Robinson, But- terworth, and Richardson, three-quarter backs: J. Faulkner and W. Pendlebury, hall-backs; W. Faulkner, Reece, Farmer, Walker, Hughes, Lightfoot, Darlington, and Taylor, forwards. Valentine started against a good breeze. Runcorn front rank went off in a dribble, to which Valentine effectively replied, and then Butterworth was injured in stopping a rush of the Swinton pack. Even play in centre was followed by Goodman dropping at goal, the ball falling just outside the posts A passing bout between J. Faulkner, Robinson, Butter- worth and: Warder ended in Makin touching down. Each end was visited in rapid succession. Valentine raising a cheer by finely punting and tackling Houghton before he could respond. The home defence was severely tested for a time, and tnen the "Lions" had ten minutes repelling attacks, which they successfully accomplished, and at half-time nothing had been scored. The record was unbroken when Mr. Referee Dilloc sounded time, but Runcorn had a decided advantage in the play in this half, and Richardson, Roninson, and Warder were each held on the line when a score seemed certain. Houghton attempted to place a penalty goal, the ball rebounding into play from the cross-bar. Towards the finish Swinton took more advantage of the wind, by high kicking, and gave the home team some consider- able trouble and two exciting runs by Lewis and Ather- ton though without tangible issue placed the home lines in danger. When time was called neither side had scored so that -a stubborn and exciting game ended in favour of neither team.

WARRINGTON "A " v. LEIGH " A."—(" A" TEAM reautiz).—The Warrington "A" team journeyed on Saturday to Leigh and played as advertised with the ex- ception of Saunders, whose place was filled by Sudlow. Leigh played two men short for the first quarter of an hour. The storm was at its height when Thornton kicked off, towards the railway. The return was weak, and Carey received the ball. A splendid chance was lost by C'Brien, who failed to catch Carey's pass. The opening was soon taken advantage of by Leigh, who dribbled the leather to midfield. The ball, however, cl,d not long remain at half-way,as the Warrington forwards made a dashing run to the homester's quarters. For a length of time the leather remained within two hundred yards of the Leigh goal line, hut without any effect. The homesters were penalised for off-side play, and Red- ford failed at the kick. Leigh now begin to realise their danger, and so forced play to neutral territory. A round of passing by Houghton, Foden, Fairhurst and Carey saw the visitors again in the Leigh quar- ters. A few minutes later Fairhurst broke away and dropped with the ball under the posts. For some reason or other the try was disallowed. A fine bit ot play on the part of the Leigh three-quarters, took the homesters to Warrington's quarters. Here they remained for a little time and made several attempts to score. Scott saved by kicking the ball dead. Biscow now saved with a brilliant run and kick sending the Leigh men to mid- field. From here the visitors forced the ball to the Leigh 2S, flag and a brilliant passit"e, movement between Carey, O'Brien. Foden, Scott and Radford resulted in the latter nearly getting over. Several scrimmages and line outs took place, and Scott received the leather and dropped a splendid goal. The game was now desultory, give, and take play at midfield being the order. Half-time was called with Warrington leading by a dropped goal to nil. On the restart Leigh began to took up and play up gamely, pressing repeatedly. Sale was conspicuous with a fine run to the visitors goal line, where he finished up with a splendid shot. A line, out and a scrimmage resulted and the ball was cleared to the homesters 25. Here Foden took possession and scored the first try. Thornton attempted to inanrcree the scr,re, but failed. From now to the finish Leigh made every attempt to score, but without success ; the nail beime chiefly stationed at half-way. Final : Warrington, 1 goal, 1 try (seven points) ; Leigh, hil. The following players tcok part :—Warrington "A " Pull back, J. Boscow ; three-quarter backa, Carey, Slott, Radford, O'Brien ; half backs, Houghton, Foden ; forwards, Fair- hurst, Thornton, Sudlaw, Andrews, Jenkins, Scholt,e, Meacock, Smith. Leigh " A : Full hack. Shovelton ; three-quarter backs, Sale, Unsworth. Maltby, Hatton ; ! half hacks, Nall, Short ; forwards, Roberts, Aldred, Arrowsmith, M'Masters, Hulme, Grogan, Carrington, and Emmings.
WARRINGTON ST. MARY'S V. FRODSHAM. —Playel on St. Mary's ground, Liverpool-roads on Saturda.c. Froasham having won the toss, Caldwell, started. for St, biarfss

The home team immediately began to press, Deakie almost scoring. Tris in quick succession were scored by Rutter and Warburton, no goals resultinz. From the kick off, the Saints got possession, and by good PK, Eden scored, Roughley failing. After te9tae ing. Froa' sham were awarded a free kick, which Burrows chargecl 'own. Warburton obtaining possession scored a try. Half-time soon arrived with the score: St. Mary's, four. tries; Frodsham, nil. The game was of a one-sidea nature, tries bein7 scored by Riitter, Deakin (two). fligginbottom, Ronghley improving two. Final score--* St. Mary's, two goals seven tries (31 points) ; Frod• sham, nil.

Here is a curious end to a humble occupation in Lotr don, which shows how the most outlying and pooreol fields of industry, which the big world would not natur ally think about, suffer from the most casual and dir tant advances in the life of the community. A poOt woman has just been driven into one of the Londoo workhouses who had been gradually deprived of a life long means of support in consequence of the Count! Council reclaiming and enclosing so many open spaced, She had made what she regarded as a good living bi collecting and selling grounthel for cage-birds, but Of conversion of the waste places into gardens has banish' the weed almost entirely from the metropolis, and tb poor woman sinks into helplessness in the rising tide 0 civilisation.

div.head: REVISLA Gl- THE id6llB. AT WARRINj-TON.
div.p: REVISLA Gl- THE id6llB. AT WARRINj-TON.
WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. The court was continued on Wednesday morning at ten o'clock.
MOTHERS AND SONS.

The Liberals made an objection to the vote of William John Lowrie Whiteman, 6, Manley-st. His mother ap- peared on his behalf and stated that her son was the tenant of the house. Mr. Clayton's objection was that be was not the tenant, but a rent book was produced and the Barrister over-ruled the objection and granted tbe woman 2s. 2d. costa for her attendance.—The blue- rals made a claim for a vete for John Connell, 11,Towa- hill. It was shown that the sou was the support of the house, and the Barrister allowed the claim.—The Con- servatives claimed a vote for William Warburton, Walker- st. The mother was the tenant of the house,but the son was the sole support.—The Barrister struck the mother off the list,she bring on division three,which entitled her to a municipal vote only, and placed the son in division one,which gives him the full tranchise.—The Conserva- tives succeeded in a number ot similar applications.

div.head: RATEABLE V !LUE INSUFFICIENT.
div.p: RATEABLE V !LUE INSUFFICIENT.

A Liberal claim was made on behalf ot James Woods, for a vote in Town Hall ward, for a shop in Allen-street. —An objection was made by the Conservativas that the rateable value was insufficient to entitle the applicant to be placed on division one.—The Barrister said he did not think he had power to place it on division three,but he would consider the matter and adjourn the applica- tion.—On Friday, the Revising Barrister placed the ap- plicant on the list for division three, which only entitles nim to the municipal vote.
AN OFFICE VOTE.

A Conservative claim was made on behalf of Lewis A. Voisey for an office in King-street.—Mr. Clayton objected to the application on the ground that the applicant was not in sole possession,he being iN partner- ship with a Mr. Worthington.—The Revising Barrister allowed the claim as there was no application for a vote by the partner.

div.head: SUCCESSION BY MARRIAGE.
div.p: SUCCESSION BY MARRIAGE.

The Liberals claimed a vote in division three on behalf of James Butler, of 4, Hill-st., on the grounds of succes- sion by marriage. In answer to the questions put by Mr. Holbrook it was ascertained that he became the tenant of the house in September 1895, but previous to that time the person who was now his wife was the ten- ant.—The Revising Barrister allowed the claim.
A MISTAKE IN THE NAME.

The Liberals claimed a vote on behalf of Maxwell Campbell, of 8, Houghton-st., for a vote successive from West-st.—The Conservative agent pointed out that tlae applicant's name appeared on the list as that of George Campbell.—The applicant's wife appeared, and the Bar sister altered the name from George to Maxwell and allowed the vote.
THURSDAY. The Revision Court was continued on Thursday. AN APPLICANT SWORN.

John Starkey applied for a lodger's vote for 2, Han- over-street. Mr. Holbrook questioned him and he said that he paid 7s. a week as a lodger. He could not bring any proof, but the Revising Barrister said that if the applicant would swear that he paid 7s. a week he would allow the vote. The applicant was sworn, and the vote was allowed.

div.head: PARTNER'S VOTE.
div.p: A PARTNER'S VOTE.

Mr. Henry Beresford Melville was the applicant for a vote in respect of offices in Bold street. The applicant was represented by Mr. Johnson,who explained that Mr. Melville was the secretary of the Warrington Mare and Foal Society, wt ose annual show was taking place that day at Walton Park, and therefore he could not appciar. In answer to Mr. Clayton, Mr. Johnson said he was prepared to swear that there is a deed of partnership in existence entered into in May last year.—The vete was allowed.

div.head: CHAPEL KEEPER'S TOTE,
div.p: A CHAPEL KEEPER'S TOTE,

The Liberals applied for a vote for Mr. Mellor for 10, Cairo-street. Mr. W. H. Woodcock repremted the ap- plicant and said that Mr. Mellor had a service occupa- tion for the Unitarian Schools. He paid no rent, but could move at any time, and still hold the position of chapel keeper. He would then receive additional wages in lieu of rent. —The vote was allowed. MR a B MATTHEWS' TOTE OBJECTED TO.

The Liberals oti,cted to the vote of Mr. Robert Bond Matthews id respect to an office in Liverpool-road, Little sankey. —Mr Clayton : Is this really an office ?—Mr. Matthews : It is an office as far as 1 make use of it.— Mr. Clayton :Is it not simply a shed -Mr. Matthews : There is a writing desk in it.—Mr. Clayton : There is no desk in the place.—Mr. Matthews: I beg your pardon there is.—Mr. Clayton : Well I was in the place myself and never saw any.—Mr. Matthews: I am very sorry for you,—ln reply to other questions, Mr. Matthews said that Mr. eickston was the owner of the premises.— Mr. Clayton informed his Honour that Mr. Pickston was on the register as a county eh-ctor and that there were other sheds in the place. —ln reply to the revising bar- rister, Mr. Tunstall said that in the premises, Mr. Picks. ton was rated at £1 104., Mr. Matthews ae £2, and Mr. Kenyon at £lO. The full rateable value of the premises was £25 10s., but there were two parts, a stable and a smithy, empty.—Mr. Clayton objected to the vote on the ground that Mr. Matthews allowed another to occupy the same place, but the Revising Barrister said thAt there was nothing to prevent a tenant allowing any other p rson to have an easement on his premises.— Mr. Clayton : Lt me see the rent book.—The book was handed to htm,and he mentioned that several sums were apparently written with the same ink.—The Re- vising Barrister: Do you suggest that Mr. Pickston's signature is a forgery.—Mr. Clayton : Oh no.—The ob- jection was disallowed, but the Revising Barrister re- fused to allow any expenses.

div.head: LOCAL WATCHMAKER AND HIS VOTE.
div.p: A LOCAL WATCHMAKER AND HIS VOTE.

The Conservativem claim-d a vote for Mr. Edward Eustance, for 122 Wdderspool Causeway. In reply to Mr. Clayton,a gentleman who represented Mr. Eustance said that the latter did not reside at Colwyn Bay,but oc- casionally went there. He always resided in Wilders- pool-road. Toe family resided at Colwyn Bay. The Revising Barrister allowed the vote.

div.head: QUESTION OF OWNERSHIP.
div.p: A QUESTION OF OWNERSHIP.

The Liberals objected to the vote of Joseph Crots for HI Rose and Crown-street. Mr. Clayton said that he had been informed by Mr. Cross's brother that his mother was the sole occtpier and owner of the premises, but this Mr. Cross deniefl,and said that he paid the rates for the shop add it was his own property. The vote was al- lowed,but on the application of Mr. Cross for expenses, the Revising Barrister declined to allow them, saying that the case seemed to be one which required a little inquiry.

A NUMBER OP OBJECTIONS.—COSTS ORDERED TO BE PAID. Mr. Clayton on behalf of the Liberals objected to the name of Wm. Kelly, near Hopwood-street, being on the list on the grounds that John Riley was the tenant and not William.—The applicant informed the Barrister that he was the only person living t here. —The Barrister quashed the obj-sction and allowed 3. 6J. costs.—Ann Emerson, 7, Back Crossley-street was objected to by Mr. Clayton. his contention being that she had been the recipient of relief during the year.—The Relieving Officer on being appealed to stated that the woman had not received any relief, but her mother had.—The Bar- rister allowed the vote to remain, and granted the woman 3. 6J. costs.—The Conservatives objected to John Walsh of 5, Blackhurst-street AR the ground that there were more houses on the list opposite his name than the number he had resided in. According to the list, Walsh had lived in four, whereas he had only occupied three.—Tne Barrister altered the list and granted 2s. costs.—The Liberals objected to James Fodell. Liverpool-road,on the ground that his name was James Thomas Foden.—Foden stated that his name was James Thomas but he very seldom used" Thomas" and he was known as James Foden.—The Revising Barrister allowed the vote, but would not order any costs to be paid on the ground that Foden could have made a declaration when he received notice that he was objected to on account of misdescrip- tion of name.

div.head: JOINT TENANCY.
div.p: A JOINT TENANCY.

James Sheldon Haynes, Grappenhall-road, and Willie Alfred Haynes, living with his parents at Sankey-street, both applied for a vote in resp:-ict of a joint-shop in Winwick-street.—ln answer to questions by Mr. Holbrook as to wh was the tenant, Mr. James S. Haynes said he took it on behalf of himself and brother. —On the Overseer being questioned he said the shop was rated in the name of Haynes Leather Campany, Limited.—Mr. J. S. Haynes said the shop did not bc•long, to the Leather Company but it was a business place for his brother and himself.—The Barrister allowed both votes.
MESSRS. NELSIN'S TANNERY.

Wm. Nelson, Chesnut, Lymm. cld med a vote for office and tanners' in Mersey-street.—Mr. Clayton asked who were the tenants of the premises, and was in- formed that the business was carried on by Wm. Nelson and his father.—The vote was allowed.

Mr. John Westgarth made a claim for an office near Wilson Patten-street and 1, Mersey-street successive which was supported by Mr. Clayton. The vote was allowed.—Mary Coates, of 10, Filars'-gate claimed a vote for a dwelling-house at 10, Friar's-gate, and Mr. Clayton objected. It was statrA in answer to a question by the Liberal agent that the premises did not belong to the trustees of the late Mr. Coates.—The vote was allowed.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S COURT.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S COURT.

The proceedings were continued yesterday but the worb was chiefly of a formal nature, known ar, " starring " when the lists ara checked. At the con- clusion, a vote of thank 3 was passed to the Rovisiog Barrister on the proposition of Mr. Clayton,seconded by Mr. Holbrook, and the compliment was duly ackuow- edged by him.

THE PRESENTATION TO A BANDSMAN. Sir,—' should like with your kind permission, through dip medium of your paper, to gratefully rknowledge tlio receipt of £2l is. 10d. from the Warrington Associ- aVon of Bands. I heartily thank them one and all for their sympathy and generosity to a brother in misfor- tune. I should also like to take this opportunity of ex- pressing my gratitude to my old workmates, who have /' en me a substantial proof of their. sympathy. my rtiest thanks are also due, and are given unstintingly he committee ef our Infirmary, but more especially to the doctors and nurses of that institution to whom, under God, I owe my life. Thanking you in anticipa- tion, I remain your truly,
GILBERT LOWE 27, Birchall-street, September 10th, 1396.
ON GAAES AD ATHLETICS.

FOOTBALL. Saturday's match at Runcorn was perhaps one of the tightest games seen on the Irwoll-lane enclosure, indeed the teams were so evenly matched that it was difficult to say which was the best fifteen. If there was any ad- vantage it rested with the cupholders who in the second half! twice looked very dangerous. Warder had very hard luck in not getting the ball down for a try while Houghton who negotiated a penalty kick had the morti- fication of seeing the ball strike the crossbar front which it rebounded into play. it may be said for Swinton that the team is almost as strong as ever it was and the name the club bears fora strong back division is by no means a fiction. : Swinton may be classed a hard nut to crack in the cup competition.

Runcorn leave their native heath for the first time this season to-morrow (Saturday) when an attempt will be made to beared the Wigan lion in his den. With a strong team and good combination this should be quite possible for the Runcoin lads who are rapidly getting into their stride.

The Runcorn Committee have received the transfer of Shepherd, a forward, sometime identified with Brough- ton Rangers. This plover has recently commenced work at the Castner Kelner Works at Weston Point, and has expressed a slasire to pose as a linnet. The committee have decided to play him and no doubt his services will be an acquisition to the club.

--- The Runcorn A. team who went to Swinton—like their first team were not able to bring their match to a defin- ite conclusion for after playing a fast and hard game the score book represented a blank and Runcorn although they pressed continually during the second half had to be content with a drawn verdict.
---- Swinton evidently have a good third string as in the A team match on Saturday, ten new me m were put on trial for the home team.

--- In the match at Swinton, Jolley was hurt in stopping Price of Swinton on the line.Jolley's plucky intervention saved his team from defeat as the Swinton man was within an ace of scoring. The rest of the game was finished with Runcorn struggling gamely with 14 men.

If Saturday's play at Warrington in the engagement with Leigh is to be taken as a criterion of the capacities of the home first team, it must be admitted at once that theyhave a very poor chance of cutting a respectable fi- gure in the Lancashire and Cheshire section of the Nort- hern Union League. But the Warrington Rugby Football Club Committeeshould be sympathisedwith rather than criticised. It must not be forgotten that they are faced with the undeniable fact that almost every other club in the League have imported playara of repute into their ranks, and the teams they now place into the field are far stronger than those which played under the Begby Unicn code. On the other hand it cannot be said that the Warrington team—so far as can be judged by their performances this ses.sou—is as good as last year, and the committee does not seem to have much choice in selecting from reserve men. The question will therefore arise must Warrington in order to maintain the prestige they have gained in the football world, folic v the example of other clubs and get outside assistance? The questicn must be left for the earnest consideration of the committee.

To revert to the match (4 Saturday, one of the most noticeable features of the Warrington team's play was the lack of combination shown—especially in the back division. Barber, who made his first appearance in the team this season, played a splendid game, but he as sadly in need of someone in the three-quarter line to back him up. Isherwood was certainly a weak link in the chain ; Cross did not play as well as usual ; and Lawless was found very little to do. Heesom at back was out-classed by "..00p, his ris•a-vis, whose judicious kicking into touch was a treat to witness, and he was given several opportunities for these displays by Flig- ginbottom who persisted in kicking the ball into Coop's hands. Bate .vorked hard,but did not receive the assist- ance from Higginbottom he should have done. Of the forwards, Taylor was far and away the best man and well deserves a place in the' county team.

div.head: PARK.-AN IMPROVEMENT SUGGESTED.
div.p: THE PARK.-AN IMPROVEMENT SUGGESTED.

- - Sir,—Will you oblige me by drawing the attention of the Town Hall and Park Committee to the great want of shelter in the garden portion of the Park. I find that there is not a single dry seat in the old garden portion of the Park. I find in my visits to the Park that a num- ber of mothers, nurse girls, and children frequent the Park and find it very incens enient for want of shelter. I suggest to meet this want with a verandah at the north end of the lawn,a little highor than the aviary, and to come out at the east end near the water founZain, about 12 feet wide, seated on both sides,which would meet the wants of both side; of the garden and would he very convenient especially during the present time of incle- ment weather.—Yours etc.,
W. DIGGLE. 23, Froghall-lane, Warrington, Sept. 15th, 1898.

"A PERFECT HELL OF DRUNKENNESS." Sir,—As a former resident in your town and an ob- server of its doings, I was very much shocked to hear that the town has gained such an undesirable title" as a perfect hell" of drunkenness. His worship must evi- dently be an observing man and one who feels the res- ponsibility of his position. This utterance of His wor- ship should have a threefold effect. First, it should put to shame those who have spent their hard earned wages in 80 wanton and foolish a manner as to earn for War- rington so undesirable a title. Secondly, it should be a great incentive to the temperance party and rouse them to a deep sense of duty to leave no stone unturned by endeavouring to bring about a better state of things. Thirdly, it should awaken the police to the feet that the poor miserable beings who are living in " hellisla " dens of drunkenness and crime,are being supplied by thought- less and unprincipled publicans who eare not whether men beat their wives and children, or wives pledge every article of furniture and clothing available to satisfy their craving for drink. so long as they (the publicans) reap financial benefit thereby. I must say lam very much surprised that there has been no prosecution of publicans during the year that has passed, notwithstanding the fact that the town has earned for itself the undesirable title before mentioned. Surely out of the largeinumber of "drinks " proceeded against some at least must have been arrested in the public house where they had obtained their excessive supply of the" stuff that demoralises," or near enough to it for the police to know who had broken the law by supplying overdoses of the" noxious drug." And yet! strange though it may appear, that Warrington should have earned the undesirable title sf " a perfect hell "of drunkenness not one publican has been fined for supply- ing drink to drunken persons. I shall rejoice to see Warringten awake from its slumbers and shake off this unenviable title of " a perfect hell" of drunkenness.— Yours truly,

div.head: WELL-WISHER. Birmingham, September 15th, 1896.
div.p: WELL-WISHER. Birmingham, September 15th, 1896.

THE LAWS OF MARRIAGE. 111 Sir.—The circumetances of the tragedy which occurred in Warrington on the 7th September. and reported in your issue of last Saturday brings to light some of the evils arising from the injustice of the present laws of marriage. In that little room in which lay the corpse of the mal-treated woman an epitome of the tragic side of life was revealed birth, life, love and death. Had the laws of marriage been less binding and more just proba- bly that tragedy would aot have occurred. The same may be said of the murder of Mr. Ma.vbrick which oc- curred some years ago and many ethers. When people are married it is so very desirable that they should live together in peace and love that to speak against the laws of marriaee may be mistaken for a want of suffi- cient regard for the holiness of love and the sanctity of domestic life. The meaning of the sentence, " Those whom God bath joined together let no man pot asueder," is very often misunderstood. When people are married without sufficient and proper affection Ide not think that God has joined them together and when peo- ple marry because they love each other,it is not right to bind them together for life for better or worse, save for certain forms of unfaithfulness, They ought to be able to obtain a separation when it can be clearly shown that their living together is no longer conducive hut injurious to each other's highest welfare and their children's interest:, for we should never sacri- fice the noble and the pure. Every man ought to desire the woman whom he loves to be unsullied by the love uncorrupted by the attentions of another man.and when a woman Levee a man if that man is not faithful to and woethy of her, she ought to withhold from him the ex- pressions of her love, but the laws f marriage render this more difficnit than it ought to be, yet we are com- pelled to submit to these frightful laws or live in dis- grace and be looked upon as being immoral and as hay- ing too little regard for the affections round which when rightly directed our sympathies revolve. The binding nature of these laws prevent people hav- ing the influence over each other for good which they would otherwise have. They lesson the Influence of affection because the injured nary cannot separate from one by whom they robe- be practically die- regarded, and affection often basely wronged must eurelv die at last. Is it not sinful to cause such persons to live together when the affections which sanctified their union have fled. Such is my opinioh of the marriage bond, and believing that an alteration of these laws is of great importance I desire to make it known. Fortunately there are persons who could live happily together under nearly nev conditions who do not feel the injustice of these ,nstrons laws, hut that is no reason why they should not be altered, for they often lead to misery, sin, and murder. I would ask all who are happily married, to whom it would make but little difference whatever the laws of marriage were or if there were no marriage laws, and I would nett them to consider this subject for the sake of their children and those who arc' not so fortunate, in order that they may in some little degree do something to promote the beauty and the heppinese of human life, that we may live in harmony with the laws of this won- drous universe in which we play though it is such an nitely little "vet it may be a never-ending part."— Yours truly,
S. KENYON.
Warrington, Setenaber 16th, 1896.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

FUNERAL 02 AN OLD EAREIISTOWN RESIDENT The remains of the late Mr. William Walton were laid in their last resting place on Saturday in the I new cemetery, Earlestown. Mr. Walton was very I well-known, and highly respected in Earlestown, and was one of its oldest residents. He was em- ployed for over 40 years at the London and North Western Railway Company's Waggon Works. When the Insurance and Provident Societies were started in connected with London and North Western Rail- way Company, now many years ago,he was elected and re-elected a representative by his fellow-work- men. He died in his seventy fourth year, on the Btle inst., and his loss will be long and deeply felt. The Roe J, Bartley officiated at the grave. RidgOW AT óxi. On Monday evening a general meeting of the members of the Horticultural Society Committee and the exhibitors at the recent show was held in the Church institute for the purpoee of distributing the money prim and making suggestions, &c., for the next annual sbow.There were present; The Rev. H. T. Clark (president), Mr. John White (vicei -zrese dent), Mr. Dwerryhouse (treasurer), the 'Rte. J. W. Gilbertson, and Messrs. J. Sacker, S. L. Jones, T. J. Weir, J. Tandy, D. Calder, W. Oulton, I'. Ilamblett, G. Hayward, I. Wilkinson, R. Wilkinson, J. Antro- bus, A. De Prez (hon. secretary), and Messrs. W. Kipps, James Lockhart, and E. Slater, judges at the show. After the distribution of the prize money the Secretary read the financial statement, showing that there was a deficit of about £2, owing to extra expendi.ture in purchasing tables for future years. The total subscriptions for the show were .£2l 10a. 6d. Mr. John White then proposed that a vote of thanks be accorded Mr. C. Reylance who had very kindly allowed them the free use of his field for the purpose of holding the show. This was seconded by Mr. J. L. Jones, and carried, After a I few comments introduced by Mr. Jones, respecting the alleged dissatisfaction in the adjudication of the premier prize for the best flower garden, to which liessrs.Kipps and Lockhart conclusively re- plied, the President asked if anyone had any sug- gestions to make, either with a view of amending the schedule for another year, or for the fixing of the date for next year's exhibition. After some dis- cussion it was decided to hold the show next year about the third Thursday in August. A vote of thanks to the hen. secretary foi the efficient way in which he had discharged the duties appertain- ing to the office was proposed by Mr. White, and carried with applause. Mr. Tandy seconded the vote of thanks to Mr. De Prez, and as a slight ack- nowledgement of the time and trouble devoted to tile show by him, he would be pleased if the com- mittee could see their way to make the secretary a present of £2. This matter the treasurer promised should be laid before the next committee meeting. The Rev. J. W. Gilbertson then proposed a vote of thanks to the judges, and the meeting terminated with the usual vote of thanks to the chairman.

To-day, Warrington journey to Stockport, and the team chosen is as follows :—Heesom, full back ;Lawless, Scott, Barber, Carey, three quarter backs; J. T. Bate and Houghton, half backs ; Taylor, Dakin, Barrett, Scholtze, Burrows, Eligham, Hill and Swift forwards. Reserve: Boscow, full back ; Radford, three-quarter back ; Savage, forward. It will be seea that a number of changes have been made in the composition of the I team from that which played last week. In the three- quarter line, Cross and Isherwood have been dropped for Scott and Carey, and Bate is to have as his partner, Houghton, in place of Higginbottom. There are also two alterations in the forwards, but many are surprised at the continued absence of Fairhurst.

The following paragraph culled from the "Athletic News" will be read with interest by Warringtonians "It is rather late in the day to mention it, but last year's president of the Lancashire section of the Northern Union has been the recipient of a handsome gold medal commemorative of the position he has vacated. There is no more popular man in the whole of the Northern Union than Mr. E. Warren, and his col- leagues appreciated his abilities to the full extent. It does not need much prnpecy to say that he will be the , President of the Northern Uniwn next year."

Whilst the first team have not yet won a match this season, the very opposite is the case with regard to the " A " team, for they have yet to taste their first defeat. Following up their victory against Swinton they, on Saturday,accounted for the "A" team of Leigh and beat that combination by seven points to nil. Scott succeeded in dropping a goal, and Foden scored a try,both of them meritorious efforts. The vistcirs had the best of the game throughout and they passed excellently and Boscow's inclusion in the team was a source of strength at back.

The Warrington St. Mary's team completely trounced the ;FrodshamiteE on Saturday on the Liverpool-road ground. To win a match by 31 pints to nil is no mean performance and one would think that it is something in the nature of a record for the Saints who are certainly making a name amongst the junior clubs. They have a god record behind them and every prospect of a bright future.

-- The monthly meeting of tlae above botard was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. Mr. S. Davies presided, and there were also present, Mrs. Clay, Revs. T. R. Matthews, and J. H. Riddette ; Dr. Patterson, Messrs. G. Pilling, W. Houghton, A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, W. Hickman, G. Thompson, J. Warburton, J. Billinge, T. B. Malkin, J. Clarke, T. Halton, J. Houghton, J. MINES. A 'letter was read from the Local Government Board approving of £7B 93 Eil being granted to Mr. H. M. Mines, the late superintent of Padgate schools, and also consenting to the appointment of Mr. and Mrs. Wright to their respective offices at the schools. INQUIRY OFFICER OF NEWTON DISTRICT. The Local Government Board assented to the discon- tinuation of the appointment of an inquiry officer for the Newton district, but consented to the re-appointment until June 24, 1597,at a salary of £95. They then consent that the salary of the relieving officer be raised from £5 to £lOO per annum to compensate Mr. Bowes for the loss of the inquiry officership. THE PORTECOMING POOR LAW CONFERENCE. The CLERK said he had received from Mr. Hagger,the secretary rf the North-Western Poor Daw Conference, the usual papers in respect to the confereace to be held under the chairmanship of Sir John flibbert on October 2nd and 3rd. Amongst the subjects to be discussed were poor law and friendly societies, old age pensions, poor law schools, the disposal and subsequent super- vision of workhouse children, and further powers of de- tention in workhouies. A PROPOSAL FROM THE LADIES COMMITTHE. A letter was read from Mrs. atelsten secretary of the Ladies Committee to the House Committee, informing thetn that the committee had passed a resolution asking that.the permission of the Board of Guardians be asked for the introduction by the Ladies committee into the Workhouse Infirmary, co both male and female sides, the scheme for light employment,known as the Brabazon employment scheme. In forwarding the resolution to the House Committee,the Ladies desired to explain what they proposed to do if the permission they now solicited be granted. The Ladies Committee would proceed to appoint from amongst themselves, a sub-committee to exclusively deal with the lirabazon employment scheme. They proposed to add to their number, subject to the approval of the Guardians, two or three ladies who were willing and competent to teach knitting, crotchet work, bc., to the women, and straw plaiting to the men. They pointed out that it was obvious that the pre- sent Ladies Committee could not undertake the teach- ing entirely themselves, many of them having neither the time nor the inclination for such work. The Brabazon Education Scheme Committee would, if per- mitted, visit the Infirmary weekly, to instruct their pupils and give out materials for the work. These materials were purchased with the grant given las the Countess of Meath. Every year, a sale of work should be held, and at the end of two years from the initiation of the work, the Brabazon Education scheme should be- gin to pay back the grant. No payment of any kind was given to the workers, usual methods of reward were being given plants, pictures, or a treat to the Infirmary generally, as the Guardians might approve. The scheme had been found to work well, and to be beneficial to the health of the patient. It was now in use in more than 100 workhouses, and the Ladies Visiting Cornmitte trusted that the Guardians of the Warrington Union would agree to give the scheme a trial. The House Committee recommended that the proposal of the Ladies Committee be agreed to with certain re- servations, embodied in rules set forth for the preserva- tion of discipline. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY,in moving the adoption of the House Committees' minutes,referred to the above proposal. He said that the object of the scheme was to benefit some of the people who were incapable of doing such work as could be found normally in the House. With regard to the object itself, he did not think there could be two opinions, as it was undoubtedly a good one. It was in operation in a number of workhouses in different parts of the country. Whether it could be successfully carried out in Warrington was a doubtful point,but he hopeci,at any rate,that :he resolution would be carried, as it was performed by voluntary workers rod involved no ex- pense. It would be extremely ungracious to put ob- stacles in the way of the ladies who were willing to give their time to it. The rules agreed to by the House Com- mittee would guard against any breach of discipline. He hoped that the Board would unanimously agree to try the scheme. Mr. CLARKE seconded the motion. Mr. KNOWLES moved that the minutes of the House Committee referring to the Brabazon Employment scheme. He said that Mr. Jolley had stated, in propos- ing the adoption of the minutes, that it would not cost anything. It, however, said in the letter from the Ladies Committee that they could not undertake the teaching entirely themselves. He undersrood that for the old ladies in the Infirmary who could knit, and the old men whe could do anything, there was always some light employment for them. He could not see why a small union should seek to adopt such a scheme. They had not a large quantity of people to look after. He would like to have the system proposed thoroughly dis- cussed as he did not know sufficiently about it to agree with it at present. He would like to know what other unions had adopted the scheme, and whether it was suc- eessful. On the su,ggesticn of the CLERK, Mr. Knowles altered his amendment to read that the subject be adjourned for two months. Mr. A. JOLLEY, as vice-chairman of the House Com- mittee, second d the amendment, as he did not approve of the scheme. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said that the scheme would not in- volve any additional expenditure, as all the work of the ladies would be voluntary. The Ladies' Committee would appoint a sub-committee to look after the work, and those ladies who were on the sub-committee would do the work gratuitously. They simply offered their services for the welfare of the inmates. Mrs. CLAY also denied that there would be any extra expenditure whatever. The CHAIRMAN said that he seconded the motion in support of the scheme in committee, on the express un- derstanding, that there would be no expenditure. Mr. G. PILLING supported the amendment, as he ob- jected to what was really another Ladies' Committee being formed. He thought that if such work was done, it ought to be done by the Board. Mr. HICKMAN said he was entirely in the dark in the matter. He was not against anything which would benefit the inmates of the Workhouse, but he would like to know something more about the scheme, and he sup- ported the amendment in order that further information could be gained,and not from any feeling of opposition

to it. The Rev. J. H. Rinnerre observed that he had no sympathy with the jealousy displayed to the Ladies' Conamittee, and he was interested in the scheme and hoped it would be adopted. It was for that reason he supported the amendment, as by adjourning the matter for two months, much more information would be ob- tained, and he was sure that when members had ob- tained that information,they would suppoit the scheme. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY, replying to the various speakers, said he did not see why, when the committee who gave their time and went patiently into the details of the work of the House. brought forward any scheme for the welfare of the inmates a certain portion of the Board should always set themselves dead against it. He hoped that the members of the Board would unite to support the committee. He did not see why they should wait until everybody else had adopted reforms, and then come in at the tail end. That seemed to be the feeling of some members of the Board. He thought that there was sufficient brain power among them to go forward themselves without waiting for others. Tile scheme under consideration was agreed upon unanimously by the committee and he sincereiy hoped that the House Committee would be supported against an obvious at- tempt to shelve the scheme. The amendment was then put to the vote, and eleven voted in favour, and seven against. The amendment was accordingly carried. PRESENTS. The Superintendent of Padgate Schools reported pre- sents from Mrs Daniel Jones, St. Peters Cherch,R Agged School, Mr. F. Menks, Mr. A. Jolley. and Lady Greenall. THE EXTENSION OF THE BOROUGH. The CLERX reported that he had received the draft of the extension order for the borough of Warrington. When that came into force, the Rural District Council would go out of office, and the Guardians representing Latchford, St. AUStiES and Fairfield Wards would repre- sent the portions which would be included within the borough, as though they had been originally elected from those townships. He further said that he had received a communication from Mr. F. C. Helton, the clerk to the County Council, with reference to the pro- posed retention of a guardian for Little Sankey, and he had asked him (the Clerk) to confer with the Town Clerk of Warrington on the tr. atter. Returns prepared for the " Board of Trade Jeurnal ' show that there was no marked change in the lah-atr market last month. DRUNKENNESS. At the Earlestown Police Station on Monday evening before Mr. C. B. F. Borron, John Mahon of Gas-street, Newton, was charged with being drunk on Saturday night in Earlestown, and was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. A.ef EAneacsiowN Tom?, LADY'S REWARD FOR BRATERY. S.ora. e time ago We gave publicity to a case in wiliest a young lady named Mary G. Price living in London-row, Vulcan Cottages, had at considesable risk to herself,gone into what is known as Thomp- son's pit, and rescued a child named Fer- guson, which had fallen in and was in danger of drowning. This happened in June ] last.and the young lady has had her bravery recog- nised by the Royal Humane Society, who have sent her one of their testimonials inscribed on vellum. This is the first occasion on which a young lady has gained this honour in this neighbourhood. OOOD TEMP-LARY. The Hope of Earleetown lodge of Good Templars had an open meeting on Monday evening. Bro. E. Newman, S.J.T., presided and there was a large attendance. After an opening hymn the Chairman gave a short address. There was afterwards a model lecture on Babylon; Anciene and Modern, illustrated by a model entrance to a Roman Temple. Short addresses were also given. by Bros. G. Clarke and W. H. Dale. After the yoenger portion of the audience had retired, Bro. Q, M. Sergeant Roberts !presided, and briefly addressed the meeting.— Musical items were given by Bros. C. H. Griffiths of Liverpool, Jno. Taylor, and Clarke, Sisters Griffiths, Whitty, and recitations by Bro. Wilson. An ddress was given by Bro. Newell, and thanks were ten- dered the chairman and speakers. . BAPTIST C/lIIRCH, EARLESTOWN. Special services in connection with the harvest thanksgiving were held in the above church, on Sunday. The preacher for the day was the Rev. J. S. Hughes, of Hill Cliff, who discoursed at the morn- ing and evening services to large congregations. Special hymns and anthems appropriate to the occasion were sung at both services by the choir. In the afternoon the rev, gentleman held a chil- dren's service, when he delivered an instractive address to the juveniles. The collections during the day amounted to £4 10s. 3d. On Monday evening an entertainment was given in the chapel, when a good programme of k acted and secular items was given by the choir, Misses Holt, Limond, Eckersley, Clarke, Mrs. Eckersley, Messrs. A. Limond, (3. Kidd and W. Limond. At the close a sale of fruit, veget- ables, &c,, with which the church was decorated, was conducted by Mr. J. G. Walton, and realised about £3, the proceeds being in aid of the church funds. VOLUNTEER PRIZE MEETING AT NEWTON. The annual prize meeting of the Newton detach- ment, G Company of the Ist V B.S.L.R. Volunteers, took place on Saturday. Through the kindness of friends and supporters of the corps a good prize list was again competed for. 35 members taking part. The meeting was held at Ilighfield Atoss,and the conditions were 7 ehets at 200 yards, and 7 at 500, the scoring being the same as practised at Bis- ley. Very inclement weather prevailed, and in consequence the marksmen laboured under a disad- vantage, a heavy downpour of rain accompanied by a strong breeze interfering with the shooting. Some fairily good scores were en the whole, compiled, Sergeant James Tunstall scoring 29 at 200 yards and 30 at 500 yards, and his brother, Sergeant Joseph Tunstall, coming second with 30 and 26, respectively. The following are the scores with the value of the prizes won :—Sergeant Thomas Tunstall, 59, prize £2 28.; Sergeant Joseph Tunstall, 53, .E 1 188.; Sergeant W. THE CHANGE OF RAILWAY OFFICIALS AT EARLESTOWN. In regard to the retirement of Mr. Harwood from the position of chief foreman at the Viaduct Works, and the appointment of Mr. D. Harrison, of Workington to the position, the " Workington Star" of September 11th has the following :—" On it becoming known that Mr. D. Harrison, foreman in the London and North-Western wagon depart- ment at Workington was about to be promoted to a better position at Earlestown, a movement was set on foot amongst the workmen to present him with a fitting token of their esteem. So loyal and un- animous was the response that on Friday evening (the eve of his departure) Mr. Harrison was the recipient of a very handsome barometer and ther- mometer combined. The present bore a silver plate, on which was the following inscription :—" Pre- sented to Mr. D. Harrison, as a mark of esteem by I the workmen of the wagon department London 1 and North-Western Railway, Workington, Septem- ber 4th, 189 d." The presentation took place at the wagon shop after work hours on Friday, and the ceremony was performed by Mr. J. Smith, foreman under Mr. Harrison. In the course of an appro- priate speech Mr. Smith referred to the good feeling that had existed between the workmen and Mr. Harrison during the 18 years that he had been over them. During all those years he had always been found to be a honest and straightforward master, and they were exceedingly sorry to part with him. On behalf of the workmen he had great pleasure in presenting Mr. Harrison with the barometer,and he wished him long life and prosperity in his new position. (Applause.)—Mr. John Coldbeck and Mr. J. W. Todhunter also spoke in eulogistic terms of their connection with Mr. Ilarrison.—Mr. Harrison thanked the subscribers and speakers for their handsome present and kind words. During the time he had been with them he only tried to do his duty, and he was pleased to receive such sub- ] stantial proof that he had succeeded. He had spent a very pleasant 18 years with them and wherever he might be he would never forget his many friends left behind ie Workington. In conclusion he again thanked them for the present and hoped that his suceessor would get on as well with them as he had. (Cheers.) THE LATE MISS Rt7TH EVANS. In this months issue of the "Liverpool and Dis- trict Congregational Magazine" there is a memorial notice of the late Miss Ruth Evans from which we extract the following :—" Congregationalism in southwest Lancashire has lost a staunch and gener- ous friend in the death of Miss Evans, of Haydock. She passed away, at the ripe age of seventy-seven, at Coed tal Glyndyfrdwy, on the 10th of August. The daughter of Richard Evans, the founder of the ereat colliery firm of Haydock, it is no small tribute to say that she surained in a worthy manner, throughout her long life, the reputation for stead- fa-tness to principle and unstinted support of every cause she believed in, which she inherited. For some veers past she had been living in Rhyl, where she founded a Ministers'Rest.And it was no small part of the enjoyment of the Rest to receive the hearty welcome which Miss Evans always gave in her own home to the ministers who came to the Rhyl Rest. But the founding of the Rest was only the last of many munificent gifts by which Miss Evans and her family have served the churches of the district. The church at Ashton was built by her father. The magnificent new church at Newton-le-WiLows is to a large extent the outcome of the generosity of the Evans family. send of la ;e years Miss Evans her- ell fuldesl to these two splendid churches, with menses et ached, one at Haydock, and the other at Rainhi'il:' s_

div.head: INSURANCE AGAINST WANT OF EMPLOYMENT IN WINTER.
div.p: INSURANCE AGAINST WANT OF EMPLOYMENT IN WINTER.
INTERES CING EXPERIMENT AT COLOGNE.

-- - The British Vice Consul at Cologne, in a recent report, describes a scheme for insuring workmen against peri- odical want of employment which has been started in that city. Herr Schmalbein, an Alderman of Cologne, succeded in interesting a number of prominent citivins in the matter, and the preliminaries have been arranged for the City of Cologne Insurance Society for the Un- emplwyed in Winter, and the statutes were approved of at a meeting of persons interested in social movements of this nature. The object is declared to be the institu- tion and maintenance of an insurance fund for the un- employed of Cologne, in connection with the Cologne General Labour Registry, from December 15 to March 15. The funds consist of the subscriptions of members, the contributions of the insured, a contribution from the city funds, and voluntary donations of societies, clubs, employers, and other persons. The Board of Manage- ment consists of the chief burgomastar of Cologne, the chairman of the General Labour Registry, and of eigh- teen other members, six elected by a committee of the insured and twelve by the general meeting of all mem- bers, but half of thesemust be employers and the ether half neither employers nor workmen. Two of each of these two classes must retire annually. The society is to begin operations when it has a working fund of £2,500, and the number of persons insured the first year must not exceed I,OOQ. The insured must be workmen over eighteen years of age, who have resided in Cologne for at least two years, and who pay the subscription of 3d. a week by purchasing insurance stamps to that value and affixing them in a book with which they are sup- plied, called the p,emiuna-book. Members who observe the rules " are specially considered as far as possible " at the General Labour Registry in procuring employ- ment, and are entitled to a daily allowance while out of work, between December 15 and March 15, for a period not exceeding eight weeks. A married man with at least one child gets 2s. a day, and an unmarried man is. 61 for the first twenty days, and after that half these amounts. But no member is entitled to this allowance until he has been insured for at least eight months,and all workmen in receipt of allowances must, ' if desired, attend twice daily at a specified place and take work if it is offered. The committee of the in- sured decide, subject to an appeal to the Board of Managemetit, whether the insured has forfeited his right , to an allowance under the rules. There are in all forty-four rules, but they are of a simple character, and the more important are summarised above. The Vice Consul adds that about £2,000 was subscribed at the meeting above mentioned, and it was anticipated the minimum guarantee fund would be easily obtained. The rules of the Labour Registry of Cologne and the re- sult of the working of this institution last year are given
7- . - in an appancitx to the report.

A great sensation was created among the passengers on the Flebburn landing stage, on the river Tyre, on Tuesday. A young woman, Elizabeth Henderson, quar- relled with a man named George Cook, and then threw herself into the river. Cook sprang after her, and was followed by her brother James Henderson and a relative named Edmund Bridget. Thc woman was rescued by Cook in a very exhausted stare, but her brother was soon in difficulties, and was drowned in sight of scores of people. The third man, Bridget, succeeded in safely reaching the shore.

Another matter I have been asked to draw atten- tion to, is the fact that Evans and Co's. private rail- way leading from Earlestown to Haydock is closed against pedestrians, and anyone found walking along the side of the line, will render themselves liable to prosecution for trepass. It appears since the making of new streets on Newton Common, a footpath leading from Clarence-street to the road near Gibraltar Cottages, Haydock, has 'seen made, and this can be used by foot-passengers and work- people. But to get into Haydock they will have to cross over the line and through Messrs. Evans' farm yard. They will, however,have to do this at their own risk.

-- The road along the line has been used for many years, as a near cut to Haydeck,and its closing will doubtless come as a great hardship. Still Messrs. Evans have a right to close it,and in doing so they put an end at once to all danger to foot passengers arising from the working of their traffic.
