THE ALLEGED WOUNDING CASE AT GOLEORNE At the above court on Thursday morning, before 'Atr. William Houghton, Abel Pimblett, Edge Green-lane, Golborne, was charged with having oa the sth inst. un- lawfully and maliciously wounded Ann 'Roberta at Gol- borne. Mr. Stuart, Newton-le-Willows, defended. Complainant said she was a marled woman. She remembered Saturday, the sth Secptember. At half-past eleven on that night she saw the defendant. He was in her yard, and he was looking through the back kitchen window. He first of all broke a broom and threw it into the house, and then burst open the door. She did not do anything. Ile threw a large pieee of mug at till.. He also broke a large mug. Witness was in the kitchen. The defendant shouted to her, "Come out, you Charley's Aunt, and I will kilt you." It was defendant's mother who put that name en her. The defendant ti,en broke the large mug. The mug was on a bench in the yard. She went to close the kitchen door, and he threw a large piece of mug, which hit her on the head. She saw the piece coming, but did net remember anything else. She became insensible. She did not remember anything until she saw the Sergeant and Dr. Part, which was next Morning. She identified the apron which she was wearing at the time of the occurrence. Pieces of mug produced were parts of the mug which belonged to her and which was on the bench in the back yard. She could not say which piece struck her. By Mr. Stuart : There were other people in the yard beside the prsoner. She had never spoken to the pri- soner. He was in the backyard when he said "Come out, you Charley's Aunt." Every one had their back yard. When she came to close the inner door she did not say, " Charley's Aunt has done you again." The inner room never got closed. He never came inside the door. There were three ether people standing there. One piece came in which hit her on the head. The piece which struck her broke and fell on the floor. Tfiere were some friends in the house. She had a quart of porter in the house. They had been singing. They were quite saber. They had only two quarts of porter. The women were quite sober. bins had had a glass of rum ; that was all she had to drink that day. She did not dare him to come in. When she looked through the kitchen win- dow she saw him push the door in. She had given him no cause to assault her. She did not know why some ens else did not go to the door. If someone else had cone to the door they would have been struck. He saw her coming to the door. Defendant never came inside any door. She was net singing " Barney's backed the winner and we are on the loose to-day: we'll have a goose for dinner and Charley's Aunt has won the

ay." Dr. Part, of Golborne, said be was called in to Mrs. Roberts. Be arrived at a quarter to five on the morning of September 6th. He found a superficial scalp wound about an inch long on the top of the head. The second wound was two inches in length on the forehead,extend- ing into the scalp. In the wound were found the frag- ments of the mug. Per two days after the woman's condition gave rise to anxiety. Had erysepelas set in the wounds might have proved fatal. She was in danger for two days. By Mr. Stuart : She came down to open the door her- self. She did not appear to be drinking. They were wounds likely to be caused by a piece of mug. They were straight cut wounds. Charles Williams, a brickmaker, residing at 75, Edge Green-lane, said he remembered Saturday, September sth. He looked tbrougla the window and heard a crash, and saw the defendant with a piece of mug in his hand. He knew there wee a mug outside the door, which was standing on a bench by the door. Fie heard defendant shouting, but could not hear what he said. Defendant then knocked the back door, open. He saw Mrs. Roberts go to shut the inner door, when the defendant threw a piece of mug at her which struck her on the head. The pieces of mug produced were all of a piece when Mrs. Roberts was struck. It broke, and some of the portions went on the stairs. He brought a neighbour in to at- tend to her. A police-sergeant picked up the pieces of the mug. He lodged with Mrs. Roberts. By Mr. Stuart : At the time the defendant broke the door open he could see through the window, and then Mrs. Roberts got up to shut the inner door. He had been in a public heuse at 7.30 and 9.30 or thereabouts. He then went straight home. He was singing and tun- ing the baby to sleep. Robert Huerdly was going in. They were trying to pacify the child. Emma Wiewell said she worked at the factory Golberne, and resided at 73, Edge Green-lane. OR the night in question she was in Mrs. Roberts's house about half-past eleven. Mrs. Roberts when about to shut the door was struck on the head with a piece of pan- mug. She saw her bleeging from the top of the head. William Chamberlain said he was a day wagernan at Messrs. Cross Tetley's Colliery.ead resided at 64,I,hton- road, Golborne. On the night in question he was stand- ing at Mrs. Itoberts's back door. He saw Abel Pimblett, hut he did not say anything. First of all he went up to the window. He was within three yards of him when the door went open, but he did not know whether he burst it open or kicked it open. tlefendant then broke the bru‘h up and knocked the mug off the bench, and broke it. He started throwing pieces on the floor. He threw a piece at Mrs. Roberts, and it struck her on the forehead. Mrs. Reberts seemed to fall down, but he could not see exactly. By Mr. Stuart : He took defendant into his house. The defendant" ketched "against the mug, but did not know whether he did it on purpose or not. Oliver Youne,, pelice sergeant, stationed at 6elhorne, said he apprehended the defendant at 13, Edge Green- lane. He charged him with unlawfully wounding Ann Roberts with intent to do her grievous bodily harm. He made no reply to the charge. Defendant was then committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions. Mr. Stuart applied for bail inE2O and two in £lO each. This was allowed subject to the defendant finding sureties to the satisfaction of the I police.

I hope they are not setting the foundation of a church scandal at Barleatown,but from what I can hear they are on a fair road for doing so. At one of the churches—it is needless to designate it,—the clergy are trying to insist upon the congregation gregation have fallen in with the but the majority refuse to standing whilst they enter and leave the chancel. Some of the con wishes of the clergy, obey their behests. Accordingly, the clergy have resorted to a means to accomplish their end, and after pronouncing the benediction they have given out a hymn,and whilst this is being sung the clergy have quietly cleared out. This was !not noticed at first, but being repeated several of the congrega- tion have resented the action of the clergy by als* leaving the church during the singing of the hymn. I thought we had done with these disagreements, but it would seem that such is not the case. I hope the responsible parties will see the wisdom of humouring the congregation.

I hear there is an intention afoot of lighting cer- tain parts of the town with the incandescent light. The streets selected are I understand, Market-St., Bridge-street, and Queen-street. The idea is very excellent for there is no doubt the town is badly lighted, and were it not that some of the shops are well lighted with patent lights, we should be badly off indeed. I think, however, the committee appointed to see to these matters have not made the best selection as to the parts to be lighted, but seeing that it is only experimental, we may shortly see some extension.

One place which &mid certainly be exception- ally well lighted, and at once, is the vicinity of Ilaydock crossing, which as every one knows is at present miserably lighted and is perhaps the most dangerous part of the town, especially on Friday night when there is an extra busy traffic. I mean of course the crossing leading to Wargrave Road. The other night about half-past ten a coach with four horses was leaving Earlestown for Warrington, and whether the driver was a stranger to the place, or it was owing to the badly lighted condition, when going over the first crossing the horses heads were turned to follow the curve of the footpath, instead of keeping straight ahead, and before the driver was aware he found himself entangled . amongst the rails leading through the gate on to the London and North-Western main line. By some good fortune the horses kept their feet, but it is wonderful that no serious damage was done. This shows at once that more light is needed at this spot, and I would recommend the Committee to give the matter consideration.

div.head: SAD DEATH_ OF A RUNCORN BOATMAN.
div.p: SAD DEATH_ OF A RUNCORN BOATMAN.

-- Mr. H. C. Yates, county coroner, held an inquiry on Monday afternoon at the Navigation Inn, Broadheath, concerning the sudden death, which took place on Sun- day of John Gretton,boatman, of Stonehills,Halton-lane. Runcorn. Fanny Gretton, wife of the deceased, stated that he was 78 years of age. She had been two years married to him. They left Run- corn on the boat on Saturday and arrived at Broadheath about three o'clock in the after- noon. Deceased attended to the steering. On Sunday morning he complained of pains in the etomach. She gave him some ginger tea and mustard. He afterwards ate his breakfast, and about ten o'clock left the boat to sit on the hank. Almost immediasely witness was called so him,and found him apparently in a fit. She loosened his collar and sent for a doctor. No one came, how ever. Deceased seemed to die in a few moments. In- answer to the Coroner, witness said deceased had been a heavy drinker for some time.—Joseph Benson, boatman of Northwich,said he had been working for the deceased two days.. He joined him on this side of Preston Brook, and came with him to Broadheath. Deceased told wit- ness on Sunday morning that he did not feel very well. Deceased was sitting on a bucket on the canal bank smoking.and witness joined him. He spoke to him for a while. Be happened to turn away to look at a boat and when he looked hack deceased was lying on the ground. His face was discoloured, and he Was frothing at the mouth. Life seemed to pass away almost immediately afterward. Be had known the deceased for 20 years. Deceased seemed to be a healthy man.—A. Juror said he should like to hear the evidence ef the person who went for the doctor, and know why the doctor had not come. —The Coroner said the juror was quite right in making the request. Doctors,however, sometimes received very strange messages. The jury must also remember that a doctor was not bound to attend. He could only be com- pelled after a relieving officer's order had been obtained. He agreed that it was very hard on people. He had on other occasions made strong remarks about it. He thought the very nature of a doctor's calline should bind him to attend to a sick call .—Samuel Ingleield, of Lyrnm, said he was at Broadheath on Sunday. He was told to go for a doctor, and he went to Mr. Cnoner, in Manchester-road. The servant told him that the doctor did not attend on Sunday. Witness then went to the Police Station.—The Coroner said the matter was thus explained. He briefly reviewed the evidence, and Stiff- gated thet death was due to syncope. What was thought by deceased and his wife to be indigestion was evidently a heart mischief.—The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the Coroner's suggestion, and gener- ously handed over their fees to the widow.

-- A shocking trazedy was perpetrated on Wednesday night in Enston-read, London, the victims being an un- fortunate namnd Elizabeth Weimott and a metal polisher named Henry Victor. Victor shot the woman dead, and then turned the weapon on 1- 'mself, inflicting a wound which is likely to prove fatal.

Detective Sergeant Floo a spoke to 'e receiving the prisoner from the SPch police, and said that when charged w•gth conspiring . A tele- gram from New York ste" that persons acquainted with Mr. Ivory, the we; -e...' tun Lexington Avenuo liquor dealer, say that the - aescription of Bell cabled to New Tork tallies in ev re , y respect with that of Mr. Ivory. A, telegram fr—,,„. . Dublin states that the preliminary steps \ have been ~:--. 4'..aken by the Irish Executive to procure the • extrau''.cion of Tynan for the part he took in the Phoenix ra'at murders in 1882.

The prisoner Bell was formally brought before the Glasgow magistrates on Wednesday,and at once handed over to two officers from Scotland Yard, by whom he was on Wednesday night escorted to London. Tynan was again interrogated by the Public Prosecutor at Boulogne on Tuesday. He is said to have repeatedly denied that he had been in any way connected with or concerned in an, dynamite plot, or that he had been guilty of any offence against the laws of France. An English detective officer informed the Public Prosecutor that be had not received the necessary documents front London,and asked that the prisoner should be remanded pending their arrival. To this course the Public Prose- cutor at once assented. An English detective on Wed- hesday tried to interrogate the prisoners flames and Wallace at Rotterdam, but both prisoners persisted in their determination not to answer any questions. A formal request was on Wednesday made by the British Embassy in Paris that Tynan should be detained pend- ing the arrival of a formal demand for his extradition. The question has been raised in Paris whether Tynan is a naturalised American citicen,as he states,and it is said that if his statement should prove to be true the diffi- culty of securing his extradition will be greatly in- creased.

WARRINGTON CHESS AND DRAUGHTS CLUE. What was formerly called the Warrington Chess Club will in future be known by the above title,aiad on Monday evening the club entered upon a new lease of life when the first raeeting of the mentors was held in the Masonic Rooms, Bold-street, The chess and draughts boards were laid aside for a few minutes for the transaction of business. The Rev. Father Firth was voted to the chair. The lion. , Treasurer, Mr. Newcombe, read the financial state- ment which showed that the subscriptions of the members and donations amounted to .E 9 19s. and after meeting all expenses there was a debit bal- ance of _EI lis. The accounts were passed. A short discussion ensued as to the desirability ot provid- ing a fresh place of meeting for the club, and it was ultimately agreed that a small sub-committee consisting of Mr. Mason (secretary), Mr. Newcombe Mr. F. H. Dunne, and Mr. Taylor should be ap- pointed to select one.—The Secretary said he had pleasure in proposing that the follow- ing five new members be admitted :—Niessrs Kitchen, Whitfield, O'Byrne, Kerby and E • Fletcher. The proposition was unanimou•ily agreed to. The question of joining the Lancashire Chess League was brought up for consideration. It wag pointed out that the Warrington team were called upon to travel to Manchester for the league engage" meets last season ,ain the opinion was expressed that some of the matches should be played at Warring- ton, if arrangements could possibly be made fq doing so. On the proposition of the Chairman it I was decided that the club should continue in the league. A vote of thanks was passed to Father Firth for presiding, and in reply he said he was sorry to tell the members that he had received orders to pack up and get out of Warrington. Tha.,t would prevent him from taking any active partici' pation with the Warrington Chess Club. He was returning to Cumberland where he had once held the honourable position of president of the county chess association and was able to add to WS' name P. C. C. C. A. (Laughter.) He would have liked to arrange a number of matches betweee Cumberland and Warrington but he was afraid tbe distance was too great. He must acknowledge that during his connection with the Warrington Ches 6 Club he had experienced many pleasant evenings. He would be pleased to keep up his connectica with it by becoming an honorary member. It 0311 Y be added that Mr. Dunne. who will be more Prc); minently associated with the draughts seetion 0' the club, i president of the Yorks hire dratigli.ttss. league, and for fifteen years has been the deaegu` editor for the '• Leeds Mercury."
